<meta>This page contains the dedication of Henri Estienne’s edition of Apollonius of Rhodes, likely the 1574 edition. The text is a formal Latin letter to the scholar Gerard Falkenburg, discussing the technical labor of editing ancient Greek poetry.</meta>

# HENRI ESTIENNE <note>Henricus Stephanus (1528–1598) was a legendary French printer and classical scholar known for his monumental editions of Greek and Latin authors.</note>
## TO HIS FRIEND GÉRARD FALKENBURG, GREETINGS.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'M' featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
I am finally fulfilling my promise regarding the edition of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the *Argonautica*, an epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts.</note> after a long time, my dear Falkenburg. Indeed, as the saying goes, it is "soon enough if it is well done." For this edition is at least such that no one should find my diligence lacking, nor should I regret how much I have achieved in it. In particular, I have taken care that the same standard of punctuation <term>interpunctionem</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "interpunction" referred not just to commas, but to the scholarly art of phrasing a text to clarify its grammatical meaning.</note> which I provided in that "large-lettered" <note>original: μεγαλογραμμάτῳ (megalogrammatō). This refers to his famous 1566 edition of the Greek poets, printed in a large format.</note> work of the principal poets should not be missing here. Now, just as this labor of punctuation is no small task, so too is it of no small use to readers; you know well enough that an appropriate and accurate punctuation can often take the place of a full commentary.

Those who are not too lazy to compare this edition with previous ones will recognize how many places I have clarified in this way. Certainly, an example of this diligence appears at the very threshold of the work. For in those earlier editions, these verses were read as follows: — *as him hereafter*

> *A cruel Fate awaits this man, whom he might see,*
> *By the promptings of the one-sandaled man from the people, to be overcome:*

I, however, foresaw that most readers would go astray here, incorrectly joining "Fate" <note>original: μοῖρα (moira)</note> with "of the man" <note>original: ἀνέρος (aneros)</note>, and the following words with "to be overcome" <note>original: δαμῆναι (damēnai)</note>. Yet the true sense of this passage is actually: *that a cruel fate awaits him [King Pelias], to be overcome by the suggestions of this man [Jason] whom he might see coming from the people with only one sandal.* Therefore, I wished to protect the readers by using two marks of punctuation, in this manner: — *as him hereafter*

> *A cruel Fate awaits; by the suggestions of this man, whom he might see*
> *Coming from the people with only one sandal, he shall be overcome.*

For you see how, by placing punctuation after "cruel" <note>original: στυγερή (stygerē)</note> and after "one-sandaled" <note>original: οἰοπέδιλον (oiopedilon)</note>, I show readers the path they ought to follow in explaining this passage, or even lead back those who have already strayed. If I wished to continue with more examples, I would not have to go much further; but this diligence, which reveals itself...

<summary>In this dedication, the printer Henri Estienne explains to Gerard Falkenburg the importance of his editorial work on the poet Apollonius, focusing specifically on how corrected punctuation clarifies difficult Greek verses regarding Jason and King Pelias.</summary>
<keywords>Henri Estienne, Gerard Falkenburg, Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica, textual criticism, Greek poetry, punctuation, King Pelias, Jason</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s dedication to Gérard Falkenburg. Estienne is arguing that even though advanced scholars like Falkenburg might not need meticulous punctuation, the majority of readers do, and even ancient commentators have been led into error by poor phrasing.</meta>

[The work] itself can testify; I will not allow myself to be said to have boasted. Indeed, someone will object that this labor is not necessary for everyone. I will certainly admit that this is true. Since I know that Falkenburg (to not go far afield) can do without such labor; but I know in turn that few Falkenburgs exist: that is, those who are equally practiced in reading the Greek poets, and who could win the same praise that he won from his work on Nonnus <note>Nonnus of Panopolis (5th century AD), author of the *Dionysiaca*. Falkenburg published an important edition of this poet in 1569.</note>. Furthermore, I add this: there are some places where proper punctuation <term>interpūnctio</term> can bring great help even to those most practiced in reading them, or at least make them more cautious.

Of this fact, we have a most clear testimony in the scholiast <term>scholiasta</term> <note>An ancient or medieval commentator whose notes (scholia) were often copied into the margins of classical manuscripts.</note> of this poet. For who is ignorant, or who does not admit, that he is by far the most learned of all those [commentators] who have reached us? Behold, however, I noticed that he was driven into a great error by faulty punctuation. It occurs in the fourth book, where these are the words of Medea lamenting:

> Fear, then, the divine things and oaths; fear the Fury 
> Of the suppliant, and the retribution of the gods—lest I go into the hands 
> Of Aeëtes, to be destroyed by grievous outrage. 
> <note>original Greek: Δεῖσατε οὖν θείας τε καὶ ὅρκια, δείσατ’ ἐριννὺν / Ἱκεσίην, νέμεσίν τε θεῶν, ἐς χεῖρας ἰοῦσαν / Αἰήτεω, λώβῃ πολυπήμονι δηωθῆναι.</note>

For here the scholiast, because he did not notice that one must punctuate after *gods* <note>original: θεῶν (theōn)</note> and not after *going* <note>original: ἰοῦσαν (iousan)</note>—which certainly was not noticed in the editions that preceded mine—falls headlong into a certain absurd explanation. He wants to persuade the reader that "retribution going into the hands of the gods" is said because "standing before the gods, we supplicate; therefore we also respect the suppliants." <note>original Greek: ἐνώπιον τῶν θεῶν ἱστάμενοι ἱκετεύομεν. διὸ καὶ αἰδούμεθα τοὺς ἱκετεύοντας.</note>

Nay, you—whoever you are who writes these things—take note that the punctuation must be after *gods*, not after *going*; and there will be no reason for you to torture yourself here <note>original: "crucem hîc figas," a Latin idiom meaning to cause oneself mental anguish or to get stuck on a "cross" of one's own making.</note>. For you will immediately see that this is the sense: "Fear the Fury of the suppliant, and the retribution of the gods; [fear] me going into the hands of Aeëtes, to be destroyed by grievous outrage." <note>Estienne is arguing that the participle "going" refers to Medea herself, not to the "retribution of the gods."</note> Moreover, what is required to support this infinitive <note>"to be destroyed" (δηωθῆναι)</note> can easily come to the mind of the reader; whether he wishes to understand it as "so that I [am destroyed]" <note>original: ὥστε ἐμὲ (hōste eme)</note> or "because of my [being destroyed]" <note>original: διὰ τὸ ἐμὲ δηωθῆναι (dia to eme diōthēnai)</note>, "going" etc., or to supply some other phrase that seems fit for this passage.

<summary>Estienne explains that his meticulous punctuation is designed to prevent grammatical misunderstandings, using a specific error by an ancient scholiast in Apollonius' 'Argonautica' as a primary example.</summary>
<keywords>Henri Estienne, Gérard Falkenburg, punctuation, Apollonius Rhodius, Medea, scholiast, Argonautica, Greek grammar, philology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s introduction to his edition of Apollonius Rhodius. Having argued that even learned readers benefit from careful punctuation, he now shifts to his editorial "cleansing" of the text—specifically, removing "ghost words" created by previous editors who incorrectly fused prepositions and nouns together.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>T iij</sig>
<warning>Faded text at the top of the page; some ink bleed-through from the reverse side.</warning>

But to move from this diligence of mine (which I have also moderated in my usual manner, so that I placed nothing unless it seemed likely to be free of controversy, rather leaving some passages that present an ambiguous sense for the reader himself to punctuate) to another method, which I also used in the edition of that work which I recently called "the large-lettered edition" <note>original: μεγαλογράμματον (*megalogrammaton*). This likely refers to Estienne’s 1566 edition of the Greek poets, printed in a large, elegant typeface.</note>: I say that I have cleansed these books of many words that were similar to those "pseudo-Homeric" terms, such as *Under-foundation*, *Under-desire*, *Under-pitiless*, *Under-embryo*, *In-blood*, *Upon-funeral-rites*, *Upon-stable*, *Down-skin*, *Around-unfortunate*, *Very-crafty*, and *They-were-herding-under*. <note>original: Ὑπόθεμος, Ὑφίμερον, Ὑπονηλεές, Ὑπέμβρυον, Ἐνάιελον, Ἐπικτέρεα, Ἐπαύλιος, Καταδέρμia, Περι-κάμμορε, Πολυκέρδιον, Καταβουκολέοντο. Estienne is arguing that these are not single compound words, but should be read as a preposition followed by a noun or verb.</note> Just as in the editions of Homer that preceded mine, such compound words had crept in against Homer’s will—or rather, without Homer even being aware of them—as I declared in my preface; so too I found that they had crept into these books of Apollonius, both others and especially these: *Weary-headed*, *Through-wide*, *In-blood* (which I also counted among the pseudo-Homeric words), *Upon-lips*, *Under-help*, *Under-youthfulness* (or *Under-youthfuls*), and *Under-rowing*. <note>original: Καρημογέοντι, Διαπλατύς, Ἐνάιελον, Ἐπικείλια, Ὑπαρωγῆ, Ὑπανεοίησι, Ὑπενεοίησι, Ὑπειρεσίησι.</note> Regarding this last one, however, I only gave a warning in the annotations. Evidently, the Greek language did not seem rich enough in compounds to some people, who therefore wished to enrich it with these. 

Nor, indeed, did they dare this only in these poets, but in others as well—even in the tragedians. Moreover, even the Greek lexicographers <term>lexicographi</term> <note>Authors of dictionaries or word-lists.</note> seemed to approve some of these words; for example, Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian (c. 5th century AD) who compiled a massive dictionary of obscure Greek words.</note> approves *Under-embryon* <note>original: ὑπέμβρυον (*hypembryon*)</note>. Although, on the other hand, it should be noted that it was not Hesychius, but the one who transcribed his book, who annexed the preposition **under** <insert>hypo</insert> to the noun *embryo*; for Hesychius explains it as "she brought forth a newborn infant," using the verb *sub-placed* <note>original: ὑπέβαλεν (*hypebalen*)</note> to explain the Homeric *sent forth* <note>original: ἧκεν (*hēken*)</note>, which was omitted through the same carelessness. For Hesychius himself had written it thus: "he sent forth under the embryo." <note>original: ὑπὸ ἔμβρυον ἧκεν (*hypo embryon hēken*)</note>. Yet Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> could be believed to have been deceived by that error, since he explains it as "a newborn to this nursing woman." As for the word *Upon-lips* <note>original: ἐπικείλια (*epikeilia*)</note>, the scholiast <note>An ancient commentator.</note> forbids me from doubting whether to place it in this category.

What, then, will they do now, whom those dictionaries printed in previous years have led to such words in Apollonius...

<vocab>Apollonius, Homer, Hesychius, Suidas, pseudohomerica, lexicographi, μεγαλογράμματον, Ἐνάιελον, Ἐπικείλια</vocab>

He critiques famous lexicographers like Hesychius and Suidas for perpetuating these errors, which he attributes to the carelessness of medieval scribes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s introduction to his edition of the Argonautica by Apollonius Rhodius. Having previously discussed his removal of "ghost words" (incorrectly joined prepositions and nouns), he now turns to his careful work on punctuation, arguing that even the most learned scholars and ancient commentators can be led astray by a misplaced comma or period.</meta>

...as much as it is able, I will not act in such a way that I might be said to have merely paraded my efforts. Truly, someone will object that this labor is not necessary for everyone. I will certainly admit that this is true. Indeed, I know that Falkenburg <note>Gerhard Falkenburg (c. 1538–1578) was a Dutch scholar and friend of Estienne, known for his deep knowledge of Greek poetry.</note> (to look no further afield) can do without labor of this kind; but I know in turn that few Falkenburgs exist: that is, men equally practiced in the reading of the Greek poets, and who are able to bring back the same praise which he reported from his work on Nonnus. <note>Nonnus of Panopolis was a Greek epic poet; Falkenburg had recently produced an edition of his *Dionysiaca*.</note> Furthermore, I add this: there are some passages where proper punctuation can bring great assistance even to those who are most practiced in reading them, or at least make them more cautious.

We have a most brilliant testimony of this fact in the Scholiast <term>Scholiast: an ancient or medieval commentator whose notes (scholia) were often written in the margins of classical manuscripts.</term> of this poet. For who is ignorant, who does not admit, that he is by far the most learned of all those commentators who have come down to us? Yet behold, I have noticed that he was driven into a great error by crooked punctuation. This occurs in the fourth book, where these are the words of the lamenting Medea:

-> Fear then the divine goddesses and your oaths; fear the Fury <-
-> of suppliants, and the retribution of the gods, coming into the hands <-
-> of Aeëtes, to be ravaged by miserable outrage. <-
<note>original: *Δείσατε οὖν θείας τε καὶ ὅρκια, δείσατ᾿ ἐριννὺν Ἱκεσίην, νέμεσίν τε θεῶν, ἐς χεῖρας ἰοῦσαν Αἰήτεω, λώβῃ πολυπήμονι δηωθῆναι.* (Apollonius Rhodius, *Argonautica* 4.385–387)</note>

For here the Scholiast, because he did not notice that the punctuation should be placed after "gods" (*θεῶν*) and not after "coming" (*ἰοῦσαν*)—which certainly was not noticed in the editions that preceded mine—throws himself headlong into a certain absurd exposition. He wishes to persuade the reader that "retribution coming into the hands of the gods" is said because "we stand before the gods when we supplicate; therefore we also respect those who supplicate." <note>original: *ἐνώπιον τῶν θεῶν ἱστάμενοι ἱκετεύομεν. διὸ καὶ αἰδούμεθα τοὺς ἱκετεύοντας.*</note>

On the contrary, you—whoever you are who wrote these notes—take note that the punctuation must be placed after "gods," not after "coming"; then there will be no reason for you to torment yourself here. <note>original: *crucem hîc figas*. This Latin idiom suggests getting stuck on a difficult mental puzzle or "pinning oneself to a cross" of one's own making.</note> For you will immediately see that this is the sense: "Fear the Fury of suppliants, and the retribution of the gods; [fear] me coming into the hands of Aeëtes, to be ravaged by miserable outrage." <note>By moving the punctuation, Estienne makes "coming into the hands of Aeëtes" refer to Medea herself rather than the gods' retribution.</note> As for what is required to assist this infinitive "to be ravaged," it can easily come into the mind of the reader: whether he wishes to understand it as "because I [am to be ravaged]" or "on account of my being ravaged," or to supply some other thing that seems appropriate to this passage.

<summary>Henri Estienne argues that even the most learned ancient commentators (Scholiasts) made significant interpretive errors due to poor punctuation, using a speech by Medea in the Argonautica as a primary example. He demonstrates how moving a single punctuation mark clarifies that it is Medea, not divine retribution, who is falling into the hands of her father, Aeëtes.</summary>

<keywords>Henri Estienne, punctuation, scholarship, Scholiast, Medea, Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Gerhard Falkenburg, editorial methods, Greek poetry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s preface to his edition of Apollonius Rhodius’s Argonautica. In the preceding section, Estienne discussed how misplaced punctuation in ancient commentaries (scholia) led to significant misunderstandings of the text. He now moves from the issue of punctuation to his corrections of the vocabulary itself, specifically targeting "ghost words" created by the incorrect fusion of prepositions and nouns.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>T iij</sig>

Truly, so that I may move on from this diligence regarding that matter <unclear>of punctuation</unclear> (which I have moderated in my usual way, so that I placed no mark unless it seemed it would be free of controversy: and I rather left some passages displaying an ambiguous sense to be punctuated by the reader themselves) to another method, which I used also in the edition of that work which a little before I called *the great-lettered edition* <note>original: μεγαλογράμματον (*megalogrammaton*). Estienne refers to his 1566 "Poetae Graeci Principes," a massive collection of Greek heroic poetry printed in a large, elegant typeface.</note>: I say that I have purged these books of many words which were similar to those pseudo-Homeric ones, such as *Under-warm*, *Under-desire*, *Under-pitiless*, *Under-fetus*, *In-nine-years*, *Upon-gifts*, *In-stalls*, *Down-bindings*, *About-fate*, *Much-cunning*, and *Down-tending-cattle*. <note>original: Ὑπόθερμος, Ὑφίμερον, Ὑπονηλεές, Ὑπέμβρυον, Ἐνάαετον, Ἐπικτέρεα, Ἐπαύλφος, Καταδέσμνια, Περικάμμορε, Πολυκέρδιον, Καταβουκολέοντο. These are "ghost words" where early editors mistakenly joined a preposition to the following word, creating a "compound" that did not actually exist in ancient Greek.</note> For just as in the editions of Homer that preceded mine, such compound words had crept in—against the will, or rather without the knowledge of Homer himself—as I declared in my preface: so also I discovered that they had crept into these books of Apollonius, specifically these: *With-head-aching*, *Through-wide*, *In-nine-years* (which I also counted among the pseudo-Homeric words), *Upon-flock-gifts*, *Under-help*, *Under-suggestions* (or *Under-promptings*), and *Under-the-mountains*. <note>original: Καρημογέοντι, Διαπλατὺς, Ἐνάαετον, Ἐπιμείλια, Ὑπαρωγῆ, Ὑπανεσίησι, Ὑπεννεσίησι, Ὑπειρεσίησι.</note> Regarding the last of these, however, I only gave warning in the annotations. Evidently, the Greek language did not seem rich enough in compound words to some people, who therefore wished to "enrich" it with these inventions. Nor indeed did they dare this only in these poets, but also in others: and even in the tragic poets. 

Moreover, even the Greek lexicographers <term>Lexicographers: compilers of dictionaries.</term> seemed to approve of some of these words: such as *under-fetus* <note>original: ὑπέμβρυον (*hypembryon*)</note> in Hesychius. <note>Hesychius of Alexandria (c. 5th century AD) authored the most important dictionary of obscure and rare Greek words.</note> Though otherwise it should be noticed that it was not Hesychius, but the one who transcribed his book, who had annexed the preposition *under* <note>original: ὑπὸ (*hypo*)</note> to the noun *fetus* <note>original: ἔμβρυον (*embryon*)</note>; since Hesychius explains it as "he placed a newborn child under" <note>original: νεογνὸν βρέφος ὑπέβαλεν</note>: explaining the Homeric word "he sent" <note>original: ἧκεν (*hēken*)</note> with the word "he placed under" <note>original: ὑπέβαλεν (*hypebalen*)</note>: which was omitted through the same carelessness. For Hesychius himself had written it thus: "under the fetus he sent." <note>original: ὑπὸ ἔμβρυον ἧκεν (*hypo embryon hēken*)</note> But Suidas <note>The Suda (formerly attributed to an author named Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia and dictionary.</note> could be believed to have been deceived by that error: since he explains it as "this newborn to the nursing woman." <note>original: τοῦτο τῇ θηλαζούσῃ νεογνόν</note> As for what pertains to *upon-flock-gifts* <note>original: ἐπιμείλια (*epimeilia*)</note>, the scholiast <term>Scholiast: an ancient commentator who wrote explanatory notes (scholia) in the margins of manuscripts.</term> prevents me from doubting whether to place it in this group. What, therefore, will they do now, those whom the dictionaries printed in previous years [misled] regarding words of this kind in Apollonius...

He demonstrates how these errors were perpetuated by famous lexicographers like Hesychius and Suidas through scribal negligence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s preface to his edition of Apollonius Rhodius. Having previously discussed "ghost words" formed by misattaching prepositions, Estienne now addresses "monstrous" words found in contemporary dictionaries and begins his critical defense of Apollonius’s poetic rank compared to Homer and other classical masters.</meta>

<warning>Black stain at top of page obscures several words in the first and second lines.</warning>

...will refer them back: No wonder <unclear>...</unclear> they might complain that they do not find their Apollonius. But it is inevitable that this happens to them with many other authors as well. For where will they find these words, which are cited in those dictionaries as if they were from the most approved writers: **Un-furrowers**, **Feeding-without-fire**, **Nose-boring-swift-Venus**, **Dust-un-smeared**, **Around-the-Hot-Gates**, **Knee-bender**, **Delicate-slave-girl**, **War-rolling-wheel**, **Acting-sparingly**, **Burned-by-bronze**, **To-be-bound-tight**, **I-conquer-many-times**. <note>original: Ἀναυλατίοντες, Ἀπυρωτροφή, Ῥινοτορωκυθέρεια, Ἀκονήλιτος, Ἀμφιθερμοπύλας, Γόναντος, Ἀβραδούλη, Ἀρεικάντροχος, Φειδωποιούμενος, Χαλκοκεκαυμένος, Σφιγεθῆναι, Πολυνικῶ. Estienne is mocking "monstrous" compound words found in unreliable lexicons that do not actually appear in classical literature.</note> See, my dear Falkenburg <note>Gerard Falkenburg (d. 1578) was a Dutch humanist scholar and a friend of Estienne.</note>, what monstrosities of words, rather than actual words, I had to struggle with while printing my *Thesaurus* <note>The *Thesaurus Graecae Linguae* (1572), Estienne’s monumental Greek dictionary.</note>: the memory of which was revived for me by those things with which I said I have purged Apollonius. But since I fear that the mention of this barbarism is not very pleasing to your ears, I will let this talk go and say what I feel about our Apollonius.

They seem to have done a great injury to him, and even to the Muses themselves, who judged that he should be "reduced to the ranks." <note>term: *in ordinem cogere* — a Roman military expression meaning to demote someone or strip them of their status. Estienne is defending Apollonius against critics who wanted to remove him from the "first rank" of poets.</note> Conversely, in my opinion, someone has also done a great injury to both Homer and the Muses themselves by daring to compare this poem with the Homeric work in which he sings of the deeds done at Troy. But if Apollonius is not one who can be compared with Homer, he should not therefore be cheated of his own honor. For (as Marcus Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman.</note> wisely wrote) among poets there is not a room for Homer alone, or Archilochus, or Sophocles, or Pindar: but also for those of the second rank, or even those below the second.

Certainly, neither "invention" <note>term: *inventio* — the creative power to devise a plot and subject matter.</note> nor words worthy of his invention seem to have been lacking in Apollonius: yet in such a way that he seems to allow himself some rather harsh liberties, and does not seem to have a vein of inspiration that flows equally everywhere. If anyone also finds "judgment" <note>term: *iudicium* — the critical ability to arrange material with taste and logic.</note> lacking in him in some places, let him know that he misses what is found missing in many other poets—and indeed, in many places even in the Prince of Poets <note>Homer.</note> himself. If anyone should say that as much genius does not appear in certain places as the subject matter seemed to require, let him remember the opinion of Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> regarding Callimachus: *Although he does not prevail in genius, he prevails in art.* <note>original: "Quamuis ingenio non valet, arte valet." From Ovid's *Amores* 1.15.14. Callimachus was a famous Alexandrian poet known for his polished, scholarly style.</note> Yet there is no one who thinks he should be reduced to the ranks...

<summary>Estienne mocks the "monstrous" fabricated words found in contemporary lexicons and defends Apollonius Rhodius as a poet of high standing, arguing that even if he is second to Homer, he remains a master of his craft.</summary>
<keywords>Henri Estienne, Apollonius Rhodius, Greek lexicography, Homer, Cicero, Ovid, Callimachus, poetic rank, Thesaurus Graecae Linguae</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s preface to his edition of Apollonius Rhodius. Having just finished mocking the "monstrous" words found in poor dictionaries, Estienne transitions to a literary defense of Apollonius by demonstrating how heavily the great Latin poets—Virgil and Ovid—relied on him as a source of inspiration.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>¶.iiii.</sig>

...would dare to say Callimachus <note>A famous Hellenistic poet and librarian at Alexandria who famously feuded with Apollonius over the nature of epic poetry.</note>. But what need is there for more words? Or do we think that Maro <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, better known as Virgil.</note> would have borrowed anything from Apollonius unless he had held him in high esteem? Yet we see that he borrowed not a few things from him; and indeed in that very book of his work which seems to be the chief among the others. For thus he begins his fourth book, concerning his Dido:

*But the queen, long since wounded by heavy care, feeds the wound in her veins:* <note>original Latin: "At regina, graui iamdudū saucia cura, Vulnus alit venis" (Aeneid 4.1-2).</note>

when Apollonius had said of Medea:

*The bolt burned deep within the girl, beneath her heart, like a fire.* <note>original Greek: "βέλος δ' ἐνεδάετο κούρῃ Νέρθεν ὑπὸ κραδίῃ, πυρὶ εἴκελον" (Argonautica 3.286-287).</note>

He adds:

*The hero's great virtue and the great honor of his lineage recur to her mind; his features and his words remain fixed in her breast, and her care gives no peaceful rest to her limbs.* <note>original Latin: "Multa viri virtus animo multúsque recursat Gentis honos: hærent infixi pectore vultus, Verbáque: nec placidam membris dat cura quietem" (Aeneid 4.3-5).</note>

Doubtless this comes from another passage of our poet [Apollonius], where he sings of the same woman:

*Everything still appeared before her eyes: how he looked, and so forth.* <note>original Greek: "Προπρό δ' ἄρ' ὀφθαλμῶν ἔτι οἱ ἰνδάλλετο πάντα, Αὐτός θ' οἷος ἔην &c." (Argonautica 3.453-454).</note>

And a little later:

*And in her ears always echoed his voice and the sweet-tempered words which he spoke.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν οὔασι δ' αἰέν ὀρώρει Αὐδή τε, μῦθοί τε μελίφρονες, οὕς ἀγόρευσε" (Argonautica 3.457-458).</note>

Nor truly does it seem he looked only to these, but also to other passages of our Apollonius when he sang those verses. To which we can also add this:

*—absent, she both hears and sees him though he is absent.* <note>original Latin: "illum absens absentē audítq; vidétque" (Aeneid 4.83).</note>

I know there are those who before me have observed that these things certainly came from the beginning of Book IV, just as many other things did; however, perhaps I myself have observed some things that others have omitted. For instance, this concerning Dido:

*She begins to speak, and stops in the middle of her voice.* <note>original Latin: "Incipit effari, mediáque in voce resistit" (Aeneid 4.76).</note>

For the poetic vein of Apollonius had previously flourished, as it were, in describing Medea:

*At one time a word would rise to the tip of her tongue, at another it fluttered deep within her breast. Often it rushed through her longing mouth to speak, but her voice would not proceed any further.* <note>original Greek: "Μῦθος δ' ἄλλοτε μέν οἱ ἐπ' ἀκροτάτης ἀνέτελλε Γλώσσης, ἄλλοτ' ἔνερθε κατὰ στῆθος πεπότητο. Πολλάκι δ' ἱμερόεν μὲν ἀνὰ στόμα θῦεν ἐνισπεῖν, Φθογγῇ δ' οὐ προὔβαινε παροιτέρω" (Argonautica 3.683-686).</note>

But someone else, on the contrary, wrongly thinks those words, *The voice stuck in his throat,* <note>original Latin: "Vox faucibus hæsit." Estienne is likely referring to Aeneid 2.774 or 4.280.</note> which are said of the astonished Aeneas, are similar to those first ones, *At one time a word...* and so forth. Nor indeed do I think that only Maro [Virgil], but also Naso <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, better known as Ovid.</note> borrowed several passages of our Apollonius, or wished to allude to several of them.

<summary>Estienne argues for the high literary status of Apollonius Rhodius by demonstrating how Virgil’s portrayal of Dido’s love in the Aeneid was directly modeled on Apollonius’s description of Medea. He provides several side-by-side comparisons of Latin and Greek verses to prove this influence, extending the observation to Ovid as well.</summary>
<keywords>Apollonius Rhodius, Virgil, Ovid, Aeneid, Argonautica, Dido, Medea, literary influence, Greek poetry, Latin poetry</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s argument that the great Roman poets were deeply indebted to Apollonius Rhodius. Having previously compared Apollonius to Virgil, Estienne now turns his attention to Ovid (Naso), demonstrating how the Latin poet modeled his descriptions of love and moral maxims on the Greek original.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

For just as our poet <note>Referring to Apollonius Rhodius.</note> says of Medea:

> *But the two of them stayed there in the vestibule of the chamber, held back by shame,* <note>original Greek: "Διὼ δ' κατ' αὐτόθι μίμνεν ἐπὶ προδόμῳ θαλάμοio, Αἰδοῖ ἐεργομένη"</note>

and what follows, we shall find that Naso <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, the Roman poet Ovid.</note> said similar things about a girl seized by love. What? Shall we deny that Naso, in a certain passage of his *Metamorphoses*, had before his eyes that long struggle of shame with love—or love with shame—which appears in that same place? But it is pleasing to show how Naso seems not only to imitate, but also in some part to wish to interpret a certain most beautiful <term>maxim</term> <note>original Greek: γνώμην (*gnomē*), a short, pithy statement of a general truth or moral principle.</note> of our poet. Apollonius sings:

> *But the races of suffering-hardened men never*
> *set foot upon delight with their whole foot; but some*
> *bitter pain always comes along with their joys.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλά γ’ οὔποτε φῦλα δυηπαθέων ἀνθρώπων Τερπωλῆς ἐπέβησαν ὅλῳ ποδί· σὺν δέ τις αἰεὶ Πικρὴ παρμέμβλωκεν ἐϋφροσύνῃσιν ἀνίη." (Argonautica 4.1165–67).</note>

Naso, however, writes:

> *...so true it is that no pleasure is pure,*
> *and some anxiety intervenes in our joys.* <note>original Latin: "uſqueadeo nulla eſt ſincera voluptas, Sollicitúmq; aliquid lætis interuenit." (Metamorphoses 7.453).</note>

Furthermore, I have observed other sentiments in the same poet taken from other Greek poets, which are otherwise thought to have flowed from the vein of his own genius (which was certainly most fertile). Among their number is this one:

> *...and praised virtue grows.* <note>original Latin: "laudatáq; virtus Creſcit." (Ex Ponto 4.2.35).</note>

For it was said many years before Ovid was born:

> *Virtue, being praised, increases.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀρετὰ ἐπαινεομένα αὔξεται."</note>

But there will be another place for speaking about these things, as well as others that pertain to this edition. To this work I have added a few annotations on Apollonius; and I was intending to add the ancient commentaries <note>The "scholia," or marginal notes found in ancient manuscripts.</note> and the emendations I had noted during the printing process—unless I had seen that it would be impossible for me to fulfill my promise regarding this edition even after a long time, but that I would remain for a long time <term>overdue</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπερήμερος (*hyperēmeros*), a legal term for a debtor who has missed his payment deadline.</note> and <term>in your debt</term>. <note>original Greek: ὀφλήματος (*ophlēmatos*).</note>

To you, I say, whom I desire to please in all ways, both for the sake of the Muses—our common friends—and because of him whom we have as a common friend both with the Muses and between ourselves, that most noble and distinguished man, **Thomas Redinger**: whom for his own merit I not only love, but also revere and respect. To him (since he is most worthy to have the first fruits of such editions come into his hands), I would like you to give another copy of *Apollonius* in my name, and at the same time I wish you to share with him the greeting I have bestowed upon you. *Farewell.*

<summary>Estienne concludes his preface by showing how Ovid imitated Apollonius's psychological descriptions and moral maxims, then explains why he is rushing the edition to print for his patrons, including Thomas Redinger.</summary>
<keywords>Ovid, Metamorphoses, Apollonius Rhodius, literary imitation, Thomas Redinger, maxims, Greek influence on Latin poetry, scholarly publishing</keywords>

# APOLLONIUS OF RHODES
## The Argonautica: Book One.

<image-desc>A large woodcut headpiece depicting a central decorative urn or fountain flanked by two winged putti (cherubs) among scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial letter 'A' intertwined with leafy vine patterns and a small central face.</image-desc>
Starting with you, O Phoebus <note>Phoebus is an epithet for Apollo, the god of music and prophecy, traditionally invoked at the start of a poem.</note>, I shall recall the famous deeds of men born long ago, who at the command of King Pelias, drove the well-benched *Argo* through the mouth of the Pontus <note>The Black Sea.</note> and through the Dark Rocks <note>The Symplegades, mythical clashing rocks at the entrance to the Black Sea.</note> in pursuit of the Golden Fleece.
For such was the oracle Pelias had heard: that a hateful fate awaited him in the future—to be overmastered by the schemes of a man whom he should see coming from the town with only one sandal.
And not long after, in accordance with your prophecy, Jason crossed the stream of the wintry Anauros on foot; he saved one sandal from the mud, but the other he left behind, held back by the force of the current.
He came straightway to Pelias to take part in a sacred feast, which the King was offering to his father Poseidon and the other gods...

<column-break/>

### SCHOLIA
### on the first book of the
### Argonautica of 
### Apollonius.

Starting] <note>The Scholia are "commentaries." They usually begin by quoting a word from the poem and then explaining it.</note> The participle is formed from a comprehensive <term>middle voice</term> verb. Comprehensive verbs are those that show both an action and a state of being; for example, "I force," "I present a gift," <margin>5</margin> "I sacrifice." There is also the form "I begin." The first meaning is "I take my beginning from you" (for it is the custom to begin a preface with the gods—"let us begin with Zeus" <note>A reference to the poet Aratus.</note>). The second meaning is "being under your power," as in being divinely inspired. For poets are inspired by the gods in a manner similar to those who are possessed. <margin>10</margin> Some say...

---

...that "starting" [the present participle] is used here instead of "having started" [the past participle]. The meaning, then, is: "Having started from you, I shall bring to memory the glorious deeds of the Argonauts." Argo] Apollonius calls the ship *Argo* after Argus, the man who built it; but Pherecydes <note>An early Greek mythographer and historian.</note> says it was named after Argus, the son of Phrixus. They say this was the first "long ship" <note>A galley or warship, as opposed to a round merchant vessel.</note> ever made. Others say that Danaus, while being pursued by Aegyptus, was the first to build one, which is why it was called a *Danaïs*. Well-benched] This means it has good seats for the rowers. For such was Pelias.] The word "Such" is used here to show cause, similar to the way it is used in poetic comparisons: "As is the generation of leaves, so is that of men." It can also be used referentially, as in: "But even so, such as she was." Now it is used either to express wonder or to refer back to the story, or in reference to the events that follow. Anauros] He refers to a wintry torrent. Rivers that are formed from heavy rains are called by this name. Outpourings] The places where rivers meet the sea are called outpourings. As Homer says: "As when at the outpourings..." <note>A reference to Homer's *Iliad* 17.263.</note>

<margin>
15
**Of Pelasgian Hera**] <note>original: "Ἥρης δὲ Πελασγίδος"</note> He calls Hera "Pelasgian" in the Homeric style, referring to the region of Thessaly. For the Pelasgians were said to be those who inhabited Phthiotis <note>A region in southeastern Thessaly.</note>, as Homer says: "Now again those as many as dwelt in Pelasgian Argos." Thus, he calls the city in the Peloponnese "Achaean Argos" to distinguish it.
20
</margin>

<margin>
**First now Orpheus**] <note>original: "Πρῶτά νυν Ὀρφῆος"</note> Herodorus claims there were two men named Orpheus, one of whom sailed with the Argonauts. Pherecydes, in his sixth book, says that Philammon—and not Orpheus—sailed with them. As for his parentage, according to Asclepiades, Orpheus was the son of Apollo and the Muse Calliope; but according to others, he was the son of Oeagrus and Polymnia. The question is asked: why did Orpheus, being physically weak, sail with the heroes? It was because Chiron, being a seer, foretold that they would be unable to pass the Sirens <note>Mythical creatures whose song lured sailors to their deaths.</note> unless Orpheus sailed with them. So says Herodorus.
</margin>

...He offered sacrifice to the gods; but for **Pelasgian Hera** he had no regard.
Soon Pelias, having seen Jason, devised for him such an ordeal: a very troublesome voyage, so that on the sea or among foreign men he might lose his chance at homecoming.
The ship itself, **Argo**, earlier poets still celebrate, saying it was built by the instructions of the goddess Athena.
But now I shall tell of the lineage and the names of the heroes, the paths of the long sea, and all they performed in their wanderings; may the Muses be the interpreters of my song.
**First then let us remember Orpheus**, whom once Calliope herself is said to have borne, having bedded with Thracian Oeagrus near the Pimpleian height.
<margin>25</margin> They say that he, with the sound of his songs, charmed the stubborn rocks on the mountains and the streams of rivers.
And the wild oaks—still signs of that song today—flourish on the Thracian shore of Zone, standing in thick, orderly rows; these he led down from Pieria, enchanted by his lyre.
Such a man was Orpheus, whom the **son of Aeson** <note>Jason.</note>, obeying the injunctions of the centaur Chiron, received as a helper in his labors, even though Orpheus then ruled over Bistonian Pieria.
<margin>35</margin> And **Asterios** came, whom Cometes begat by the waters of the eddying river Apidanos, dwelling near Mount Phyllium;
There, the great Apidanos and the divine Enipeus both come together from afar, flowing into one stream.

---

**Pimpleis**] <note>original: "Πιμπληΐδος"</note> Pimpleia is a place in Pieria. Others say it is a mountain in Thrace. Others call it a spring and a village of Pieria.
**Charmed**] <note>original: "Θέλξαι"</note> To deceive and to delight. This word is often used for a "deception" that causes harm, but here it is used as a poetic exaggeration for the power of music.
**With the sound of songs**] Meaning the rhythm of the odes. The word "sound" <note>original: "ἐνοπὴ"</note> is also sometimes used to describe a loud noise or shouting.
**Thracian Zone**] Zone is a mountainous place so called, and also a city of the same name, as Nicander says.
**Standing in rows**] They are arranged in a line, one after another, and are very dense.
**From Pieria**] Pieria is a mountain in Thrace where Orpheus spent his time. Herodorus says that the centaur Chiron advised Jason to take Orpheus along with the Argonauts.
**Apidanos**] The Apidanos and the Enipeus are both rivers in Thessaly. Mount Phyllium is in Macedonia. Piresia is a region or city located near Mount Phyllium.

The marginal notes provide historical and geographical context, explaining why the centaur Chiron insisted Orpheus join the physically stronger heroes to help them bypass the Sirens.</summary>

**Leaving Larissa, among these**] <note>original: "Λάρισσαν δ' ἐπὶ τοῖσι"</note> He refers to the Thessalian Larissa, which was founded by Acrisius <note>The grandfather of Perseus</note>; it was named after Larissa, the daughter of Pelasgus, as Hellanicus says. There are three Larissas: the most ancient is the "Argopolis," which is the acropolis itself. The second is the one in the Pelasgian region of Thessaly, which Homer calls Argissa, located near Gyrtone—this is the one Apollonius mentions now. There is also one near Troy, which Homer remembers as the "tribes of the Pelasgians." As for **Polyphemus**, Apollonius calls him the son of Elatus, but Isocrates and Euphorion say he was the son of Poseidon. Others...

-> **Nor did Iphiclus** <-
<meta>catchword</meta>

---

**The Lapiths** were named after Lapithes, the son of Apollo and the nymph Stilbe.
**Iphiclus**] Iphiclus was the son of Phylacus and Clymene, daughter of Minyas. Hesiod says of him that he could run across the **ears of corn** <note>original: "πνείων ἀθέρων"</note> without bending them, while Demaratus says he could run upon the surface of the sea. It is worth noting that whether it is Hesiod or Pherecydes speaking, they agree that Iphiclus sailed with the Argonauts. The phrase **"Nor long"** <note>original: "Οὐ δηρὸν"</note> is used instead of "very quickly," a figure of speech known as antiphrasis. It should be known that Pherecydes agrees with Apollonius in saying that Alcimede, the daughter of Phylacus, was the mother of Jason; however, Herodorus says Jason’s mother was Polymede, daughter of Autolycus. Andron, in his *Register of Families*, says Theognete, daughter of Laodicus, was the mother of Jason.
**For he had married his sister**] <note>original: "Κασιγνήτην γὰρ ὄπυιεν"</note> Through a secondary meaning he indicates the primary one: that he had taken her as a wife. The word *opuiën* (married) was formed either from the *opes* (eyes), meaning one who looks upon and watches over his bride, or from the *ops* (voice), due to the intimate conversation between husbands and wives; from which we also get the word for "women."
**Nor did Admetus of Pherae**] Pherae was named after Pheres, the son of Cretheus and father of Admetus. **Fair-flowing** <note>original: "ἐϋρρύοισιν"</note> means "well-watered." **Chalcolonion** is a mountain situated above Pherae.
**Nor did they stay in Alope**] A city of Thessaly or Magnesia. **Rich in grain** <note>original: "Πολυλήϊοι"</note> comes either from *leion* (a crop-bearing field) or from *leia* (plunder)—the latter is better, as he follows it with "skilled in deceits." They are recorded as being sleepless, clever, and hardworking.
**Aethalides** is a proper name, though it has the form of a patronymic <note>A name derived from a father's name</note>.
**Amphrysian**] Dionysius also writes this with a "b" (Ambrysian). It is a river in Thessaly.
**Coronus of Gyrtone**] Which Homer calls Gyrtone. It is a city of Thessaly or Perrhaebia. It was named after Gyrtone, the daughter of Phlegyas. **Coronus** was the son of Caeneus. The myth-tellers say that **Caeneus** was originally a woman, but after Poseidon had been with her, he transformed her into a man. For she requested this, as well as invulnerability. He was later defeated by Apollo, and having been conquered, he commanded those passing by to swear by his spear. Hence also...

There is a proverb: "the spear of Caeneus." <note>original: "τὸ Καινέως δόρυ"</note> Some say that Caeneus himself sailed with the Argonauts, and not his son Coronus. The poet Apollonius has taken this account from Pindar, who says: "And those struck by the green pines went, Caeneus, cleaving the earth with an upright foot." <note>original: "Οἳ δ᾽ χλωρᾶς ἐλάτῃσι τυπεῖς ᾤχετο Καινάς, χίσας ὀρθῷ ποδὶ γαῖαν."</note> This happened to him because he would neither sacrifice to the gods nor pray, but instead honored only his own spear. Therefore, Zeus stirred up the Centaurs against him, who pushed him down into the earth.

...son of Caeneus, a noble man, yet not better than his father.

But unbroken and unbending, he sank into the depths of the earth,
Struck down by the weight of massive pine trees.

**Valiant Eribotes**] <note>original: "ἀλκήεις Ἐριβώτης"</note> This means "strong." It is derived from his surpassing <note>original: "ἐξῆκον"</note> and total strength <note>original: "ἀλκήν"</note>, just as "voiced" <note>original: "φωνήεις"</note> comes from "voice." Herodorus, in his *Argonautica*, calls this man Eurybates and says he is the son of Teleon. The sons of Actor were Menoetius and Irus. Of these, Menoetius was the father of Patroclus, and Irus was the father of Eurytion. **And to rush upon**] <note>original: "Καὶ ἐπαΐξαι"</note> This is used instead of "to pursue." For "from behind" implies a pursuit. The word "and" is missing in the phrase "and when they break their ranks," meaning they would turn them to flight. **Canthus came**] <note>original: "Κάνθος κίε"</note> Cleon also lists Canthus. There is a son of Canthus from whom a mountain in Boeotia takes its name. He was the son of Abas, from whom the Euboeans are called Abantians. **To be slain**] <note>original: "δῃωθῆναι"</note>...

<meta>This page continues the "Catalogue of Heroes" from Book One of the Argonautica. Following the description of the Lapiths and Mopsus, the text now introduces the sons of Eurytus, the exiled brothers Peleus and Telamon (the Aeacids), and the Athenian heroes including Phalerus and Butes. FIRST [BOOK]
a.iii.

...to be shown more generally now as "to perish." Next, the poet, as if grieving over the loss of the heroes, exclaims: *How not for men [is there an end] to evils.*

How there is no end to the evils men must suffer,
Whenever those heroes were buried even in Libya,
As far from the Colchians as the distance seen
Between the setting of the sun and its rising.
Then Clytius and Iphitus joined the gathering,
The guardians of Oechalia, sons of harsh Eurytus;
Eurytus, to whom the Far-Darter <note>The god Apollo</note> gave his bow, yet he did not
Enjoy the gift, for he willfully challenged the giver himself.
Nor were they from the same place; for they lived apart, exiles
From Aegina, when they killed their brother Phocus
In their recklessness. Telamon settled on the Attic island,
While Peleus made his home in Phthia, having been driven away.
After them from Cecropia <note>The ancient name for Athens/Attica</note> came the warlike Butes,
Son of noble Teleon, and Phalerus of the sturdy ashen spear.
Alcon, his own father, sent him forth; for he had no other
Sons to care for his old age and his life;
Yet, though he was his late-born and only child,
He sent him, that he might shine among the bold heroes.
And Theseus, who surpassed all the sons of Erechtheus...

<column-break/>

**How not for men**] The meaning is: "There is no great evil that man does not encounter." Therefore, because of this, they had to "suffer." Or, that there is no evil so great that it is not burdensome for men to endure <note>original: "ἐπαυρᾶν"</note>, which means to meet with or experience.
**Sunset and sunrises**] He says they are separated from the land of the Colchians by as much as the east is distant from the west. Since Libya is toward the west, while Colchis is toward the east.
**Guardians of Oechalia**] The children of Antiope. The more recent writers say Oechalia is in Euboea, but Homer, in the "Pelasgian Argos" section, lists it as: "Those who held Oechalia, city of Eurytus the Oechalian."

<column-break/>

Others say the cities simply share the same name.
**Nor were they from the same place**] Not from the same location. For they were settled in different places because of the murder of Phocus. One settled in Salamis, which he called an Attic island; the other, Peleus, in Phthia.
**After them from Cecropia**] Meaning, "with these men from Attica." For Attica is called Cecropia after Cecrops, who was its king. This Teleon, the father of Butes, is a different person from the previously mentioned father of Eribotes.
**Of the ashen spear**] Meaning warlike; named from the *melia* <note>the ash tree, whose wood was used for spear shafts</note>.
**Alcon**] Proxenos says that Alcon, the father of Phalerus, was the son of Erechtheus. He says Alcon fled from Attica with his daughter Chalciope to Euboea. When his father demanded her back, he would not hand her over to the Chalcidians.
**Late-born** <note>original: "Τηλύγετον"</note>] Here it does not mean "only-born" (since the phrase "and being his only one" is added afterward), but rather a child born to him when he was already aged. Such children are especially dear to their parents.

**And Theseus, who surpassed all**] Theseus and Pirithous; one descended from Zeus, the other from Poseidon. They rivaled one another in their deeds. When Theseus fell in love with Helen, he had Pirithous present with him; when Pirithous wished to kidnap Persephone, it was necessary for Theseus to follow him. And so, having descended to Hades through Taenarum, and having sat upon a certain rock <note>The "Chair of Forgetfulness" which caused those who sat on it to be fused to the stone</note>, they were unable to stand up again. Later, when Heracles descended to fetch Cerberus, he rescued Theseus, on the grounds that he had not descended of his own will; but he left Pirithous behind, since he had gone down by his own choice.

### ARGONAUTICA

...he came. The Dioscuri <note>The twin brothers Castor and Pollux</note> marched against Troezen on account of their sister <note>Helen of Troy</note>, while Theseus was away in the underworld; after plundering the city, they took Aethra, the mother of Theseus, as a captive.

---

<margin>
**Taenarian**] Pherecydes <note>An early Greek mythographer</note> says in his ninth book that Elatus, the son of Icarus, married Erymeda, the daughter of Damasiclus. 
From this union was born Taenarus; <margin>105</margin> from whom the city, the headland, and the harbor are called Taenarum. 
**A fruitless journey**] He [the poet] is pleased with that phrasing. "A fruitless journey," meaning empty and <margin>110</margin> vain; he uses this term in the Phoenician manner. Except for the bravery of each of the heroes, which Apollonius touches upon, he says <margin>115</margin> that if both had sailed with the Argonauts, they would have relieved them of great toils. He also provides the reason <margin>118</margin> why they did not sail together. 
**To foresee**]
</margin>

But a bond in the unseen world beneath the earth held the Taenarian <note>From Cape Taenarum, a legendary entrance to the underworld</note> Pirithous fast, for he had followed Theseus; a fruitless journey. Truly, both would have made the labor's end easier for everyone.
But Tiphis, son of Agnias, left the people of Siphae among the Thespians; he was skilled at foreseeing the rising waves of the broad sea, skilled at predicting the storms of the wind and the voyage by the sun and stars.
Athena herself, the Tritonian goddess, urged him into the company of the noblemen, and he came to those who longed for him. 
For she herself also fashioned the swift ship; and with her, Argus, son of Arestor, built it according to her instructions. 
For that ship was the most excellent of all that have ever tested the sea with oars.
After them came Phlias from Araethyrea, where he lived in wealth by the grace of Dionysus his father, dwelling near the springs of Asopus.
From Argos then came Talaus and Areius, sons of Bias...

---

...fully learned. For this is the highest art of a helmsman... and the meaning is: "He was good by day using the sun, and by night using the stars to determine the right time for the voyage." 
**Tritonian**] There are three Tritons: in Boeotia, Thessaly, and Libya; in the 27th book it is said Athena was born at the Libyan one. 
**Came from Araethyrea**] Araethyrea is a city in the Peloponnese, situated near Sicyon; it is now called Phliasia, named after Phlias, the son of Dionysus and Chthonophyle. Dionysus himself was also called "Phlyus," from the word "to swell" <note>original: "φλύειν" (phlyein)</note> regarding wine, which means "to bloom." 
**Asopus**] Asopus is a river in Thebes, having its springs in Araethyrea. He was struck by a thunderbolt by Zeus while pursuing him, because Zeus had snatched away his daughter Aegina, as Callimachus says. 
**From Argos then Talaus**] From Amythaon (son of Cretheus, son of Aeolus, son of Hellen, son of Zeus and Dorippe) was born Melampus, as Demeiodas says. He was named thus <note>Melampus means "Black-foot"</note> because his mother, after giving birth, exposed him in a shady, wooded place; his feet were blackened by the sun while the rest of him was in the shade. 
In the so-called *Great Ehoiai* <note>A lost Hesiodic genealogical poem</note> it is said that Melampus, while traveling abroad, stayed with Polyphates; while the latter was sacrificing, a serpent crawled up and ate the servant. The serpent was killed and buried by Melampus. Its offspring, having been reared by him, licked the ears of Melampus and inspired him with the gift of prophecy. 
Later, he was caught stealing the cattle of Iphiclus, son of Phylacus, and was seized by him. When the roof of the house was just about to fall, Melampus, perceiving this through his prophetic power while held in the prison, told the servant girl. Iphiclus, learning of the prediction, escaped the danger himself, and out of respect, released Melampus, giving him the very cattle he had come to steal.

# ARGONAUTICA

Athamas. <note>original: "Ἀθάμας"</note> Of Cretheus was born Aeson. Of Aeson was born Jason. And Abas was the son of Melampus, the son of Amythaon, who was the son of Cretheus, the son of Aeolus.

<margin>
**Aetolian | appropriately**
Leda is called Aetolian because Thestius <note>Leda's father</note> was an Aetolian. The poet names her from her land, just as one might call a man from Syracuse a "Sicilian." However, Ibycus calls her "Pleuronian" <note>from the city of Pleuron</note>, while Hellanicus calls her "Calydonian." She was the daughter of Thestius, the king of Aetolia, who was the son of Ares and Androdice. Eumelus, or perhaps Panteidyas, says in the *Corinthian History* that she was the daughter of Glaucus, the son of Sisyphus, from her father’s side, and her mother was Panteidyas. He records that while searching for lost horses,
</margin>

The son of Leto <note>Apollo</note> himself taught him <note>Idmon</note> the arts of prophecy,
<margin>145</margin> To heed the omens of birds, and to interpret the signs in the sacrificial fire.
And truly, from Aetolia came the daughter of Thestius, the strong Leda,
Who sent Castor and Polydeuces <note>The Gemini twins, Pollux</note>, skilled with swift-footed horses,
From Sparta; she had borne them in the halls of Tyndareus,
As dearly loved children <note>original: "Τηλυγέτοις", often meaning late-born or beloved</note> in a single birth. Nor did she refuse
<margin>150</margin> To let them go; for she was worthy of the bed of Zeus.
The sons of Aphareus, Lynceus and over-mighty Idas,
Came from Arene, both greatly confident in their strength.
Lynceus excelled even with his most piercing
Eyes; if the fame of that man is truly told,
<margin>155</margin> That he could easily see even deep beneath the earth.
With them arose Periclymenus, the son of Neleus, to join the voyage,
The eldest of all the sons born in Pylos.

---

Glaucus came to Lacedaemon; there he lay with Panteidyas, who later married Thestius. Thus Leda, though biologically the daughter of Glaucus, was called the daughter of Thestius. She is called "Aetolian" either because of her country or after the hero Aetolus. Pherecydes says in his second book that Leda and Althaea were born to Thestius from Laophonte, the daughter of Pleuron. But he hints that she is the daughter of Glaucus and Althaea when he says, "the blessed daughter bore them to Glaucus." <note>original: "τοὺς τέκε θυγάτηρ Γλαύκῳ μάκαιρα"</note> They say Polydeuces was the son of Zeus, and Castor the son of Tyndareus. The term "late-born" <note>original: "Τηλυγέτους"</note> is used here to mean "beloved," though Homer uses it for children born in old age. 

[The sons of Aphareus came from Arene]: Pherecydes says the mother of Idas and his brother was Arene, after whom the city was named; Peisander calls her Polydora; Theokemptos calls her Laokoösa. These brothers were contemporaries of the Dioscuri <note>Castor and Polydeuces</note>. Arene is a city in the Peloponnese near Pylos. Homer also says, "And those who dwelt in Pylos and lovely Arene." <note>original: "Οἳ δὲ Πύλον τ’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Ἀρήνην ἐρατεινήν"</note> This Pylos is the city of Nestor, which is described as "sandy." 

[With them Periclymenus]: Neleus had children by Chloris: Nestor, Periclymenus, and Chromius. By various other women he had Taurus, Asterion, Lycaon, Deimachus, Eurybius, Epilaus, Phrasius, and Antimenes. Asclepiades says he also had Alastor. The poet <note>Homer</note> says, "For we were twelve sons of the noble Neleus." <note>original: "Δώδεκα γὰρ Νηλῆος ἀμύμονος υἱέες ἦμεν"</note> It is clear that Periclymenus is the son of Neleus, for the poet says, "Nestor, Chromius, and the proud Periclymenus." <note>original: "Νέστορά τε, Χρόμιόν τε, Περικλύμενόν τ’ ἀγέρωχον"</note> 

Because he was his descendant, Poseidon (for Neleus was the son of Poseidon) bestowed many gifts upon him, granting him the power to transform into anything. As Euphorion says, "He who could resemble all things, like the sea-god Proteus." <note>original: "Ὅς ῥά τε πᾶσιν ἔϊκτο, θαλάσσιος ἠΰτε Πρωτεύς"</note> Herakles killed him during the war against the Pylians after he transformed into a fly; on the advice of Athena, Herakles struck him with his club while he sat, like a bee, with his stinger ready. Hesiod, however, says that after transforming into one of his usual shapes, he perched on the navel of the yoke of Herakles' horses, wishing to join battle with the hero. But Herakles shot him at the right moment with an arrow, after Athena pointed him out. He describes it thus: 

"And proud Periclymenus, the blessed one, to whom Poseidon the Earth-shaker gave gifts of every kind. At one time he would appear among the birds as an eagle; at another he became a marvel to see—an ant; at another, the glorious swarms of bees; and at another, a dread and ruthless snake. He possessed gifts of every kind, beyond description, which later deceived him through the counsel of Athena." <note>original: "Περικλύμενόν τ’ ἀγέρωχον, Ὄλβιον, ᾧ πόρε δῶρα Ποσειδάων..."</note>

battle. **And he went wearing the hide of a Maenalian bear:** Maenalus is a mountain and a city in Arcadia, named after Maenalus the son of Arcas, whose father was Lycaon. **Storeroom** <note>original: "καλιὴ"</note> refers to the house itself. More specifically, it refers to a structure made of logs <note>original: "κάλων"</note>. *Kala* are pieces of wood. For in ancient times they used wooden houses, as the use of stone had not yet been devised. **And Augeias also went:** According to legend he was the son of the Sun [Helios], but in truth, he was the son of Phorbas, or Neleus, or Hyrmine. Achaia is a part of Thessaly, where this Pellene is located. **Taenarum:** A promontory of Laconia, named after Taenarus, the son of Poseidon. **Europe, daughter of Tityos:** The child of Elara. Tityos is punished in Hades because he attempted to seize Leto while she was on her way to Pytho. As Homer says: "Tityos, son of Earth." <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 11.576</note> But Euphorion says he was shot by Artemis and is punished for that reason.

They say the city was first called Pityoussa, then Asteria, then Anactorion, and finally Miletus. And Eisokeipis says that Areia was the daughter of Cleochus. From her and Apollo a child was born, and she sought to expose him in a brier-bush. Cleochus took him up and named him Miletus after the brier. When he reached manhood and was being pursued by Minos, he withdrew to Samos; hence there is a place called Miletus there. For Imbrasus is a river of Samos, which was renamed Parthenius because Hera was raised there while still a maiden <note>original: "παρθένον"</note>. Callimachus also mentions this. But Tarraeus says: Parthenia [Samos] was named after Parthenia, the wife of Samos. **Ancaeus of Parthenia**: Aristotle says of Ancaeus that being a lover of farming and planting a vineyard, he was harsh toward his servants. One of the servants prophesied that the master would never taste the fruit of his labor. When the fruit ripened, Ancaeus, rejoicing, harvested it and ordered the servant to mix wine for him. As he was about to bring the cup to his mouth, he mockingly reminded the servant of the prophecy. The servant replied: "There is many a slip between the cup and the lip." While these words were being spoken, someone arrived announcing that a giant boar was ravaging the orchard. Ancaeus, casting aside the drink, rushed after the boar, was struck by it, and died. Hence the proverb used for things that happen unexpectedly. Pherecydes says in his eighth book that Ancaeus died from a wound to the thigh by the Calydonian boar. **But a servant-woman**: A "thessa" <note>original: "θῆσα"</note> is a female slave. The Athenians also call poor women "thessas" from the verb "to serve for hire," because they lack necessities. Just as "Cretan woman" <note>original: "Κρῆσσα"</note> corresponds to "Cretan" <note>original: "Κρὴς"</note>, so "servant-woman" <note>original: "θῆσσα"</note> corresponds to "servant" <note>original: "θής"</note>.

And well-skilled in fighting face-to-face in the field,

**200 Iphiclus**] Althaea and Iphiclus were siblings born from Deidameia, daughter of Perieres. **Olenian**] There are two places named Olenus in Achaea. Homer says: "Those who dwelt in Pylene and **205 Olenus**." **Maimed** <note>original: "Σιφλός"</note>] This means "deformed." Others interpreted it as "lame-footed" and "worthy of blame." For *siphlos* means "reproach." **From the Phocians**] The Phocians were named **210 after Phocus**, the son of Aeacus. They trace the genealogy of Iphitus to Naubolus and Perinice, daughter of Hippomachus. **Pytho**, a city of Phocis where the **215 oracle** is; it was so named from "inquiring" <note>original: "πυνθάνεσθαι"</note> at the oracles, or from the dragon "rotting" <note>original: "σαπῆναι"</note> there.

---

**Zetes and Calais**: They say these men joined the Argonauts from various places. For some say they came from Thrace, as Apollonius does; but Herodorus says they came from Daulis; and Doris says from the land of the Hyperboreans <note>a mythical people of the far north</note>. Antimachus also lists them. Phanodicus, in his *Delian Matters*, says they came from the Hyperboreans for the voyage. Simonides says Oreithyia was snatched from Brilessus and carried to the Sarpedonian Rock in Thrace. There is also a place of the same name in Cilicia, as Callisthenes says. Stesichorus, in his *Geryoneid*, says there is a certain Sarpedonian island in the Atlantic sea. Regarding the Thracian Sarpedonian Rock, Pherecydes says it is near Mount Haemus, recording the story of Oreithyia's abduction. Choerilus says she was snatched while gathering flowers by the springs of the river Cephisus. Isagoras, in his *Megarian Matters*, says that the Boreas who snatched Oreithyia was the son of Strymon, and not the wind itself. Oreithyia was the daughter of Erechtheus. Boreas snatched her from Attica and brought her to Thrace, and there they united and she bore Zetes and Calais, as Simonides says in *The Sea-Fight*. Previously, Cleopatra, daughter of Oreithyia, married Phineus. After that, he married Idaea, daughter of Dardanus; she, having a hatred for her stepsons—I mean the sons of Cleopatra—tried to blind them. Others say their father blinded them because their stepmother slandered them to him. The daughters of Cecrops were Creusa, Oreithyia, and Procris. From Oreithyia and Boreas came Chione, Chthonia, Cleopatra, Zetes, and Calais. Boreas, seeing Oreithyia playing by the Ilissus, fell in love with her and snatched her away. **From the land of Cecrops**: The acropolis of Attica was formerly called Cecropia. **Where the Sarpedonian [Rock] is**: A city in Attica named after Sarpedon, the king of Thrace and brother of Poltys. The following parts are an addition, since there is also another Sarpedonian Rock in Cilicia.

**Nor did the son of [Pelias] himself**] Acastus, the son of Pelias, married Cretheis (or Hippolyte, according to some). She fell in love with Peleus, but when she was rejected in her advances, she struck first and accused Peleus to her husband, saying he had tried to seduce her. Acastus then led Peleus out to Mount Pelion as if for a hunt and left him there unarmed so he would be killed by wild beasts. But Hermes (or Chiron, in some versions) intervened and gave Peleus a sword forged by Hephaestus. With this, Peleus killed the beasts and, returning to the city, killed Acastus’s wife and, as some say, Acastus himself. Now, if Pelias was sending the Argonauts into danger, why did his own son go with them? This author says he went against his father’s will. However, Demachitus claims Pelias tried to force the *Argo* to be built with oak pegs <note>instead of stronger metal or seasoned timber</note> so they would quickly perish. But Argus did the opposite. Having faith in the builder, Acastus joined. This is why the poet says the ship was built by the counsel of Athena.

**Argus, [assistant] of the goddess**] Because he built the *Argo* through the foresight of Athena. **Since [of the blood] of the daughters of Minyas**] For Minyas had many daughters. # FIRST BOOK <note>original: "ΠΡΩΤΟΝ"</note>

<warning>Ink smudges on verses 7 and 8.</warning>

All the gates of Magnesia were closed; and around them a 
Multitude of people came running together; and they [the heroes] 
Shone out like bright stars among the clouds. Thus each person 
Spoke as they watched them rushing in their armor: 
"Lord Zeus, what is Pelias' intent? To what place does he cast 
This great crowd of heroes away from the Pagasean land? 
In a single day they would lay waste to the halls <unclear>of the palace</unclear> 
Of Aeetes with deadly fire, if he does not <unclear>willingly</unclear> hand over the fleece. 
But the paths are not to be escaped, and an inescapable <term>unshakable toil<note>original: "aphrektos," meaning a labor that cannot be avoided or is difficult to complete</note></term> awaits those who go." 
So they spoke here and there throughout the city; and the women 
Raised their hands many times to the heavens to the immortals, 
Praying that they might grant a heart-pleasing end to the return. 
And one woman lamented to another, weeping: 
> "Wretched Alkimede, even to you evil has come late at last, 
> Nor did you finish your life in the glory of living. 
> Aeson, too, is truly ill-fated; surely it would have been 
> Better for him if, wrapped in his funeral shrouds before this, 
> He lay beneath the earth, still ignorant of these evil labors. 
> If only [the ram] had also [destroyed] Phrixus, when the maiden Helle perished,"

<column-break/>

<margin>
**Pagasae**] A promontory in Magnesia. It was named from the fact that the *Argo* was "put together" <note>original: "pepêchthai"</note> there. But Skymnos says it is because the places are surrounded by springs <note>original: "pêgais"</note>. There is also a temple of Pagasean Apollo. **Stars as if in clouds**] Looking at their old age, their fortune, and their bravery, he calls the heroes "stars," and the common crowd "clouds." **Where such a crowd**] The word "where" <note>original: "pothi"</note> is not used soundly here. For it indicates a relationship to a fixed place. How then does he say "he casts them out from a place" instead of "he sends them away"? He calls Thessaly **Pagasean** because it was first called Achaea, after 
</margin>

---

Achaius the son of Xuthus. **Lay waste with fire**] Burn together. Or "make war upon," having overturned them. By **halls**, he means the country, or perhaps the tongue, used as a metonymy <note>a part representing the whole</note>. **But the paths are not to be escaped**] That is, the journey is not one they can flee from. For it was by necessity. Thus the labor is **unshakable** <note>original: "aphrektos"</note>: unfinishable, or not easily done, or impossible to set right. **But the paths are not to be escaped**, because of the dangers in between. **And an unshakable toil for those who go**] Namely, the dangers in the voyage. Or taking it together: "not that it might be, but neither are the paths escapable, nor is the toil unshakable." This refers back to "In a single day they would lay waste to the halls of Aeetes with deadly fire, if he does not willingly hand over the fleece." Others say the word **unshakable** means hard to fence in, difficult to work, or hard to set right. **Heart-pleasing end of return**] Heart-fitting. And this is written in regard to female nature. He fashioned the speech and nature of both [genders] quite wonderfully. For to the men, since their nature is bolder, he introduced praise and the outcome of future events; but for the women, since they are weaker, he creates pity and supplications. Such are women during great and fearful events. **Wretched Alkimede**] Her mind is inspired <note>or troubled</note>; even if it was late, nevertheless evil did come to you, Alkimede (the preposition "through" is missing here), and you did not finish your life brilliantly, boasting of such a son. **Surely it would have been better for him**] This refers to his voice [Jason's father] in enduring the labor. **Of evils**] Either his own, or those destined to be completed by the Argonauts. **If only it had also [taken] Phrixus**] For it is said that after Helle fell off, the ram spoke by the will of Zeus to the Argonauts <gloss>actually to Phrixus</gloss> to encourage him, saying it would save him and bring him to Scythia. This was destined to become an evil for Alkimede herself, as her son was now being sent there. That the ram spoke is also mentioned by Hecataeus. But some say he sailed on a ship with a "ram" figurehead. Dionysius, in his second book, says a man named "Ram" <note>original: "Krios"</note> became Phrixus' tutor and sailed with him to Colchis. For this reason, the myths about the sacrifice of the ram were created there.

# THE ARGONAUTS <note>original: "ΑΡΓΟΝΑΥΤΙΚΩΝ"</note>

<margin>**At the porch** <note>original: "Epí promolêisi"</note>] At the exit of the nobles. From the phrase "to go forward" <note>original: "to eis toumprosthen molein"</note>. From this, they also call the first slopes of mountains "promolas."</margin>
"...[wishing] that the black wave had overwhelmed [Phrixus] along with the ram; but the

Bring sorrows and myriad pains to Alkimede hereafter."

Thus then they spoke as the men were going toward the porch.

As in Homer: "As when the sharp bolt [of labor] holds a woman in travail." **Sorrow** <note>original: "Achos"</note>] is a confusion of the soul, an intertwined grief. This is clear from the poet saying: "And she wasted away even to the point of her child's [departure]."</margin>

<margin>»</margin>...one who is wrapped around the face in such a way that the "type" <note>the shape or form</note> of the body is seen through the garment. **Downcast** <note>original: "Katēphées"</note>] Cast down because of grief. As for **they lifted** <note>original: "ēeíronto"</note>, the passive is used instead of the active "they were lifting." <margin>»</margin>**She threw her arms around** <note>original: "Epecheúato"</note>] Instead of "she placed upon" or "she cast over." <margin>»</margin>**More intensely, like a young girl** <note>original: "Adinṓteron ēΰte koúrē"</note>] This phrasing is similar to "blacker than pitch." For the comparative form is used in place of the absolute. **Like a young girl** <note>original: "Ēΰte koúrē"</note>] The poet has arranged this comparison somewhat unusually <note>original: "akatallêlôs"</note>. For Jason is cast in the role of the old woman [the nurse], and the mother in the role of the girl. It would seem, one says, that these roles should be reversed. But we shall say that Jason is fittingly cast, in terms of his age, as the one providing care <note>old-age-care</note> for his mother. For just as the old woman raises the girl, so the mother [raised him], but now he is her strength due to her age (for old age and infancy are neighbors) and her need for a nurturer. The **stepmother** who lies heavy and harsh upon her is Pelias. The word **Guardians** <note>original: "Kēdemonēes"</note> is a lengthened form of "kedemones." This refers to relatives by marriage, kinsmen, or protectors. **For she has no others**] This also applies to Alkimede, for she has no other children. **A heavy life** <note>original: "Bíoton barùn"</note>] The word "being" is missing here. Being under a stepmother, she leads a bad life. For "biotos" is used for "life" (as it is here) and also for "wealth." The word **leads** <note>original: "hēgēlázei"</note> or "hegelaskei" is the same expression. It means to spend time in the same place, to be held there, or to turn about in the same spot. Regarding animals, Homer says: "Those which wander <note>original: "hēláskoisin"</note> through the farmstead." And: "Because that fate of mine wanders <note>original: "hēlakázei"</note>." **To pour out** <note>original: "Ekphlýxai"</note>] Instead of "to speak out." We say that cauldrons "bubble over" <note>original: "phlýzein"</note> when they are heated, throwing up water by the heat. **To desire/groan** <note>original: "orechtheîn"</note>] refers to the action. It is the sound of an inarticulate voice <note>a moan or sob</note>. Homer says: "Many..."

# BOOK ONE <note>original: "Π Ρ Ω Τ Ο Ν"</note>
b.iiii.

...[as when] oxen bellow <note>original: "orechtheon"</note>. One should rather understand it in the sense of strangers, but also of those who are acting roughly. Homer says, in another place, "stretching <note>original: "orechthon"</note> his spirit." It seems the word with the accent on the third-to-last syllable is due to the *eta* [long 'e' sound], while the word with the accent on the last syllable is due to the *epsilon* [short 'e' sound], as in "erechtho" <note>This is a technical note on how different vowel sounds changed the stress and meaning of words in Homeric Greek</note>.

...of gates or doors, this etymology is found in Apollodorus: that 'bull' <note>original: "tauros"</note> is so named from 'stretching the tail' <note>original: "teinein tēn ouran"</note>, but he transferred this explanation to doors. **Standing over** <note>original: "Epistadon"</note>] Having stood by. **So excessively** <note>original: "Hode lien"</note>] This is a very common expression. For it is impossible for a mother not to weep when her child is going out into such great danger. **Since indeed [not]** <note>original: "Epei ou mēn"</note>] This refers to the passage in Homer: "For there is no profit in chilling grief." **But still you might** <note>original: "All’ eti ken"</note>] This also refers to the Homeric phrase: "before suffering another evil." **You might gain** <note>original: "Aroio"</note>] You might receive. From this, some derive the name of the god Ares from "receiving" or "profiting" in war. The meaning is: you will add evil to evil. **Even though you are grieving** <note>original: "Aniazousá per"</note>] The word 'ar' is often used instead of 'ge' [at least] or 'de' [truly]. He says it thus, 'being good.' This is how the scholar Aristarchus explained it. In the phrase 'being good,' he takes 'ar' to mean 'truly.' And here, at any rate, he takes 'ar' as 'truly': 'truly being good.' And in the phrase, 'fleeing from steep destruction,' he reads it as 'truly fleeing.' Or the meaning is as follows: 'though you are grieving in your heart for your fate, nevertheless endure to bear it.'
