<note>The following section consists of "scholia"—ancient academic commentaries often found in the margins or foot of manuscripts to explain difficult words or mythological references.</note>

apocope <note>the loss of a final sound</note>. Homer was the first to use it, saying, "—both brothers and companions." Therefore, it is mostly expressed in full. "For I have no companions <note>original: "etai"</note> or oarsmen present." **Forward** <note>original: "Proterōse"</note>] Instead of "into the front." Homer: "He did not say I should go forward to the ships." **As when from the temple** <note>original: "Hoios d' ek nēoio"</note>] This is a fitting simile; for both Jason is young, and Apollo is young. **Through holy Delos** <note>original: "Delon an' ēgatheēn"</note>] Delos is one of the Cyclades islands, sacred to Apollo. Previously it was called Delos, but later Asteria, because of its shape. Again, it was called Ortygia, after the sister of Leto. **Or Claros** <note>original: "Ē Klaron"</note>] Claros is a city near Colophon, sacred to Apollo; an oracle of the god was established there by Manto, the daughter of Tiresias. Or it was named after a certain hero, Claros, as Theopompus says. But Nearchus says that Apollo received the city by lot <note>original: "klēron"</note>, and it was named thus after the lot. Those who have written the *Thebaid* say that Manto, the daughter of Tiresias, was dedicated as a first-fruit offering by the Epigoni and sent to Delphi; and going out according to an oracle of Apollo, she encountered Rhacius, the son of Lebes, a Mycenaean by race. Having married him (for this was the meaning of the oracle, that she should marry whoever she first met), she went with him to Colophon. And being distressed there, she wept <note>original: "edakryse"</note> because of the destruction of her homeland. Therefore it was named Claros, from her tears <note>the Greek for 'tears' sounds similar to the city's name</note>. For the stream from them is "watery" <note>original: "hydrēloi"</note>, or as some say, "watery" <note>original: "hydrēroi"</note>. It is also said that a spring gushed up from the tears of Manto at Claros, and she established a sanctuary of Apollo there. Others say Claros was so named because Poseidon and Ares cast lots <note>original: "klērōsasthai"</note> there. Rhacius was so named because of his poverty and wretchedness. **From those calling out together** <note>original: "Keklomenōn amydis"</note>] All shouting and cheering at once. **There met him** <note>original: "Tōi d' xymblyto"</note>] The omen was good, because Iphias the priestess was aged. **Not able to say anything** <note>original: "Oude ti phasthai"</note>] One must understand the word "and." However, though she was eager to speak, she did not manage to. For the word "empēs" here means "nevertheless."

<note>The following section contains the Scholia, or ancient commentaries, found at the bottom of the manuscript page.</note>

And so Delos is not, as the myth goes, named from the transformation of Asteria, the sister of Leto, but because all the places named Ortygia are colonies of the Ortygia in Aetolia. **Embarkation-offering** [Epibathra]: A sacrifice for boarding. In this context, a fee or payment for the sake of boarding the ship for the first time. **We set before** [Prothetheimetha]: Instead of "we make." For "to place" [theinai] is used for "to make." **Barley-meal** [Prochytas]: Some say this refers to the barley grains, others to the water they were accustomed to pour into the ear of the sacrificial animal so that the victim would nod its head <note>Signaling its "consent" to be sacrificed</note>. The word "with" is implied here. **To gird oneself** [To zōsasthai]: Instead of "to rise up" or "to be prepared." It also signifies "to arm oneself." **With a bronze axe** [Chalkeio pelekei]: Apollonius says in the first book of his commentaries that iron was called "bronze" [chalkos] by the ancients; he was unaware that because iron had not yet been discovered, they actually used bronze. As Hesiod also says: "They worked with bronze, for black iron did not yet exist." **Tumbling forward over its horns** [Perirrhedēs keraessin]: Being carried down headlong with force. Breaking forward or being carried over. Just as in the Poet <note>Homer</note>: "Eurymachus fell tumbling over the table." From the word for "turning around." Falling in a circle is described this way. But here, it means being carried forward. **Fat** [Dēmō]: Before they burn them, they wrap the sacrificial parts in plenty of fat so that they are easily consumed by the fire. **Watching** [Theeumenos]: Homer uses this word to mean "wondering at," as in "wondering at the stag." But Apollonius uses it to mean simply "looking."

Stop now the bright fire from the sacrifices, and the soot
That darts in purple-edged spirals, as is fitting;
Straightway he spoke the mind of Leto's son <note>Apollo</note> unerringly:
"For you indeed it is the fate and necessity from the gods to care for
The fleece, bringing it here; but countless trials lie in the midst,

But for me, it is fated by a hateful divine lot to die
Far away somewhere on the mainland of Asia.
Knowing my fate thus from evil omens even before now,
I departed from my fatherland, so that I might embark
Upon the ship, and that fair fame might be left for my house after I have gone."
So he spoke; and the youths, hearing the prophecy,
Rejoiced at the return, but grief seized them for Idmon's fate.
And when the sun passes the burning day,
And the fields are newly overshadowed by the cliffs,
As the sun declines under the evening darkness,
Then indeed they all upon the sands,
Having poured out a deep bed of leaves near the hoary shore,
Lay down in order. And beside them lay countless
Foods, and sweet wine drawn in pitchers by the
Cupbearers. Afterwards, they conversed in turn with one another,
Such things as young men often at feast and wine
Joyfully toy with, when insatiable insolence is absent.
Then again Aeson's son <note>Jason</note> was helpless within himself.

<column-break/>

**Purple-edged** [Porphyreais]: Referring to those things turning purple. The turnings and spirals from the fire, as if turning purple. The phrase is quite vivid.
**Spirals** [Elikessin]: The coils of the smoke.
**Bringing the fleece** [Koas agontas]: It was possible for others to say "to you" (plural). And the poet says: "Truly, Aea is dear to someone, though I am far away."
**Asia** [Asidos]: Asia was named after Asia, the mother of Prometheus and Atlas. Others say it is from having much "asis" <note>original: "asin" - meaning silt or mud</note>.
**Knowing thus from evils** [Ode kakois dedaos]: Not regarding general things, but regarding my own harmful circumstances. It is a hyperbaton <note>a transposition of natural word order</note>, and the "in" conjunction is redundant. The preposition "from" is missing. And there is an exchange of the genitive case for the dative. The verb is also in the intensive form, meaning "I went out." The meaning is this: "Having known my own fate from evil omens, I went...

---

...out from my fatherland, so that by fulfilling your glory I might carry it away."
<margin>**So that I might embark** [ophr' epibaio]: This is a hyperbaton.</margin> The sequence is: "so that I might embark upon the ship, and the good reputation of embarking upon the ship might be left for my household."
<margin>**Burning** [Zapheron]: Instead of</margin> hot and boiling. He refers to midday by what happens then; since the sun, having reached the middle of the sky, heats everything because it is equally distant from all things below. Or because it seems to stand still. Or where the sun does not seem to move at that time.
<margin>**Hoary** [Poliou]:</margin> Because of being whitened by the waves washing over it.
<margin>**Bed of leaves** [Phyllada]: A pile of leaves used as a mattress.</margin>
<margin>**Sweet** [Laron]:</margin> This means "very pleasant." Or it is formed from "lao," meaning "I wish." Hesiod says "sweet feet," meaning those pleasant to look upon.
<margin>**They toy with** [Epsioontai]:</margin> From "epsia" <note>play/sport</note>, or because it is a playful speech, like a "word-jest" <note>original: "epesia"</note>, from "epos" <note>word</note>. This is why it is not aspirated. But when it is aspirated, it means "they follow."
<margin>**Insatiable** [Aatos]:</margin> That which is "greatly harmful." For the prefix "a" is intensive, as in "gaping" or "harsh."

->## ARGONAUTICA - BOOK ONE ##<-

[The god] shall signify [the path]. You yourself are the cause of the voyage and the labors.

<margin>
**The voyage itself** <note>original: "οἷον"</note>: referring to the voyage and the end of the road.
**Cause** <note>original: "Ἐπαίτιος"</note>: Because the god provided helpful oracles. Rhetorically, as if the god were the one responsible for the voyage, the poet says the whole matter belongs to him as his own concern.
</margin>

415 Guide now the ship yourself, with my companions unharmed,

<margin>
**Hellas**: Some say Hellas is synonymous with Phthia; however, we understand Hellas to be the whole region, not just the same as Phthia. In this context, it refers to all of Greece.
</margin>

Both myself and them, back to Hellas; and hereafter, for the return
Of as many of us as shall come home, we will place splendid
Sacrifices of bulls upon your altar again. And other gifts to Pytho,

<margin>
**Ortygia**: Concerning Ortygia, Phanodikos has recorded history in his *Delian Tales*; and Nikandros, in the third book of the *Aetolian Tales*, says that Delos was named after the Aetolian Ortygia, writing these words: "Those setting out from Titanian Ortygia..." Some say this, while others say it was formerly called Delos; others say it is the island bordering Sicily. Hence all "Ortygias" are celebrated. And Delos was not named, as the myth says, from the transformation of Asteria, the sister of Leto, but because all the settlements are from the Ortygia in Aetolia.
</margin>

And others I will bring as infinite gifts to Ortygia <note>An ancient name for the island of Delos, Apollo's birthplace</note>.
420 Now come, Far-Darter, and receive this sacrifice of offerings,
Which we have set before you as a "boarding-offering" <term>epibathra: a ritual payment or sacrifice made for the favor of safely boarding a ship</term> for this ship
As the first-fruits. May I loose the cables, O King, with a harmless fate,
Through your wisdom; and may a gentle breeze blow,
By which we may travel over the sea in fair weather.
425 He spoke, and with the prayer he threw the barley-groats. And for the bulls,
The exceedingly strong Ancaeus and Heracles girded themselves.
Indeed, one [Heracles] struck the middle of the head upon the forehead
With his club, and the bull fell in a heap right there, sinking to the earth.
Ancaeus struck the wide neck of the other
430 With a bronze axe, and cut through the powerful tendons.
It fell, collapsing forward upon both horns.
Their companions quickly slaughtered them and flayed the hides;
They carved the meat and cut it up, and sliced the sacred thigh-bones <note>original: "Δημῷ" — these were covered in fat for burning</note>.
Covering them all together with a thick layer of fat,
435 They burned them upon split wood. And Aeson's son <note>Jason</note> poured
Libations of unmixed wine. And Idmon rejoiced, seeing the flame shine with gladness.

---

**Boarding-offering** [Epibathra]: Offerings made for embarking; here it means a "reward" or payment for the sake of stepping onto the ship for the first time. 
**We have set before** [Protheithemetha]: Instead of "we are making." For to set before is to perform. 
**Barley-groats** [Prochytas]: Some say these are barley grains, others say it is the water they were accustomed to throw into the ear of the sacrificial victim to make it nod in "consent." 
**Girding** [To zôsasthai]: Instead of "to reach up" or "to be prepared." It also signifies arming oneself. 
**Bronze axe** [Chalkeio pelekei]: Apollonius says in the first of his commentaries that iron was called "bronze" by the ancients; he was unaware that because iron had not yet been discovered, they used bronze. As Hesiod also says: "They worked with bronze, for black iron did not exist." 
**Collapsing forward upon both horns** [Perirrhedês keraessin]: Being carried down headlong with force. Bursting forward or being carried over. As the Poet <note>Homer</note> says: "falling forward headlong." Or as Eurymachus "fell down." It is always used for falling in a circular or tumbling motion. But here, it means being carried into the forward space. 
**Fat** [Dêmô]: They wrap the sacrificial parts in the omentum (fatty membrane) so that they will be consumed by the fire. 
**Gladly** [Thethumois]: Meaning "rejoicing." Homer uses it for the movement of wondering, "marveling at the deer." But Apollonius uses it in the sense of "looking" or "beholding."

**Embarking**: as for the following, "that I might board the ship," it means that the good reputation of embarking on the ship might be left to his household.

# ARGONAUTICA #

**He brooded**] <note>Greek: Porphyresken</note> Instead of "pondering deeply." For "purple" <note>Greek: porphyra</note> is a type of fish found in the deep sea. Therefore, it means he was considering the depths of the danger on both land and sea. **465**

**Zeus so much**] Concerning the Cyclops, Homer says: "Neither would I, to avoid the enmity of Zeus, spare you." Through these words, Idas's arrogance is made clear. Homer also calls him impious—and **470** "he very easily left behind his bow."

**Such a champion among the distinguished**] "Arizelos" is a city in the Peloponnese; now it is called Hierana, as Geisandros says. But here it means "conspicuous" or "notable." Is it that you do not carry me as a comrade, but as a helper? **475**

**Strongly mixed**] <note>Greek: Chalikreton</note> Meaning "unmixed wine," that which relaxes the mind. The Athenians call unmixed wine *chalis*. Aeschylus in the *Bacchae* says it is called *Chalimias*. **Idmon** appropriately makes Idmon—who is divinely inspired—oppose Idas, who is an enemy of Apollo. **485**

<column-break/>

"He brooded <note>original: Porphyresken</note> on each detail, looking like one downcast.
But Idas, noticing him, rebuked him with a great shout:
'Son of Aeson, what plan is this you revolve in your mind?
Speak your thought in our midst! Does some terrifying fear 
Dismay you as it approaches—the kind that scares cowardly men?
Let my impetuous spear now be witness, by which beyond all others
I win glory in wars; Zeus does not help me 
So much as my own spear does! No grievous pain 
Shall there be, nor shall the labor be unfinished,
Even if Idmon follows and a god himself should oppose us.
Such a champion do you bring among these distinguished men!'
He spoke, and holding the large cup with both hands,
He drank down the unmixed wine <note>original: chalikreton</note>, the sweet liquor; wine soaked 
His lips and his dark beard. And they all made a clamor 
Together; but Idmon spoke out openly:
'Wretch, you think destructive thoughts even now. 
Does the unmixed wine make your bold heart swell <note>original: oidanei</note>
In your chest to your ruin, and has it driven you to mock the gods?
There are other words of comfort with which a man 
Encourages a comrade; but you have spoken utter wickedness. 
Such talk as this once caused the sons of Aloeus <note>Otus and Ephialtes, giants who tried to storm heaven</note> to boast against the 
Blessed gods—you do not even equal their 
Manliness; yet both were destroyed by the swift arrows 
Of the son of Leto <note>Apollo</note>, mighty though they were.'
So he spoke. But the reckless, erring Idas laughed out loud,
And answered him mockingly with biting words..."

---

**Swells**] <note>Greek: Oidanei</note> It raises up, elevates, or emboldens, used here in an active sense. The metaphor is taken from the sea when it begins to rise and swell. **To boast against the blessed ones**] The word "Epiphlyein" itself means to babble or insult. **Sons of Aloeus**] Homer also knows of their god-like size. Eratosthenes says they were called this because they were brought up by the wife of Aloeus; thus it was mythologized that they were his sons. But Hesiod says they were sons of Aloeus and Iphimedeia by name, but in truth, they were the sons of Poseidon and Iphimedeia. He also says the city of Halos in Aetolia was founded by their father, which Homer mentions: "those who held Halos." **He laughed out loud**] This too is a sign of shallow character. Indeed, Isocrates says: "Do not love reckless laughter." **Biting words**] <note>Greek: Kertomioisin</note> Ironic words, those capable of "cutting the heart" <note>Greek: kear temnein</note> and causing pain. **Looking askance** with his eyes, snorting in derision. Lovers are also said to "look askance."

"Begin now, tell us this with your prophetic powers,
If for me too the gods bring such destruction,
As your father once pledged to the sons of Aegeus.
Take care how you might safely escape my hands,
Protecting your <term>fate</term> <note>original: chreiō; often meaning need or destiny</note> in vain if you should be caught."

Had not the comrades, shouting to the combatants,
And the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note> himself, restrained them. And Orpheus too,
Raising his lyre in his left hand, attempted a song.
He sang how the earth and sky and sea,
Which were once joined together in a single form,
Were separated each apart out of deadly strife.
And how the stars, and the moon, and the paths of the sun,
Always have their fixed mark in the upper air.
And how the mountains rose up, and how the sounding rivers
With their very nymphs and all creeping things were born.
And he sang how first Ophion and Eurynome,
The daughter of Ocean, held power over snowy Olympus.
And how by force of hand, one yielded his honor to Kronos...

<column-break/>

**Begin now**] <note>Greek: Arche nyn</note> Through both of these he mocks him; first he gives a single [insult] as if he were unskilled and mad, and later as one who is **490** excessively proud of his father Apollo, as if he were greatly able to strike down the arrogant. He does this with a threat while reviling him. **Fate**] <note>Greek: Chreiō</note> 
**495** It indicates both what is said according to need and destiny, or that which is to come. **In vain**] <note>Greek: Metamōlion</note> Worthy of regret. Or also "metamōnion," which means **500** useless, carried along with the winds. From the feminine plural comes a possessive form ending in "-os," as in the case of "strength-anchor." For example, Ammon becomes Ammonios; Anemōn <note>Wind</note> becomes Anemonios. 
**505** **He spoke wandering in anger**] He was enraged and angry, speaking ill and blaming. **Left hand**] <note>Greek: Laiē</note> By euphemism <note>The left side was often considered an ill-omen, so "left" was sometimes avoided or renamed</note>, meaning the left hand. **Attempted**] Either he struck the strings or he adjusted them. The benefit was the song. The sequence of the text is: "and Orpheus too..." Unless it means that from the rising up... [text unclear] Orpheus, through the utility of music, put an end to all the rivalries. **He sang how the earth**] He wishes to sing of the first confusion of the elements, and how from a kind of strife each thing came to participate in its own nature and received order. The song is appropriate to the underlying circumstances; for it is fitting to cease from the battle and return to one's proper disposition. **Out of deadly strife**] Empedocles says that when all things were previously confused, Strife and Love were <unclear>sent forth</unclear> and created the separation. Without these, nothing can come into being. From this it follows that, as is likely, nothing is truly destroyed. Thales, however, established water as the beginning of all things, taking this from the Poet <note>Homer</note> who says: "But may you all become water and earth." And Zeno says that the "Chaos" mentioned by Hesiod is water; when it settles, it becomes silt, and as the silt solidifies, the earth is made firm. Third, he says Love was born according to Hesiod, so that he might represent fire; for love is a more fiery passion. Anaxagoras, calling the sun a "red-hot mass" <note>Greek: mydron</note>, says that all things come from it. Therefore Euripides, having become his pupil, called the sun a "golden clod." The same Anaxagoras declares the moon to be a wide land, from which the Nemean lion is thought to have fallen.

**Dictean**] The Cretan [mountain], where Zeus was raised, as Callimachus records. **Mountains**] Duris says that these were the stones thrown down by the Giants; those that fell into the sea became islands, and those on land became mountains.

<margin>
**As is the custom**] <note>original: He themis</note> It was a custom for the ancients to mix a bowl when they were about to sleep, and to offer the tongues of the sacrificial victims to Hermes, and to pour wine over them. Perhaps there is a natural reason: since Hermes is handed down as the god of Reason <note>logos</note>, and his organ is the tongue—which rests when sleep falls—they rightly sacrifice the tongue to Hermes. And Homer says: "They threw the tongues into the fire." Dieuchidas in his *Megarian Histories* relates that Alcathous, son of Pelops, having been exiled from Meidra for the murder of Chrysippus, went to settle in another city. Encountering a lion that was ravaging Megara (against which others had been sent by the king of Megara), he overcame it; and putting its tongue in a pouch, he returned again to Megara. When those sent on the hunt reported that they were the ones who had overcome the beast, he produced the pouch and refuted them. Therefore, the king, having sacrificed to the gods, placed the tongue on the altars last; and from that time, this custom remained among the Megarians. But Philochorus in his *On Sacrifices* says: "They do not cut off the most beautiful part of the body [as a sacrifice]." And Homer says: "But come, cut the tongues," meaning: "cease your talking."
</margin>

<margin>
**For within her was a beam**] <note>original: En gar hoi dory</note> He plausibly says the wood is from the oak of Dodona <note>a famous oracle of Zeus</note>, because of which the Argo was "vocal." For she herself spoke. As Homer says: "...so that he might hear the counsel of the god from the high-leafed oak."
</margin>

Or perhaps in Ortygia <note>An ancient name for the island of Delos</note>, or by the waters of Ismenus, 
Striking the ground all together with swift feet 
In time to the lyre around the altar— 
So they, to the sound of Orpheus’s lyre, struck with their oars 
The rushing water of the sea, and the surges splashed over. 
The dark brine bubbled up with foam here and there, 
Seething terribly from the might of the sturdy men. 
Their armor flashed in the sun like flame as the ship 
Moved on; and the long wakes were forever turning white, 
Appearing like a path through a green field. 
All the gods looked down from heaven on that day 
At the ship and the might of the demigods, who were the best of men 
Then sailing the sea. And upon the highest peaks, the 
Nymphs of Pelion <note>Mountain nymphs from Mount Pelion</note> watched in wonder as they saw 
The work of Itonian Athena <note>A title for Athena, likely referring to a sanctuary in Thessaly or Boeotia</note>, and the heroes themselves

<column-break/>

**And they to the benches]** <note>original: "Hoi d' ana selmata"</note> This refers to the seats of the rowers, the deck-planks. Generally, 
any wide timber is called a *selma* or a *selidoma*. From this we also 
speak of the "columns" <note>original: "selidas"</note> of epic poems <note>original: "rhapsody"</note> because of their width. 

**Submerged beneath his feet]** <note>original: "Possin hypeklysthē"</note> 
Because he <note>Heracles</note> sat down, the keel of the ship was submerged 
more deeply beneath his feet and was pressed into the depths of the 
sea by the hero's great weight. 

**Or perhaps in Ortygia]** <note>original: "E pou en Ort."</note> This refers to Delos. The 
sequence of the thought is: Just as youths in Delphi, or in Delos, or 
by the Ismenus river, having arranged a dance around the altar of Apollo, 
strike the ground with their feet in harmony with the melody of the lyre; 
so these men, charmed by the lyre of Orpheus, rowed more 
strenuously. 

**Strike together]** <note>original: "homartē rhēssōsin"</note> The preposition *hypo* 
is redundant here, as seen in Homer: "under the lowest foot of Ida." 

**Ismenus]** <note>original: "Ismēnoio"</note> Ismenus is a river in Boeotia; from it 
comes the temple of Ismenian Apollo. 

**Brine bubbled up]** <note>original: "Kēkien halmē"</note> The sea rose up and leaped 
on both sides of the ship. 

**Seething]** <note>original: "Mormyrousa"</note> Terribly stirred up and moving 
fearfully. In the pre-edition <note>an earlier version of the text</note>, it says: 
"Seething from the strikes of the oars by the might of the men." 

**Armor]** <note>original: "Teuchea"</note> It was customary to hang weapons 
around the ship for decoration. 

**And the long wakes ever]** <note>original: "Makra d' aien"</note> The meaning is: 
The water turned white, just like a path through a grassy field. 
Alternatively: Just as a road is visible in the middle of a grassy field, 
so the track of the ship appeared. 

**All from heaven]** <note>original: "Pantes d' ouranothen"</note> By this, he 
confirmed that the gods also watched and marveled at the voyage. 
For they were not simply sailors, but demigods. The fact that the 
ship was built by Athena adds to the wonder. 

**Itonian]** <note>original: "Itōnidos"</note> Or perhaps "the Builder" <note>original: "Tektonidos"</note>. 
There is a temple of Itonian Athena in Coroneia in Boeotia. However, 
Apollonius is not saying that Athena built the Argo using her title 
from Itonia.

**The Mast-step:** <note>original: *Mesodmê*</note> The socket or box where the mast is placed and tilted. **The Forestays:** <note>original: *Protonoi*</note> The ropes extending from each side of the mast toward the prow and the stern. **The Mast-head:** <note>original: *Êlakatê*</note> This is said to be the thinnest and highest part of the mast, according to Eratosthenes, below which is the mast-head fitting. **The Deck/Yard:** <note>original: *Ikrion*</note> Some say this is part of the mast, but it is better to understand the *ikrion* as the so-called "yard-arm." The ends of this are called the "tips." The term *ikria* is also used for the planking where the pins are located. **The Pins:** <note>original: *Peronas*</note> These are the pegs on the planking, or what are called the "rollers," around which they bind the ropes. **The Cables:** <note>original: *Kalōas*</note> The ropes, specifically those by which the mast is made strong from each side of the ship. Generally, every rope is called a *kalos*. Therefore, sailors distinguish them: those which hold the sail are called "middle-stays" <note>original: *mesourai*</note>; those that strengthen the mast from each side toward the prow are "forestays" <note>original: *protonoi*</note>; those at the corners are "feet" <note>original: *podes* - technically the "sheets" of the sail</note>. Next to these are the "side-ropes" <note>original: *pertides*</note>, after which are the "extremity-ropes" <note>original: *terthrioi*</note>, and then those they call "middle-ropes." **Separately:** <note>original: *diakridon*</note> Instead of "distinctly" or "spread out." [The Pelasgians are] the Thessalians, named after Pelasgus, the son of Inachus. Or the name comes from the Pelasgians, a foreign tribe that inhabited Thessaly and Argos. **Cliffs** <note>original: "Eripnas"</note> refers to broken hills or craggy caves. Some also call houses by this name because they are "roofed over." The word "clifftop" is used for a headland because it is "heavily pressed" by the elements. 

**Sepias** is a headland in Iolcos, so called because Thetis <note>A sea nymph and mother of Achilles</note> transformed herself into a cuttlefish <note>original: "sepia"</note> there while being pursued by Peleus. 

**Sea-girt Skiathos:** Meaning "by the sea." Skiathos is an island near Thessaly, close to Euboea; Simonides also mentions it. 

**Peiresiae** is a city of Magnesia. **Magnesia** is a city named after the region, located on a low-lying coast by the sea. 

**Magnesian:** He is referring to the Magnesia in Thessaly. There is another Magnesia near Ephesus, founded by Leucippus the Carian, who moved there with Magnesians from Crete. 

**Along the mainland shore:** The meaning is that the coast was not rough or rocky, but smooth and level.

<margin>
**And honoring him:** This refers to Dolops. This Dolops was a son of Hermes who died in the city of Magnesia and had a tomb there upon the shore, as Cleon records in the first book of his *Argonautica*. It is the custom to offer sacrifices <note>original: "enagizousi," specifically refers to offerings for the dead or spirits</note> to the gods of the underworld at sunset, but to the heavenly gods at dawn as the sun rises. The term for victims <note>original: "entoma"</note> refers specifically to those sacrificed to the dead because their heads are cut off facing down toward the earth. This is how they sacrifice to the chthonic <note>underworld</note> deities; for the heavenly gods, they pull the neck backward and upward to slaughter them. Homer says, "First they drew back [the heads]" <note>original: "Au erysan men prōta"</note>. Others say these "cut victims" were offered to the dead as "sterile things for the sterile," while they sacrificed uncastrated animals to the heavenly gods. The preposition "beside" is implied here: they sacrificed to Dolops *beside* the swelling of the sea.
</margin>

**They lingered:** They stayed in the same place. Or they were delayed, being hindered in their journey. **Meliboea:** A city in Thessaly. **Homolin:** Homole is a mountain in Thessaly so named, or perhaps a city in Thrace. **Not much longer:** The meaning is that it would not be long before they passed the currents of the river. To "pass beyond" <note>original: "hypekbalein"</note> means to cross the streams of the river Amyros. **Chasms or clefts:** These are openings that spread out in width. **Streams of Amyros:** Amyros is a river flowing out of Thessaly, located after Meliboea; it is named after Amyros, the son of Poseidon. There is also a city there of the same name. **Ossa:** Ossa is a mountain at the edge of Thessaly, after which Macedonia begins. **Slopes:** <note>original: "klitea"</note> the inclines and bases of the mountains. **Pallene:** A mountain in Thrace and also a city, where Proteus lived. **Canastra:** A headland or cape of Pallene. **Olympus:** There are six mountains named Olympus: in Macedonia, Thessaly (where Apollodorus says the Olympic games were held), Mysia, Cilicia, Elis, and Arcadia. **Athos:** Athos is a very high mountain in Thrace. The meaning is: at daybreak, Athos appeared to them, which is as far from Lemnos as a ship sailing from midday could cover in distance. And despite Lemnos being so far away, he says the mountain's height casts a shadow over it when the sun declines. Not only over the island, but even as far as **Myrina**, which is a city at the edge of Lemnos. Lemnos is a "double-city" island, possessing both Hephaestia and Myrina. It was named after Myrina, the wife of Thoas and daughter of Cretheus. **And as far as:** <note>original: "kai esachri"</note> used here as a conjunction.

**Sintian:** Lemnos is called Sintian as a descriptive title. The Tyrsenians <note>Often identified as the Etruscans</note> were the first to inhabit it, being most harmful <note>original: "blaptikotatoi," derived from a root meaning to damage</note>. Or it refers to the island being settled by barbarians. Even Homer says: "He went to Lemnos among the wild-spoken Sintians." Hellanicus says the Lemnians were called Sintians because they were the first to forge weapons of war, for the purpose of harming <note>original: "sinesthai"</note> and injuring their neighbors. **There, all together:** The Lemnian women, having long neglected the honors due to Aphrodite, provoked the goddess to anger. For she cast a foul odor <note>original: "dysosmia"</note> upon all of them, so that they no longer pleased their husbands. When those men were later at war with the Thracians, and 

---

often took captives from there and returned with them, the men neglected their legitimate wives. Due to the goddess's anger, the women voted to kill the men by night. Not only did they do this, but they also killed the captives. Fearing that their sons would eventually avenge their fathers, they killed the entire male race together. **Across from:** Opposite. This is how Thrace is situated in relation to Lemnos. **Captives:** The women taken as plunder. **Unhonored:** Lacking status. One should know that while others agree they became foul-smelling due to Aphrodite’s anger, Myrtilus in the first book of his *Lesbica* disagrees; he says Medea, while sailing past, threw a drug into Lemnos out of jealousy, causing the foul smell for the women. He says that even until now, there is a certain day each year when, because of this stench, men and sons keep away from the women. **Alone of all:** Rightly, Hypsipyle did not kill her father. First, because a father gave her life, she gave Thoas the safety he deserved; second, because of his age; and because he was not an accomplice in the men's mistreatment of the women. **Drew him to Oinoe:** He took this story from Theolytus. **Sicinus:** This is an island near Euboea, formerly called Oinoe because it was planted with vines. Xenagoras records the name change, saying it was renamed after Sicinus, the son of Thoas and the nymph Neis. Cleon of Curium also records that Thoas was saved here, as does Asclepiades of Myrlea, showing that Apollonius took everything from Cleon. **Fishermen:** Meaning those who work the sea. One should not say "hunters" <note>original: "kynēgous"</note> on an island.

The word *teos* (meanwhile) is extended here, used in place of *heos* (until). **His own:** The poet uses the dual form inappropriately here instead of the singular. **Unspeakable:** Meaning those things that cannot be voiced or expressed. **Forgetfulness overcomes:** It is said that the dead receive forgetfulness (*Lethe*) of the events of their lives. But the poet says that even in death, this man did not fall into forgetfulness; and having been reincarnated <note>original: "metempsychotheis"</note>, according to the philosophical doctrine, he knew who he had been through the will of Hermes. Pherecydes says that Aethalides received a gift from Hermes: that his soul would be sometimes in Hades and sometimes in the places beneath the earth. The Pythagoreans say that this Aethalides—since the soul is immortal—lived again during the Trojan War as Euphorbus, son of Panthous; then later as Pyrrhus the Cretan; then as a certain Eleian whose name is unknown; and after these as Pythagoras himself. Pythagoras, regarding the changing of souls and their entry into other bodies, says that first he was Aethalides, then Euphorbus the Trojan, then a certain Hermotimus, then a Samian, and finally Pythagoras. He says the gift of memory was granted to Aethalides by Hermes in the world above.

# BOOK ONE

But his soul <note>Referring to Aethalides, the herald</note> is allotted an unchanging path, 
At one time numbered among those beneath the earth, and at another 
In the rays of the sun, among living men. But why must I 
Recount the stories of Aethalides at such length? 
He then persuaded Hypsipyle to receive the men as they came 
Through the dusk of the parched day. Yet even at dawn 
They did not loosen the ship's cables, despite the blowing of the North Wind. 
The Lemnian women went through the city and sat 
In the assembly; for Hypsipyle herself had summoned them. 
And when they were all gathered together in a great throng, 
At once she spoke among them, urging them on: 
"O friends, come, let us provide pleasing gifts 
To these men, such as is fitting for them to carry on a ship, 
Provisions and sweet wine; so that they might remain 
Steadfastly outside our towers, lest out of necessity they come among us 
And truly come to know us, and a foul 
Report spreads far and wide; for we have done a great deed, <note>A veiled reference to the Lemnian women murdering all the men on the island.</note> and it will 
Not be at all pleasing to them, if they should learn of it. 
Such is my own counsel that is now offered; 
But if any of you can devise a better plan, 
Let her stand up. For this reason I have called you here." 
So she spoke, and she sat upon her father’s 
Stone throne. Then her dear nurse Polyxo rose up, 
Limping on feet shriveled with age, 
Leaning on a staff. She was eager to speak to them. 
Near her sat four maiden companions, 
Unmarried, their hair beginning to turn white. 
She stood in the middle of the assembly and held up her neck— 
Scarcely able to do so from her hunched back—and spoke thus:

<column-break/>

<margin>640</margin> **Allotted** <note>original: "Μεμόρηται"</note>] It has been assigned, that is, it has been divided or portioned out. Aethalides, the herald of the Argonauts, was famous, as the poet says, for spending <margin>650</margin> one day in the underworld and one day in the daylight.

**Persuaded** <note>original: "Μειλίξατο"</note>] He called upon her. He convinced her with his speech, being a man of understanding. This is based on the Homeric line: <note>original: "Ἔσθλὸν καὶ τὸ τέτυκται ὅτ' ἄγγελος αἴσιμα εἰδῇ."</note> "It is a good thing when a messenger knows what is fitting."

**The parched day** <note>original: "Ἤματος αὐχμηροῖο"</note>] Referring to the day drying up toward its setting (dusk).

**Cables** <note>original: "Πείσματα"</note>] The ropes of the ships. The meaning is: although the <margin>660</margin> North Wind was already favorable for the Argonauts to sail, they nonetheless did not loosen the ropes.

**Sweet** <note>original: "Λαρόν"</note>] Pleasant, enjoyable. It is derived from the word <term>lo</term> <note>original: "λῶ"</note>, which means "I wish" or "I want." 

**Provisions** <note>original: "ἤϊα"</note>] Here meaning travel supplies or food.

**Lest they... among us** <note>original: "Μηδ' ἄμμε"</note>] "Let us give them what they need so that they stay <margin>670</margin> outside the towers, away from us; lest by the necessity and need for supplies, they enter the city and learn the truth..."

---

<margin>...of our situation.</margin> **Such is my own [counsel] now** <note>original: "Ἡμετέρη μὲν νυν"</note>] The word "now" <note>original: "νυν"</note> should be read as an enclitic; for it does not indicate a specific time, but is equivalent to "indeed." It is lengthened here for the sake of the meter. 

**But if any of you** <note>original: "Ὑμέων δ' εἴ τις"</note>] <margin>This follows the Homeric style: "Now let there be someone who might tell a better counsel than this."</margin> 

**Shriveled** <note>original: "Ῥικνοῖσι"</note>] Wrinkled. The word is found in Callimachus: "Yes, by my wrinkled skin." <note>original: "ναὶ μὰ τὸ ῥικνὸν σύφαρ ἐμόν"</note> The poet describes the old woman in the Homeric style, thus: "Who was stooped with age." 

**Beginning to turn white** <note>original: "Ἐπιχνοάουσαι"</note>] <margin>Having white hairs beginning to grow.</margin> 

**Scarcely** <note>original: "Μόλις"</note>] With difficulty, due to the lameness. <note>The scribe notes a spelling or grammatical point regarding the letter lambda.</note>

# THE ARGONAUTICA
### BOOK ONE

<margin>
**675**
**With difficulty**, because of the toil.
**To enjoy** <note>original: ἐπαυρέσθαι</note> if accented on the second-to-last syllable, it is the aorist tense, meaning "to have enjoyed"; if accented on the third-to-last, it is the imperfect, meaning "to continue enjoying."
**Others hereafter** [line 680]: Many other things, even worse than battle and war, will come.
**Childless**: Without seed, because of not being with a man. Because the word "hereafter" refers to **old age** [line 685], she made her speech even more grim by calling it "hateful old age."
**You shall live** <note>original: βώσεσθε</note>: instead of "you shall survive." The sense is: "How will you younger women live and survive when you grow old? When the older women have passed away and you are no longer able to work?
**Will oxen of their own accord** plow and harvest for you as the year comes around, without any sun-burnt laborer <note>original: αἰθιόπου, literally "burnt-faced," likely referring to men weathered by field work</note> overseeing the work?
**And for free** [line 688]: suddenly or without cost. Some copies read "at the beginning of the year."
**I for my part** [line 700]: she says these things "in character" <note>a technical term in ancient literary criticism suggesting the speaker's tone matches their age and status</note>.
**If the Fates have spared me**: as if the Spirits of Death <note>original: κῆρες (Keres)</note> are afraid to come for me, yet now I am secretly consumed by fear.
</margin>

"Let us send gifts to the strangers, such as would please Hypsipyle herself,
To be given to the guests; for it is better to grant them.
But for you, what plan is there to enjoy life,
If a Thracian army falls upon you, or some other 
Host of enemies? Such things often happen among men,
Just as now this group has arrived unexpectedly.
But even if one of the blessed gods should turn this away, yet hereafter
A myriad of troubles worse than war await you,
Whenever the aged women eventually perish,
And you younger ones, childless, reach hateful old age.
How will you live then, you luckless ones? Will oxen
Of their own accord yoke themselves for you in the deep fields,
To pull the earth-cleaving plow through the fallow land,
And for free harvest the grain as the year comes around?
I for my part, even if the Spirits of Death have spared me 
Until now, I think that in the coming year I shall 
Be covered by the earth, having received my share of funeral rites,
Just as is right, before this evil draws near.
But I urge all the younger women to consider these things.
For now, safety is within your reach,
If you would entrust your homes and all your property
To these strangers, and let them dwell in your glorious city."
So she spoke; and the assembly was filled with noise, for the speech
Pleased them. But immediately after her, Hypsipyle
Rose up again, and spoke these words in response:
"If this purpose truly pleases you all,
I would now send a messenger to the ship."

---

She says this because of her extreme old age. **Just as is right**: exactly as is fitting. **Within reach** <note>original: ἐπήβολος</note>: successful or having power over a fortune of evils; or that which saves and is beneficial. **Property** <note>original: ληΐδα</note>: used loosely here for "wealth," though properly it refers to spoils of war. **City** <note>original: ἄστυ</note>: Eumolpus explains the etymology of the word as coming from "to stand" <note>original: ἵστασθαι</note>, because cities are situated in high places. **This purpose**: this counsel. She speaks cleverly; since she herself liked what was said, she calls it the "common purpose" of all, so that she might not be accused of being driven by her own desires <note>literally "wantonness" or "lust"</note>. **To the ship and a messenger**: meaning "a messenger to the ship." The word "and" here is just a connective.

->**THE FIRST**<-

She spoke, and then called to Iphinoe who was standing nearby:
"Go for me, Iphinoe, and meet this man,
Whoever it is that leads the fleet, to come to our house;
So that I may speak to him a word from the people that pleases his heart.
And the men themselves, both to our land and our city, if they wish,

And so Iphinoe came to the Minyans; and they questioned her,
Asking what need had brought her there. Quickly she
<margin>710</margin>
Addressed them all together as they questioned her:
"The daughter of Thoas, Hypsipyle, has sent me here,
To call the leader of the ship, whoever he may be,
So that she may speak to him a word from the people that pleases his heart.
And you yourselves, to our land and our city, if you wish,
<margin>715</margin>
She invites you right now to enter, with all hospitality."

They thought that Hypsipyle was ruling now
As the only-born daughter of the deceased Thoas. Quickly they
<margin>720</margin>
Sent him [Jason] to go, and they themselves prepared to follow.
As for him, about his shoulders he fastened a work of the Itonian goddess,
A purple double-folded mantle; which Pallas gave to him
When first she laid the keel-blocks of the ship
Argo, and taught him how to measure the cross-beams with rules.
<margin>725</margin>
It would be easier to look upon the rising sun...

<column-break/>

**Go for me, Iphinoe** [line 703]: The sequence of the thought is: "Go for me, Iphinoe, meeting this man who leads the fleet, to come to our house." The word **meeting** <note>original: ἀντιόωσα</note> is used instead of "about to meet." Or perhaps "to request," that is, "to ask." A **fleet** <note>original: στόλος</note> is a crowd traveling for some action, whether by ship or on foot. Or it refers to nearly any sudden movement and major preparation. Here, the poet called the crew of a single ship a "fleet." Palamedes <note>an ancient scholar</note> notes it is written with an acute accent on the final syllable. **Hospitality** <note>original: ἀμφιέποντας, literally "tending to" or "managing"</note>: <term>He said this</term> in response to what they had feared—in case the men were actually enemies. **The daughter sent me** [line 711]: By using the word "daughter" or "maiden" <note>original: κόρη</note>, she hides the fear the Lemnian women felt (for she herself had been afraid, seeing them armed) and she turns the situation around. For the one who called them is a maiden. The word...

---

**Thoantian** [line 711]: instead of saying "the daughter of Thoas." **They thought** [line 717]: instead of "they reasoned." They supposed. **Late-born** [line 718] <note>original: τηλυγέτην</note>: This must now be understood to mean "only child." The sense is: they reasoned that Hypsipyle, being the only child born to Thoas, had inherited the kingdom from her father. **Itonian** [line 721]: In Thessaly the goddess Itonis <note>a title for Athena</note> is honored, and also in Coroneia, a city of Boeotia, named after Itonus the priest. It is a witty touch that he [Jason] does not go out in military gear, but adorned in fine clothing. First, because the Queen called him a non-combatant; second, because the city belongs only to women, who especially delight in such finery. As the playwright Menander says: "I shall be easily-despised because of my dress," and this specifically in front of women. Already, by mentioning the goddess who gave the gift, the poet signals the beauty of the cloak. **Keel-blocks** [line 724]: The wooden blocks on which the keel is fixed are called by this name. Homer says: "Set them in order, like keel-blocks, twelve in all." Therefore, **keel-blocks** <note>original: δρύοχοι</note> are the internal ribs or supports of the ship. **Rules** <note>original: κανόνας</note>: the measuring rods or levels with which carpenters align the wood and the walls. **Taught** <note>original: δάε</note>: the goddess instructed him. **Easier than she** [line 725]: In the earlier edition of the poem, after the phrase "Easier than she," the next line is "A purple double-folded mantle." The two lines in between were not present.

### ARGONAUTICA

<margin>
**Reddish** <note>original: Ἐρύθοιος</note>]: from "blushing" or "redness." It is also a species of red plant, or refers to those things you might cast your eyes upon. **Reddish** <note>original: ἐρυθρήεσσα</note> is used instead of "flame-colored" or "ruddy." This is also found in the works of **Sappho** <note>Sappho was a famous Greek lyric poet from Lesbos</note>: "Mixed with all-various colors."
<note>730</note> **Cyclopes**: Those who fashioned the thunderbolt for Zeus. As **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet, author of the *Theogony*</note> says: "They gave Zeus the thunder and forged the bolt." **At their immortal work**: At a divine, wondrous, and undying task. **Which so much**: Either referring to the quantity—so much—or to the wonder—to such a great degree—instead of "greatly." **Lacked yet one**: Because the thunderbolt was unfinished by one ray. He hints that the craftsmanship truly captured the thunderbolt, though it was slightly diminished from the true brilliance; or that it is impossible for a craftsman in a work of art to make a brilliance equal to the real thing. **Consuming** <note>original: Μαλεροῖο</note>]: The younger poets say "bright," but others say "wasting" or "withering." **Antiope**: There were two Antiopes; one the daughter of Nycteus, the other of Asopus.
</margin>

...than to look upon its redness <note>original: ἐρύθοιο</note> or to gaze directly at it.
For its middle was wrought a reddish hue,
But the edges were purple all around; and at each
End, many intricate designs were excellently and distinctly fashioned.
<margin>730</margin> In it were the **Cyclopes** <note>One-eyed giants of myth, famous as master blacksmiths</note> sitting at their immortal work,
Laboring over a thunderbolt for the King; it was already wrought
In such brilliance, though it still lacked one single
Ray, which they were beating out with iron
Hammers, as it seethed with the breath of a consuming fire.
<margin>735</margin> In it were the two sons of Asopian Antiope,
**Amphion and Zethus** <note>Twin brothers who founded the city of Thebes</note>; and Thebes, still without its towers,
Lay nearby, whose foundations they were just now laying
In their eagerness. Zethus was hoisting on his shoulders
The peak of a towering mountain, looking like one who toils hard;
<margin>740</margin> But Amphion followed him, singing clearly to his golden
Lyre; and a rock twice as large moved behind his footsteps.
Next in order was fashioned deep-tressed **Cytherea** <note>An epithet for Aphrodite, the goddess of love, named after the island of Cythera</note>,
Holding the swift shield of Ares; and from her shoulder
The fastening of her tunic had slipped down over her left arm...

---

**Antiope**: There were two Antiopes; one the daughter of Nycteus, the other of Asopus, of whom Apollonius now speaks, and of Zeus. **Amphion and Zethus**: Those who walled Thebes, just as **Homer** says: "Who first founded the seat of seven-gated Thebes." **Pherecydes** <note>A 5th-century BC mythographer</note> also provides the reason for the building: because they were guarding against the Phlegyans, who were enemies, while Cadmus was king. **Lay nearby**: He used the word "lay" loosely, referring to the site of the city's walls and its position. **Hoisting on his shoulders**: He carried it upon his shoulders, he lifted it on his shoulders. By using the word "looking like" <note>original: ἐοικώς</note>, the poet softened the description, because this was in a painting or embroidery; for in the depiction, he was not truly suffering the hardship. **Followed him**: Following Zethus himself. The phrase "twice as large" means double; the rock of Amphion followed him. **Antimylides** also records in his first book that the stones followed Amphion’s lyre of their own accord. He says the lyre was given to Amphion by the **Muses**; but **Dioscorides** says it was by Apollo, and **Pherecydes** in his tenth book of histories says by the Muses. **Twice as large**: Double compared to what Zethus was carrying. Through this figure, he shows nothing other than the excellence of music and education compared to the lack of it, and compared to irrational bravery; advising that reason <note>represented by Amphion's song</note>, being exceedingly strong, carries a small amount with little effort, while the uneducated man <note>Zethus</note> can only carry what is massive with great labor. **Swift** <note>original: θοὸν</note>]: This means immovable and unchangeable, from the word *thoazein*, which means to move quickly. **Holding** <note>original: Ὀχμάζουσα</note>]: Grasping, carrying. Though she is not warlike, she does this as a lover pleasing **Ares**; properly, *ochmasai* means to lead a horse under a bridle or a chariot. It also means to conquer in battle, from the word for a spear-point.

# FIRST.

Beneath the breasts; and opposite, just as it was,
   A bronze **likeness** <note>original: δίκηλον</note> appeared to be seen on the shield.
In it was a shaggy pasture of cattle; and around the cattle
   The **Teleboans** <note>A tribe of pirates from the islands off western Greece</note> and the sons of **Electryon** <note>The King of Mycenae and father of Alcmene</note> were fighting.
Some defending, others wishing to plunder them,
   The Taphian pirates. With blood the dewy
Meadow was soaked, and the many were overcoming the few herdsmen.
   In it two chariots were fashioned, competing;
And one was in front, and the master guided
   The reins, and with him was his horse-taming companion.
The other, **Myrtilus** <note>The charioteer of King Oenomaus</note>, drove the horses in pursuit.
   With him was Oenomaus, grasping a forward-reaching spear in his hand,
Even as the axle was breaking in the hubs...

<column-break/>

<margin>745</margin> **Likeness** <note>original: Δίκηλον</note>]: Primarily a statue resembling **Zeus** <note>King of the gods</note>; but it is used loosely for any image, as it is here. They also call satirists **dikelitai** <note>original: δίκηλίτας</note>, those who imitate someone while mocking them. In the shield, he says, being made of bronze, a form similar to her appeared.
<margin>750</margin> Wishing to show that certain reflections were occurring in the shield, he says that when **Aphrodite's** <note>The goddess of love and beauty</note> shoulder was bared down to the breast,

->On the opposite side of the shield, the likeness of Aphrodite appeared, because it was smooth or <unclear>etc.</unclear><-

Or **Taphos** is one of the **Echinades** islands, where the **Teleboans** dwelt <gloss>lived</gloss>, who formerly inhabited Acarnania—men who were great pirates. They came to Argos and drove away the cattle of Electryon, the father of **Alcmene** <note>The mother of Heracles</note>. When a battle occurred, both the sons of Electryon and the sons of Taphos were killed. Therefore, Alcmene moved away and announced her marriage to whoever would avenge the murder of her father's sons. **Amphitryon** <note>A general and the eventual husband of Alcmene</note>, having taken vengeance, married her. This history is clearly told in **Hesiod**. But concerning the battle, **Herodorus** <note>A Greek historian and mythographer</note> records that **Perseus** and **Andromeda** had four sons: Alcaeus, Sthenelus, Mestor, and Electryon; and they held the kingdom in common after the death of Perseus. Mestor’s daughter was Hippothoe, who with **Poseidon** <note>The god of the sea</note> had a son, Pterelaus. Taphos had five sons, who came from Argos and drove away the cattle. Some say Teleboas and Taphos were the sons of Pterelaus, and from them came those called Teleboans. They came demanding from Electryon the property of their grandmother, the mother of Hippothoe. When the sons of Electryon refused them, they were killed by them. Pterelaus's sons were Teleboas and Taphos, from whom the island is named. The Teleboans are the same as the Taphians, either because they lived "far off" <note>from "tele," meaning far</note> from Argos when they drove the cattle, or after Teleboas, the son of King Pterelaus, or his brother Taphos, after whom the island is named. **To plunder** <note>original: Ἀμέρσαι</note>]: to deprive. **Competing** <note>original: Δηριόωντες</note>]: struggling. For **Oenomaus** <note>King of Pisa and father of Hippodamia</note>, being the son of **Ares** <note>The god of war</note> and Sterope (daughter of Asopus, or Eurythoe, or Danaus), had a daughter named **Hippodamia**. Having received an oracle that he would be killed by his own son-in-law, he refused to give her in marriage except to the man who could defeat him in a horse race. The **Cladeus River** was the starting point for them, and the **Isthmus** was the finish line. He killed thirteen suitors, as **Pindar** <note>A famous lyric poet</note> records. But when **Pelops** <note>The legendary founder of the Peloponnesus</note> came for the contest with horses given to him by Poseidon, Hippodamia fell in love with Pelops. She persuaded Myrtilus—the son of **Hermes**, who was Oenomaus’s charioteer and driver—to insert a waxen pin into the axle-box, or simply to insert the pin, as **Pherecydes** <note>An early Greek mythographer</note> records. Thus, when the wheel rolled off Oenomaus's chariot, he died, and Pelops took Hippodamia. The horses of Oenomaus were named **Psilla** and **Harpinna**. Myrtilus was the son of Hermes by Phaethusa, one of the daughters of **Danaus**. Others say he was the son of Myrto, one of the **Amazons**. **Companion** <note>original: Παραβάτης</note>]: Not just one who stands beside the leader, but a soldier, wanting to show both the race and the victory. He has done this. **Forward-reaching** <note>original: Προτενὲς</note>]: Having the spear extended. **Swerving** <note>original: Παρακλιδὸν</note>]: As if leaning out further. **In the hubs of the axle**: There is a difference between **hub** <note>original: πλήμνη</note> and **flood** <note>original: πλήσμη</note>. The former means the box of the wheel; the latter, the flood-tide where a river overflows. Therefore, what is in Hesiod should be read thus: "Again in the floods <note>original: πλήσμησι</note> of the heaven-fallen river." And not as some say, "in the hubs." Unless we take the word "with" from the outside, meaning "with the hubs."

<margin>
**Ox-boy** <note>original: Βούπαις</note>]: A huge boy, or a full-grown man. **Great Tityos**: Elara was the mother of Tityos. After the mother's death, he is said to have been turned over to the Earth. As Homer records: "And I saw Tityos, son of glorious Gaia <note>The Earth</note>." Pherecydes says that Zeus, having coupled with Elara, daughter of Orchomenus, pushed her under the earth while she was pregnant, fearing the jealousy of Hera. Tityos was then brought forth by the Earth. Therefore, he is called **earth-born**.

He fell, falling on his back, to mangle the Pelopian back.
And Phoebus Apollo was also fashioned there, shooting arrows,
760 A **huge boy** <note>original: Βούπαις</note> not yet fully grown, boldly drawing his bow against **great Tityos**, who was pulling at his mother's veil;
He whom divine Elara bore, though Earth nursed him and brought him to a second birth.
And there was Phrixus the Minyan, as though he were truly
Hearing the ram, while the ram seemed to be speaking.
765 Looking at them, you would be struck dumb and deceive your soul,
Hoping to hear some wise speech from them;
And you would gaze long in that hope.
Such were the gifts of the goddess **Tritonian Athena**.
In her right hand she held a far-reaching spear, so that **Atalanta**...

---

**Another interpretation.** Elara was the mother of Tityos; she died after conceiving him by Zeus because she was unable to give birth due to the massive size of the child. The story seems improbable and unbelievable because it suggests the Earth gave birth to Tityos a second time. However, we say that poets call those with extraordinary bodies "sons of the earth." Thus Callimachus said, "the terrible things of the beastly sons of the earth." That Tityos was indeed massive is also stated by Homer: "and he lay stretched over nine plethra" <note>A plethron was roughly 100 feet</note>. It is clear then that when he was born as Elara’s child, he seemed to belong to her because of his small body; but as he grew and became monstrous, they said he was both born and raised by the Earth.

<term>Great Tityos</term>]: The word "great" is used to inspire wonder, because even while he was a "huge boy" <note>original: βούπαις</note>, he overwhelmed a great figure. This must be understood either in relation to his divine nature or in view of the outrage committed against his mother. For often the terror of events knows how to violate both age and nature. To this end, the poet did not use his proper name, but the natural one, calling her "mother."

<term>And there was Phrixus the Minyan</term>]: The Iolcian. For the Minyans inhabited Iolcus, as Simonides says in his *Miscellanies*. It could also refer to him being from Orchomenus, for many say Athamas lived in Orchomenus.

One must ask what the poet intends with these varied embroideries. We shall say that through the cloak, the poet describes nothing other than the **cosmic order** and the affairs of the world. First, through the lightning and the Cyclopes, he allegorizes the power and divine nature; hence he says, "they were seated at their immortal work." After this, he records cities being built through the lyre of Amphion, then all things that happen in cities: loves and wars. For this is what the armed Aphrodite signifies to him. Violence and battles are shown through the history of the Taphians; contests and marriages through the trials of Pelops; impiety and punishment from the higher powers through Tityos; and he shows plots, snares, good counsel, and unexpected salvation through the story of Phrixus. In this way, he poetically expressed through the cloak almost everything that happens in human cities. He says the cloak is a gift of **Athena**, since the world was created by **Divine Wisdom** <note>original: θεία πρόνοια</note>, and of the things done by men within it, nothing would be done rightly without wisdom.

<term>Hearing</term>]: Upon which a messenger-like figure is shown, confirming salvation to Phrixus by the will of Zeus.

<term>So that Atalanta</term>]: Daughter of Iasos, whom Meilanion married. She is different from the Argive Atalanta, daughter of Schoeneus, whom Hippomedon married. Maenalus is a mountain in Arcadia where Atalanta passed through, named after Maenalus the Arcadian, as Hellanicus says. But the followers of Aristarchus <note>A famous Alexandrian scholar</note> write such names differently, as Heracleon says in his commentary on the *Iliad*: "Taking it from the greenery." <margin>770</margin> is defined. Regarding the phrase, **He checked the troublesome quarrels**, referring to the suitors of Atalanta <note>original: Ἀταλαύτης</note>; it says he checked her from coming, lest he kindle them into sedition, and a dispute arise between them—with some wanting to be with her, and her wanting to maintain her virginity. That the Argonauts did mingle with the Lemnian women, 
<margin>780</margin> **Herodorus** records in his *Argonautica*. 
**Aeschylus**, in his play *Hypsipyle*, says they came upon the women in arms while the Argonauts were distressed by a storm, until they received an oath from them that upon landing they would mingle with them. 
**Sophocles**, in the *Lemnian Women*, says they even joined in a great battle with them. 
**In huts** [Καλύβησιν] <note>line 775</note>: those constructed with garments, which they call *pasoi* <note>curtains or hangings</note>. He says they were shut in either through love or through helplessness. 
**Newly-built** [νηγατέαις]: those recently constructed.

---

**Dark blue** [Κυανέοιο]: here meaning "bright." The image is entirely fitting and appropriate; for a maiden was also waiting for him in love, as he was shining with beauty. 
**Along the path** [Ἀνὰ στίβον]: along the road. Derived from *seibo* <note>to tread or walk</note>. 
**Surged** [Ἐπεκλονέοντο]: he used the word "surged" well to describe joy. For *klonos* <note>commotion</note> means "turmoil." 
Homer says: "As the thick ranks surged under the son of Tydeus." 
**Without turning** [Ἀπηλεγέως]: meaning "directly" or "swiftly." 
**Herodian** says this in the third book of the *General Grammar*. 
**As he appeared** [Προφανέντι]: the prefix "pro-" is useful. 
**Handmaidens** [θεράπναι]: or by contraction, "therapainai." 
**With panels** [Σανίδεσσιν]: let it be said that he refers to the long, wide pieces of wood, like planks, named from their "extension" <note>original: tasis</note>. 
**There him** [Ἔνθά μιν]: in the earlier edition, it says: "There Iphinoe through the well-built house / quickly seated him, leading him through a beautiful chair." 
**Through a beautiful porch** [Καλῆς δι’ ἀναστάδος]: what we now call a *pastas* <note>a colonnade or porch</note>. It is called this because we "draw" ourselves [spasthai] into it, as if to "rest" [pasasthai]. It is called "beautiful" either because the dwellings are royal, or because they are erotic. For such are the things of love. As **Anacreon** says regarding a beloved girl.

<margin>
**You sat in vain** <note>original: Ἦσθ' αὔτως / Hesth' autos</note>] You sat idly. Either truly, or as a general sketch of why she called him when he came, and thus she put forward these signs of weakness.
**Under men** <note>original: Ὑπ' ἀνδράσιν / Hyp' andrasin</note>] In place of "the mainland of men." Homer says, "he led the Trojans." This usage is peculiar to the Ionians.
**Hypsipyle invents these things**—that the men are living abroad in Thrace.
**They plow** <note>original: ἀρόωσι / aroōsi</note>] They till the earth. From which we must understand the word for plowing. She invents this and conceals what truly happened: the murder of the men.

> “Why do you sit thus in vain? <note>Hypsipyle begins her deception here, pretending the men are simply away at war or farming in Thrace.</note> Since the city is no longer inhabited by men,
> 795 But they have settled upon the Thracian mainland

**Farmsteads** <note>original: Ἐπαύλεις / Epauleis</note>] The folds or the pens. Or, by a misuse of the term, the Lemnians were plundering the houses of the Thracians.
**And with them, boundless** <note>original: Αὐτῇσι δ' ἀπείρονα / Autēisi d' apeirona</note>] Expressed with wonder. For he says they were carrying off the women both as plunder and as mistresses over us. In another version: "From the ships they brought together both sheep and cattle, and with the girls, boundless plunder to this place."

> But then the counsel of the destructive goddess
> Cypris <note>A common title for Aphrodite, the goddess of love, who was offended because the Lemnian women had neglected her worship.</note> was fulfilled, who cast a heart-destroying delusion upon them.
> For they grew to loathe their lawful wives, and from their halls
> 805 Yielding to their own folly, they drove away their women.
> Instead, they lay with the captive women they had taken in war,
> Wretches! We endured it for a long time, hoping that perhaps
> They might eventually change their minds. But the double evil
> Ever progressed: the legitimate children were dishonored
> 810 In the halls, and a base-born race began to arise. <note>The "base-born" refers to children fathered by the Lemnian men with their Thracian captives.</note>
> Just so, the unwedded maidens and the widowed mothers
> Wandered neglected throughout the city.
> Nor did a father care even a little for his daughter,
> Even if he saw her being mistreated before his eyes
> 815 By the hands of an insolent stepmother. Nor did the children
> Protect their mother from shameful outrage as they did before;
> Nor did a sister care for a sister in her heart.
> But the captive women were held in honor throughout the homes...”

---

“Then an unavoidable madness fell upon the people, I know not whether from a god or through their own foolishness.” **Destructive** <note>original: Οὐλομένης / Oulomenēs</note>] Instead of "terrible," or according to the outcome, "productive of destruction." Like "tearful Ares," meaning productive of tears. **Yielding to folly** <note>original: Ἦ ματίῃ / Ē matiē</note>] Conquered by their own vanity, foolishness, and mental distraction. **If perhaps eventually** <note>original: Εἴ κέ ποτ' αὖτις / Ei ke pot' autis</note>] The particle *ke* is used without focus. The sense is: "We endured for a long time, waiting to see if they would ever repent." Lest she should accuse the women of jealousy or lack of self-control, she says the suffering took hold of them for a long duration. **And the widows upon them** <note>original: Χῆραί τ' ἐπὶ τῇσιν / Chērai t' epi tēisin</note>] To avoid accusing the maidens of lewdness, she says they were distressed on account of their mothers who were being neglected, and they took it to heart. Generally, the word "wandered" <note>original: ἀλάληντο / alalēnto</note> applies here. You could also take it to mean that none of us were approaching marriage, for we had the widowhood and insult of our mothers as a teacher of what would happen to us. **Nor did a father** <note>original: Οὐδὲ πατὴρ / Oude patēr</note>] For the sake of greater pity and emphasis, the poet uses the names of natural relations.

<summary>Hypsipyle recounts a fabricated history to Jason, claiming the men of Lemnos abandoned their wives for Thracian captives, leading the women to eventually exile them. The commentary clarifies that this story is a lie designed to hide the fact that the women actually murdered the men.</summary>

### BOOK ONE

> "In dances, in the marketplace, and at feasts, they <note>The Lemnian men</note> were devoted to them <note>The captive Thracian women</note>.
> Until at last some god cast into us an exceeding bold courage,
> so that when they returned back from the Thracians, we would no longer 
> 805 receive them within our towers—so that they might either learn 
> what is right, or depart elsewhere to some other place
> taking those same captive women with them. 
> Then they, having requested whatever generation of male children 
> remained, went back again to the city <note>Hypsipyle claims they went to a city in Thrace</note> where even now 
> 810 they dwell in the snowy fields of Thrace. 
> Therefore you should remain here as residents. And if you should wish 
> to dwell here, and if it should please you, 
> you may indeed have the office of my father, Thoas. I do not think 
> you will find fault with this land, for it is more deep-soiled than the other 
> 815 islands that lie in the salt sea. 
> But come now, go to your ship and tell your comrades 
> our words, and do not remain outside the city."
> She spoke, glossing over the end of the slaughter, as it had happened.

<column-break/>

<margin>820</margin> **Exceeding** <note>original: Ὑπέρβιον / Hyperbion</note>] Great and marvelous. For she knows it is a terrible and unbelievable thing if women mastered men. Therefore, she attributes the source of the plan to the divine.

<margin>825</margin> **With the captive women themselves** <note>original: Αὐταῖς ληϊάδεσσιν / Autais lēiadesin</note>] The preposition "with" <note>original: σύν / syn</note> is omitted here. It should be understood as: "together with the women."

**Having requested** <note>original: Θεσσάλμενοι / Thessalmenoi</note>] Having taken them up by request, or having asked for them. For "thessai" means to ask or to supplicate. As **Hesiod** says:
<margin>830</margin> *Having requested the lineage of the glorious Cleodaea.*
And **Archilochus**:
*Many times praying to you in the depths of the gray-haired sea for a sweet return.* <note>The commentator notes that the poet uses this word "divinely" or with great skill in this context.</note>

***

<note>This section continues the commentary on the previous column's text.</note>

...She invents this so that the god <note>Jason</note> might not wonder if the men died, even the younger male children.

<margin>Snowy]</margin> Some say because Thrace is a "white-soiled" land; others say because it is constantly covered in snow due to being a wintry place. This latter view is better. For the country is cold. Therefore, some mythologists say the winds blow from there. **Dionysaphanes** says there is a pit in Thrace from which the gusts of the winds originate, and thus it was mythologized that Thrace is the home of the winds.

<margin>Aegean]</margin> He refers to the Aegean Sea. It was named after an island called **Aigai**. **Homer** says: *They bring gifts to Helike and Aigai.* This island is sacred to Poseidon; there is a story that no one sleeps there because of the apparitions of the god, as **Nicicrates** says. Others say the sea was named after Poseidon himself, who is addressed as "Aegeus," as **Pherecydes** says. However, **Nicocrates** claims it is from **Aegeus** <note>The father of Theseus</note> who threw himself from the acropolis into the sea. This is doubtful, for the acropolis is very far from the sea for a traveler.

<margin>Glossing over]</margin> <note>original: Ἀμαλδύνουσα / Amaldynousa</note>] Obliterating, and hiding the truth with her fiction. She culpably shifts the entire cause onto the men. The wording implies they <note>the women</note> murdered them—not only the men but also the male children and the women—yet she claims they went away to Thrace with the Thracian women and the boys, and lived there. She has not yet fully cleared the women of potential blame in the eyes of the listeners. Indeed, the whole speech of Hypsipyle contains much cleverness. She makes her statement in a way that shifts the blame; she magnifies the men's crime, showing through many points that the women's "sin" <note>the exile of the men</note> was far smaller. She says the women endured this insult for a long time. Furthermore, the fact that the lawful wives were hated and cast out of their homes while the men consorted with women taken by the spear greatly increases the crime of the men. It is also a great magnification to say that the legitimate children were dishonored while the bastards flourished. It was a great reproach that she calls the legitimate girls and the abandoned women "widows"—or perhaps she calls them all widows now because they have been deprived of their own husbands. All these women, she says, wandered neglected about the city, while strangers took their place. It is particularly provocative that the fathers did not care for their own daughters...

<margin>835</margin> **Very much** <note>original: Μάλα κεν / Mala ken</note>] Thus it is very pleasing to us to obtain what we have need of; but you do not give in the same way. Now, the word **you grant** <note>original: ὁπάζεις / opazeis</note> is used instead of **you give**. 

<margin>840</margin> **Return back** <note>original: Ὑπόστρεφε / Hypostrephe</note>] Having gone back to the ships, I will come again to the city. 

**With his right hand** <note>original: Χειρὸς δεξιτερῇ / Cheiros dexiterē</note>] Already he gives her a symbol of partnership by the touch. 

<margin>845</margin> **When now the story** <note>original: Μῦθον ὅτ' ἤδη / Mython hot' ēdē</note>] Afterwards the handmaidens came carrying guest-gifts, since Jason had completed telling his comrades everything spoken by Hypsipyle.

<margin>851</margin> **By the grace of Hephaestus** <note>original: Ἡφαίστοιο χάριν / Hēphaistoio charin</note>] For Lemnos is sacred to Hephaestus. And the word **resourceful** <note>original: πολυμήτιος / polymētios</note> is used because of his "skilled mind." 

**Heracles remained** <note>original: Ἡρακλῆος αὖθι / Hēraklēos authis</note>] Here, for the sake of the...

<column-break/>

...to the men. But he <note>Jason</note> addressed her in return:
"Hypsipyle, very much might we meet with heart-pleasing 
kindness, which you grant to us who are in need. 
I will return back again to the city, when I have
told everything in order. But let the sovereignty 
of the island be a care to you yourself. It is not that I 
shun it in disregard, but bitter labors press upon me."
He spoke, and touched her right hand. Quickly back 
he went to go; and around him, like a swarm of bees, 
countless women hovered, rejoicing, until from the gates
he went forth. And then, with well-wheeled wagons, 
they came to the shore, carrying many guest-gifts.
When he had already told the whole story through, 
which Hypsipyle had instructed him after calling him aside,
then indeed they easily led the strangers to their homes.
For Cypris <note>Aphrodite</note> stirred a sweet desire within them, 
for the sake of resourceful Hephaestus; so that again 
hereafter Lemnos might be inhabited by men, unharmed.
Then the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note> set out for the royal palace 
of Hypsipyle, while the others went wherever they happened, 
except for Heracles. For he had been left behind by the ship.

<column-break/>

...regarding those whom, even if he saw them being beaten by their stepmother, he would neither defend the mother for the sake of the children, nor would the brothers care for one another. It especially rouses anger that the city-born women—both girls and children in all political communities—remain in the status of resident aliens <term>metics: foreign residents with limited rights</term> and newcomers, while the captive women enjoy all these things without stint. There is a sufficient defense on behalf of the women, in that they did not utterly drive the men from the island, but gave them a choice: either to maintain their duties toward their wives, or to go elsewhere and live with the captives. Generally, the speech has a descriptive and formative quality, through which it makes the listener sympathetic toward the unfortunate women. Having made the situation "self-accusing" <note>taking the blame for the conflict</note>, she then redirected the core of the matter to a shift of focus, saying it seemed best to send the men away after they <note>the women</note> received courage from the gods. For in this way, the expulsion becomes not only just but also necessary. Things judged by a god are necessary. The prologue not only makes the Argonauts more confident, saying that the men are merely away from the city, but also releases the women from blame; for she all but says "we did not kill them, as the rumor holds, but they are away in Thrace." The epilogue wins Jason over completely. Not only is "the sweet" put forward (which was to yield to her), but also "the profitable" and "the useful." For she promises him the kingdom of Thoas. The word **he spoke** <note>original: ἴσκεν / isken</note> here is used instead of **he said**, whereas in Homer, it is used instead of **he likened**.

He [Heracles] stayed willingly, and a few chosen companions.
