Scorning our own countrywomen? Does it please us to dwell here
And plow the rich soil of Lemnos?
Surely we shall not become famous here for long, cooped up
With foreign women; nor will any god take the Fleece
And give it to us of his own accord in answer to our prayers.
Let us return each to our own; and let him [Jason] stay all day
In the bed of Hypsipyle, until he has repeopled Lemnos
With sons, and great fame reaches him."

First he reproaches their lack of self-control before he reveals what is beneficial. Among the natural philosophers, Heracles is understood as "intelligence" and "strength." Thus the passage shows that although the heroes gave in to pleasure, they recovered themselves through reason. For example, he thinks: "O blessed ones, are we exiled from our own country by the blood of our kin? Or did we come here because we lacked marriages, blaming our own countrywomen? And are we to inhabit Lemnos, dividing it by lot?" Or perhaps: "O blessed ones, having committed murder of kin, are we exiled from our fatherland?" This is because such people were punished with eternal exile from their homeland. 

**Scorning our countrywomen** <note>original: Ὀνοσσάμενοι πολιήτιδας / Onossamenoi poliētidas</note>] He specifically used the word "countrywomen" to say: "Having rejected Greek women, have we come to live with barbarians?" For he implies they are fleeing the beauty of their own. Perhaps in reality, the women left in Lemnos were the older ones. 

**Famous** <note>original: Εὐκλεεῖς / Eukleeis</note>] Meaning illustrious. He uses this to highlight their lack of sense. For he knows each of them joined the voyage for glory, and they would lose this if they delayed a long time. 

**Cooped up for a long time** <note>original: Ἐπὶ δηρὸν ἐελμένοι / Epi dēron eelmenoi</note>] Through this, he skillfully and technically blames the duration of their stay. Neglecting labor for a short time might be forgiven, but to do so for a long time is foolishness for any man. They allowed this despite the saying: "There is satiety [a breaking point] in all things." 

**Let us return each to our own** <note>original: Ἴομεν αὖτις ἕκαστοι ἐπὶ σφέα / Iomen autis hekastoi epi sphea</note>] The word *sphea* (their/own) is used correctly here. It is equivalent to "their" when assigned to the third person. Strictly, he should have said: "Let us return each to *our* own." For this is the conjugation of persons: "ours," "yours," "theirs." 

**Repeopled with sons** <note>original: Ἐσομβρώσῃ / Esombrōsē</note>] Meaning "to fill with men," spoken ironically.

---

...is not sound <note>A scholarly critique of the poet's use of the bee simile.</note>, nor does it harmonize in all respects. For it is possible to liken the women to bees, the heroes to flowers, and the city to a hollow hive; but how could the remainder not be discordant? For instance, he says "the meadow rejoices and is glad"; yet the city is grieving, as shown by his saying "wailing," and again the phrase "plucking now one sweet fruit and now another" is discordant. Or perhaps, more greedily, each woman was eager to take her portion of the heroes. These details were harmonized according to their first meeting and union. <margin>**Otherwise.**</margin> To those who find fault with the simile, saying that not everything mentioned fits the subject at hand, it must be said that some parts of a simile are taken for the sake of the user's clarity, while others contribute only to beauty and expression. <margin>**Diligently** <note>original: Ἐνδυκέως / Endukeōs</note>] Attentively. Earnestly.</margin> As for the word **wailing** <note>original: κινυρόμεναι / kinyromenai</note>, it does not mean "lamenting," but rather they are weeping. And "a tear fell from them." <margin>**Praying** <note>original: Εὐχόμεναι / Euchomenai</note>] Because</margin> due to weakness, the nature of women always turns toward prayer, as is clear from the earlier lines where he says: "and the women raised their hands much to the immortals in the ether." <margin>**Go** <note>original: Νείσεο / Neiseo</note>] An extremely</margin> erotic greeting and prayer. For first she prays for them generally, and then—since her entire effort and affection for Jason is nothing other than the safety of his comrades—she prays for this for him as well; not so much to gratify them as to gratify Jason. <margin>**Easily could you** <note>original: Ῥηϊδίως δ' ἂν ἐοῖ / Rhēidiōs d' an eoi</note>] He means to say,</margin> "easily would you gather a great many people for yourself." Since he used the word *eoi* <note>original: ἐοῖ</note>, which is indicative of the third person, just as in Homer: "Whenever he [sent] his own (*eous*) attendants back behind him (*eoi*)." <margin>**Desire** <note>original: Μενοινῶ / Menoinō</note>] Instead of</margin> opinion or intention, or concern.

**I foresee** <note>original: προτιόσσομαι / protiossoi</note>] To look forward.
**I might carry out** <note>original: ἐξανύσαιμι / exanysaimi</note>] I might fulfill.
**Leave some word for me**] The sense is: "Tell me some advice, if I happen to give birth, so that I may give instructions to the child." The phrase is elliptical, meaning some words are left out for the reader to fill in.
**Marvelling** <note>original: ἀγαιόμενος / agaiomenos</note>] Marvelling at her disposition and her love.
**Keep a better heart within you**] The meaning: Have a better soul and opinion regarding me, looking at my own homeland. For we are incomplete—as if we have abandoned our own home—if we move to settle in another.
**By the will of Pelias**] That is, because of Pelias I must live there.
**Land of Hellas**] Here meaning Thessaly. Homer, however, knows only one city in Thessaly called "Hellas."

---

**Pelasgian**] That is, Thessalian, named after the Pelasgians <note>an ancient, pre-Greek people</note> who once lived there.
**And you [bear] a male**] This is said as if in wonder, asking if even a single male could ever be born in a city of women.
**Cure for sorrow**] Like a consolation or a remedy for their misery. From this comes the word *endykes* <note>meaning "kindly" or "intent"</note>, with the 'k' removed as Tryphon <note>A famous Greek grammarian from Alexandria</note> says. For *endykes* refers to something pleasant and sweet that comes after much hardship; the word *endykeos* comes from it.
**At their hearth** <note>original: ἐφέστιοι / ephestioi</note>] Inhabitants. The Spartans call a house a "hearth" (*hestia*).
**First of all** <note>original: παροίτατος / paroitatos</note>] Instead of "earlier." It is derived from the word for "before" (*paros*). Homer also says: "Other horses seem to me to be ahead."
**As the others also**] The poet defends the heroes' character by showing a pattern: the leader did not start the union with the Lemnian women while they simply followed him; rather, now that the voyage begins again, he is the first to lead and they follow.
**Sea-washed** <note>original: ἁλιμυρέος / halimyreos</note>] Surrounded by the flowing sea. "Sea-washed" rivers are those that empty into the sea.
**Island of Electra**] He refers to Samothrace. Electra, daughter of Atlas, lived there, and the island was called "Strategis" by the locals. Hellanicus <note>A 5th-century BCE historian and chronicler</note> says she was called "Electrione." She bore three children: Dardanus, who settled in Troy (whom the locals call "Polyarchus"), and Eetion, whom they call Iasion; they say he was struck by a thunderbolt for insulting an image of Demeter <note>The goddess of the harvest</note>. ## BOOK 1

Harmonia, whom Cadmus married. According to Hellanicus in the first book of the *Trojan History*, and Idomeneus in the first book of the *Trojan History*, the Electrian gates of Thebes were named after her mother, Electra.

<margin>Unbreakable and gentle] This refers to the initiation rites <note>original: τελετὰς</note> held in Samothrace; if someone is initiated into these, they are kept safe during storms at sea. They also say that Odysseus, having been initiated in Samothrace, used a mystical veil instead of a regular headband. For those who are initiated tie purple headbands around their waists for protection. It is also said that Agamemnon was initiated, and while there was great turmoil at Troy due to the divided state of the Greeks, he was able to stop the strife while wearing a purple garment.</margin>

> "By unbreakable and gentle initiations, they might learn the laws,
> "And so sail more safely across the chilling sea.
> "Of these things I will speak no further; but may the island itself
> 920 Be gracious, as well as the local gods who received those secret rites,

> By day, and by night they were within the Rhoeteian shore.

...wearing. They are initiated in Samothrace to the Cabiri <note>A group of enigmatic underworld deities</note>, whose names Mnaseas records. They are four in number: Axieros, Axiokersa, and Axiokersos. Axieros is Demeter <note>Goddess of the harvest</note>; Axiokersa is Persephone <note>Queen of the Underworld</note>; Axiokersos is Hades <note>King of the Underworld</note>. The fourth added to these is Kasmilos, who is Hermes <note>The messenger god</note>, as Dionysodorus relates. Athenion, however, says that Iasion and Dardanus were born to Zeus and Electra. The Cabiri seem to be named after the Cabiri mountains in Phrygia, since they moved from there. Others say there were originally only two Cabiri: an elder, Zeus, and a younger, Dionysus. Samothrace used to be called Leucosia, as Aristotle relates in his *Constitution of Samothrace*. Later it was named Samos after Saos, the son of Hermes and Rhene; the 'm' was inserted into the name. When Thracians came to inhabit it, it was called Samothrace <note>Literally "Thracian Samos"</note>.

<margin>918</margin> Safe] Free from danger. It is said that those initiated there are heard in whatever they pray for. As Acesaeus says: "But since you happen to have been initiated in Samothrace, now is a good time to pray." For those who know the mysteries seem more likely to be saved.

<margin>919</margin> Of these I know no further] The word "further" <note>original: προτέρω</note> is used here to mean "more than this" (just as in Homer: "the ships did not go further for me"). Here it is used loosely in the context of the narrative. The sense is: "I will say nothing more of such things; but may the island and the gods of the mysteries rejoice. It is not fitting for us to speak of them <note>The secrets of the mysteries were strictly forbidden to be told to the uninitiated</note>."

<margin>921</margin> Secret rites] The mysteries <note>original: ὄργια / orgia</note>, so called from "keeping out" <note>original: εἴργειν / eirgein</note> the uninitiated from them. Or because they happen on mountains <note>original: ὄρεσι / oresi</note>. "Orgades" refers to places that are overgrown and well-watered.

<margin>922</margin> Black] The Black Sea <note>original: Μέλας πόντος / Melas Pontos</note> is so called as Eudoxus relates in the fourth book of his *Circuit of the Earth*. They say the Sarpedonian rock is behind it. Homer also uses the term: "he leaped into the black sea." It was named after Melas, the son of Phrixus, who fell into it; or after a river called Melas that flows there.

<margin>923</margin> On one side the Thracians] Meaning on the right hand.

<margin>924</margin> Imbros] Lying on the opposite side. For Imbros is directly across from Thrace. Homer says: "Between Imbros and Samos and Lemnos." He calls Samothrace "Samos" in that passage.

<margin>925</margin> Chersonese] The "Peninsula" located after Thrace. Originally it was an island. It lies directly opposite Troy. There is also another Chersonese in Caria, which is where Alexander, the author who wrote about Caria, was from.

<margin>927</margin> Daughter of Athamas] This refers to the Hellespont <note>The Dardanelles</note>, named after Helle, the daughter of Athamas, who fell into the water there.

<margin>929</margin> Rhoeteian] Named after Rhoeteia, the daughter of Proteus. Rhoeteion and Sigeion are the two famous capes of the Trojan territory.

# BOOK ONE. 45

They measured their course, keeping the land of Ida <note>Mount Ida, near Troy</note> on their right,
<margin>930</margin> and leaving Dardania behind, they approached Abydos;
after it they passed Percote, and the sandy beach
of Abarnis, and the holy land of Pityeia.
And indeed, as the night was split by the ship’s passage,
they crossed the Hellespont, dark with swirling eddies.
<margin>935</margin> There is a steep island within the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>,
a short distance from the fertile Phrygian mainland,
leaning toward the sea, where an isthmus is washed by waves,
enclosed on the landward side. On it are double shores,
lying above the surging water;
<margin>940</margin> the people living around it call it Bear Mountain.

<column-break/>

**Of Abarnis]** Abarnis is a city of Lampsacus. It was named for the following reason: Aphrodite, having fallen in love with Dionysus, lay with him. But when he departed for India, she lay with Adonis. When Dionysus returned, she made a crown and went to meet him. When she saw him, she was ashamed to follow him because she was already pregnant; withdrawing to Lampsacus,

---

she wished to give birth to the child she was carrying. But Hera, out of jealousy, touched Aphrodite’s belly with a hand smeared with charms, and caused her to give birth to a child who was deformed in every other way and possessed an oversized phallus; this child was named Geloeus <note>A name related to mocking or laughter; better known as Priapus</note>. When Aphrodite saw him, she was seized with shame and hated everything about the child because of the unseemliness of his genitals. Because Aphrodite then denied the child there, the city was called Aparnis <note>original: "Ἀπαρνὶς" from "ἀπαρνηθῆναι" (to deny)</note>; later, by a shift of the letters, it was called Abarnis. **Percote** is a city of Troy, which Homer also mentions. **Pityeia]** Lampsacus was formerly called Pityeia, as some name it Pityia. Some say that Phrixus, having separated his treasure, placed it there, and the city was named from this, for the Thracians call a treasure "Pityo." Homer also mentions it, calling it Pityeia. **Darkened]** Referring to the sea being made dark by the spray and having very large waves. **There is a certain steep island]** The Propontis is the sea after the Hellespont; next is the Thracian Bosporus. In this Propontis there is an island which later became a peninsula, or it has a certain isthmus. For any land jutting out into the sea is called an isthmus. Near this peninsula lies **Bear Mountain**, properly so called; for they say the nurses of Zeus spent time there and were transformed into bears. Alternatively, it is because the place is full of wild animals and was named after the bear. Or, due to the height of the mountain, it seems to approach the northern constellations <note>The Great and Little Bear</note>. Certain earth-born people lived there as natives. The peninsula itself and the isthmus were inhabited by the Doliones, over whom Cyzicus ruled. The passage follows like this: There is a certain high island in the Propontis, a short distance from Phrygia and the current of the isthmus, lying upon the land above the Aesepus river, having shores on both sides; they call the mountain "Bear." It is a peninsula on which the city of the Cyzicenes is situated. He called it an island because, though it was formerly an island, it was later joined to the mainland. It is called **double-shored** because the harbor of Cyzicus has two entrances on either side. **From Phrygia]** Phrygia lies next to Troy. These are the nations of Asia. Thus, for those traveling to Colchis, Asia is on the right and Europe is on the left. He called Phrygia **fertile** <note>original: "πολυληΐου"</note>, meaning it is rich in wheat or rich in livestock. **Where the isthmus is washed]** He means as much distance as there is of an isthmus. Others hear "as much" as an expression of wonder; this is better. It means the peninsula, lying in the sea and having an isthmus—then, wonderingly, how much that isthmus roars as it is struck by the waves! A place that has sea on both sides is called an "isthmus," as if it were a "passing place" <note>original: "ἰσμός"</note>. It is called an isthmus from the word "to go" <note>original: "ἰέναι"</note> because it is where one travels. This is also why the parts of the throat are called "isthmian" <note>tonsils</note>. A "strait" <note>original: "πορθμὸς"</note> is either a place with land on both sides or a place having a narrow sea. **Enclosed]** Flowed around, or pressed down, or covered with plants.

>> **It received them, a safe harbor]** A harbor of Cyzicus, which has a namesake city in Sicily. **And the anchor stone]** The preposition is missing here. It means: they released the stone that served as their mooring and anchor because it had been worn away by the sea, and they took another. They left the old one at the Artacia spring. The Milesians <note>Greek colonists from Miletus</note>, having settled there according to an oracle of Apollo, took the anchor and dedicated it in the temple of Jasonian Athena. **The Spring of Artacia]** A spring near Cyzicus; Alcaeus mentions it, as does Callimachus, noting that it belongs to the land of the Doliones. **Neleids]** The Ionians who emigrated from Attica with Neleus, son of Codrus, and occupied Caria and Phrygia; following the oracles of Apollo, they dedicated that stone to Athena. **Small stone]** He called it "little." Just as Homer speaks of a "little table," and Theocritus a "little boy." **All together]** Deilochus does not name the Doliones specifically, but says that Cyzicus, having learned of the arrival of the heroes, hosted them. By "voyage" <note>original: "stolon"</note> he means the journey they were making. The sense is: the Doliones and Cyzicus, when they learned who they were, hosted them kindly. For the Doliones are also colonists from Thessaly, which is why they received them as being of the same race. **Persuaded them]** He convinced them to moor the ship further inside the harbor, for they had originally moored the vessel outside the city.

# THE FIRST BOOK

<margin>965</margin>
**I**n the harbor of Chytos they bound the ship’s hawsers.
<margin>**There he established an altar to Apollo of the Disembarkation]** <note>original: "Ekbasios"</note> This name comes from the "disembarkation" of the ship onto the land of the Doliones. The historian Deilochos says the temple was dedicated to Apollo of the Disembarkation, but others say it was to Jasonian Apollo. Socrates, in his work on the *Invocations of the Cyzicenes*, says he is called Cyzicene Apollo. **The expedition]** <note>original: "solos"</note> This is a collective noun used here with a plural verb, "they reached." **Equally with him]** Apollonius says this because King Cyzicus was the same age as Jason.</margin>
**T**here they established an altar to Apollo of the Disembarkation;
**S**tanding along the shore, they attended to the sacrifices.
**T**he king himself gave them pleasant wine for their thirst,
**A**nd sheep as well. For a prophecy had come to him that, whenever
<margin>970</margin>
**A** divine expedition of heroic men should arrive, he must immediately
**G**reet them with kindness and have no thought of war.
"**L**ike him, perhaps, the downy hair was just beginning to bloom on his cheeks.
**N**or had he yet been blessed with the joy of children,
<margin>975</margin>
**B**ut his wife was still in his house, untouched by the
**P**angs of labor—Cleite of the beautiful hair, daughter of Merops of Percote;
**H**er he had recently brought from her father's house from the opposite coast,
**H**aving given countless wedding gifts.
**B**ut even so, leaving his chamber and the bed of his bride,
**H**e prepared a feast among the heroes, and cast fear from his 
<margin>980</margin>
     heart.
**T**hey questioned one another in turn; the king indeed
<margin>A variant reading says: "**Fittingly, perhaps, the downy hair was beginning to sprout on him.**" This means he was just now, recently, beginning to grow a beard. The word **ioulos** refers to the first bloom of hair on the chin.</margin>
**L**earned of their voyage and the commands of Pelias;
**A**nd they, in turn, learned of the cities of the neighbors and all the gulf
**O**f the wide Propontis. But he had no further knowledge
**T**o tell them, though they desired to learn.

The word **ioulos** <note>the first growth of beard</note> also refers to the growth of hair on the chin. However, Eratosthenes, in his work *Hermes*, treated it as the name of a song, saying: "The woman of the house, working by the high gate, sang the beautiful **iouloi** songs." But Didymus says it is not just any song, but a hymn to Demeter, much like the *epielos* is a hymn to Artemis among the people of Troezen. For a "hilos" or "ilos" is a bundle gathered from the sheaves of grain, and "Oulo" is a name for Demeter. **Ioulos** is also said to be a type of animal, a many-footed woodlouse <note>original: "heleidion polypoun"</note>; for it has many feet on both sides, like a centipede. Theophrastus, in his *Letter to Phanias*, says it is also called an "onos" <note>donkey-bug</note>, as in Sophocles' play *The Mute Satyrs*: "Rolled up like a woodlouse." **Had been allotted]** <note>original: "memorēto"</note> It had been fated for him; he was destined by fortune. The construction is "nor had he yet been blessed with children" (using a participle instead of an infinitive). **Untouched by the pangs of labor]** Meaning childless and "clean" of birth-pains. **Cleite]** She was the daughter of Merops, a seer from Percote. She married Cyzicus, as recorded by Deilochos and Ephorus. **From the opposite coast]** This either indicates she came from Europe (since Europe lies opposite Asia) or from the side of the Propontis opposite Cyzicus. Merops of Percote ruled over Pityeia, as Homer shows in the *Catalogue of Ships*. **Cast fear from his heart]** This implies that he seemed to fear a certain oracle, as he was destined to be killed by the Argonauts. **The voyage]** <note>original: "agisin"</note> Referring to the sailing and the purpose for which they were traveling. He asks them this pressing and useful question politely. **Neighbors]** <note>original: "periktionōn"</note> Those living round about. **But he had no further knowledge]** Regarding what lay ahead of the land of the Doliones. Through this, the poet shows the "inexperience of the world" <note>original: "apeirokosmian"</note> typical of Cyzicus.

# ARGONAUTICA

<margin>
**Indeed they ascended]** To see the advantage of the view from here. **Dindymon** is a mountain of Cyzicus, sacred to Rhea because two breast-like peaks <note>original: *didymous mastous*</note> rise up from it, as Philostephanus says, or at least that is how it was named. All of Phrygia is sacred to the Goddess because it is "difficult to hold" <note>original: *dysechein*</note>; that is why it is called so.
**The Mounded Harbor]** <note>original: *Chytos limenos*</note> A harbor in Cyzicus named thus. For the Pelasgians attempted to heap it up <note>original: *chosai*, to mound or dam</note>, as Deilochos says, out of their hatred toward the Thessalians by whom they had been expelled. The poet says the word "Earthborn" was used by the locals.
**Earthborn]** Deilochos says they are Thessalians who are "hand-bellied" <note>original: *encheirogastoras*, a term often used for manual laborers or giants who live by their hands</note>. But some say the "Earthborn" were bandits who seemed to be plotting against the Argonauts.
</margin>

985 Indeed they climbed up great Dindymon, so that they
might behold the paths of that sea; and then they
drove the ship from its previous mooring to the Mounded Harbor.
And the road they went upon is called the Ikonian road.
But the Earthborn, rushing from the mountain on the other side,
990 blocked the mouth of the vast mounded harbor below with rocks,
like hunters lying in wait for a beast inside.
But Heracles had been left there behind with the younger men;
he immediately drew his back-bent bow
and brought them to the ground one after another. And they in turn
995 were lifting and throwing jagged rocks.
For surely even those terrible monsters were raised by the goddess
Hera, wife of Zeus, as a labor for Heracles.
And the others indeed returned and turned back,
coming from the lookout point, and the heroes joined the slaughter
1000 of the Earthborn, some with arrows
and some with spears, until they had slain them all
as they rushed incessantly in opposition.
And as when woodcutters cast down long poles, newly struck
by axes, in rows upon a beach,
1005 so that, being soaked, they might receive the strong bolts:

---

**Jagged rocks]** <note>original: *amphirhogas*</note> Meaning broken through, split, or eaten away by the sea. **The goddess raised them]** He says mythically that the Earthborn were raised by Hera to oppose Heracles. The myth generates them from the Nemean Lion. <note>This refers to Hera's habit of breeding monsters to test Heracles.</note> Polygnotus, in his writings on Cyzicus, says they were bandits. Callimachus also mentions them, saying: "Celebrating the one who fled by the river, Hera raised him as a labor for Heracles; later, so that he might become thick, the thunderous one received him." **The others]** <note>original: *olloi*</note> This is the newer Ionic form for "the others." The word *dethen* is a filler adverb, sometimes used for "clearly" or "as indeed." The phrase is transposed; the logical order is: "as the others indeed returned and joined the slaughter." **Rushing incessantly]** They slew them as they were being disturbed without ceasing or without flinching. Or thus: they killed them as they were unceasingly opposing with their strengths. **As when long poles]** This comparison is fitting and sound in every respect. For he likens the giants to wood because of the unworkable size of their bodies and their dwelling in the mountains, and he likens the heroes to woodcutters. The phrase **"so that, being soaked, they might receive the strong bolts"** refers to the proximity of the shores and another technical point: craftsmen soak wood so that they might be spared extra labor when working and when driving in the wooden ship-pegs. Similarly, the heroes killed the giants so that their ascent to the mountain would be safe from then on. **So that being soaked]** So that having been dampened, they might become receptive to the wedges.

<summary>The Argonauts move their ship to the Mounded Harbor and climb Mount Dindymon, but are attacked by the Earthborn giants. Heracles and the returning heroes slaughter the giants, a scene the poet compares to woodcutters laying out timber on a shore.</summary>

# BOOK ONE

<column-break/>

**At the narrowing]** <note>original: *eni xynochê*</note> In the circumference and the mouth of the harbor.

**Diving heads]** This refers to the act of diving headlong. The poet uses the ongoing tense <note>original: *paratatikon*, imperfect or present</note> instead of the completed tense <note>original: *syntelikou*, aorist</note> "having dived." For they were cast down into a dive head-first. "To dive" <note>original: *dyptsein*</note> means the same as "to go under" <note>original: *dynein*</note>; as in Callimachus:
<margin>101</margin>
"The divers <note>original: *dyptai*</note> coming out of the sea."
It is better than Antimachus's line: "Like some new one who dives into the salty sea."

**Fearless]** Without danger and without fear, since the enemies had perished.

**The blast remained]** The breeze of the wind was no longer steady or the same, but became contrary. One must understand the definite article "the" here. The sense follows in order:
<margin>102</margin>

***

<margin>101</margin> **In what kind of night]** The breeze of the wind no longer remained the same. **But storms]** Wintry squalls and blasts. Whence Homer uses "storms" and "Harpies" <note>the "Snatchers"</note> as synonyms to mean these very squall-like blasts, naming them from the act of "snatching" <note>original: *harpazein*</note>; as in the line: "when the storms took away the daughters of Pandareus," and then, "meanwhile the Harpies snatched up the girls," treating them as the same thing. One name comes from "snatching," the other from "rushing" <note>original: *thyein*</note>, which means to move with violence. The word "snatchingly" <note>original: *harpagden*</note> is derived from "to snatch," just as "by carrying" <note>original: *phoraden*</note> comes from "to carry" <note>original: *pherein*</note> and "by rushing" <note>original: *aiden*</note> from "to rush" <note>original: *aissein*</note>. **And they stepped out]** They disembarked and were driven back again to the Doliones. He uses the term "well-hosted" <note>original: *euxeinoisi*</note> as if he himself is lamenting the tragic outcome of what happened. **It is called sacred]** This is said by euphemism <note>using a "good" word for a "bad" thing to avoid ill omens</note>. For people often call great sufferings by auspicious names like "sacred" and "beautiful"; just as the son of Xenias calls shackles "armlets," or as one might call the plague "leprosy." Others called the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note> the "sacred disease," as even Callimachus says: "They lie who call it sacred." <margin>102</margin> **They did not recognize]** They did not, he says, truly realize that these were the colonists of the Euboeans. For this reason they were also called Macrones, since Euboea was called "Macris" <note>Long Island</note>. He said "Pelasgian" because Euboea is near the Peloponnese, which was formerly called Pelasgia. The Macrones were neighbors of the Doliones. Others say the Macreans are a tribe of the Becheires who are always at war with the people of Cyzicus. They were practiced in the arts of war, as Philostephanus or Herodorus records in their writings on their lives. Dionysius of Chalcis says they are called Macrones because they are colonists of the Euboean Macrones. Others say they are called Macrones because many among them are "long-headed" <note>original: *makrokephalous*</note>, just as the Persians are said to be "hook-nosed" <note>original: *kyrtous*</note>. He mentions...

# ARGONAUTICA

Herodotus writes of these things in his second book. He called the Pelasgian Ares that of the Macedonians, as they are colonists of the Euboeans; Euboea lies near the Peloponnese, which in ancient times was called Pelasgis. <note>The Pelasgians were an ancient, somewhat mysterious people who preceded the Greeks in many areas.</note>

<margin>1025 **And they clashed]** This marginal note references the Homeric style: "They clashed their ox-hide shields, and their spears and the might of men."
**Among the bushes]** Referring to the stems of trees, derived from "heaping up." As in: "A thick-leaved bush of olive grew." 
This passage is also modeled after Homer: "He raged as when spear-shaking Ares, or a destructive fire, rages in the mountains in the thickets of a deep forest."
1035 **Mighty]** <note>original: *zamenês*</note> Very strong; the prefix *za-* is used for intensity, as in "very wealthy" <note>original: *zaploutos*</note>, "very angry" <note>original: *zakotos*</note>, or "most divine" <note>original: *zatheos*</note>.
**Beyond fate]** <note>original: *hyper moron*</note> One must understand "of the struggle" or something similar. It means that Cyzicus was for a time surpassing the doom of battle.
**Was shattered]** <note>original: *errhaisthê*</note> Instead of "was broken."
1045 **Fulfilled his fate]** He completed the command of destiny.</margin>

Then, donning their armor, they raised their hands against one another.
They clashed their ash-spears and shields together,
Like the sharp blast of a fire that falls upon dry
Bushes and rises in a crest; and a dread and mighty
Uproar fell upon the Dolionian people.
<margin>1030</margin> Nor was their king destined to escape the doom of battle
And return home to his bridal chamber and his bed.
Instead, the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note> leaped upon him as he turned
To face him and struck him full in the chest; the spear
Shattered the bone, and he, huddled in the sand,
<margin>1035</margin> Fulfilled his fate. For it is the law that mortals never
Escape it; a great fence is stretched around us everywhere.
So it was for him: thinking he was safe from the bitter ruin
Of the heroes, fate shackled him that very night
As he fought against them. Many other defenders
<margin>1040</margin> Were also slain. Heracles killed Telecles
And Megasthenes; Acastus stripped the armor from his foes;
Peleus slew Zelys and the swift-in-war Gephyrus.
Then Telamon of the ashen spear killed their king;
Idas killed Promeus, and Clytius slew Hyacinthus;
<margin>1045</margin> Both the sons of Tyndareus <note>Castor and Pollux</note> slew Phlogius and Megalassaces;
And the son of Oineus <note>Meleager</note> slew the bold Itymoneus.

***

**For it is the law]** This serves as proof that fate is inescapable, as Homer demonstrates in many places. **Out of bitter ruin]** <note>original: *adeukeos atês*</note> Not sweet. *Deukos* means sweet. This is where the name Polydeuces <note>Pollux</note> comes from. For even while living, he is most unpleasant <note>perhaps referring to his shared mortality/immortality with his brother</note>. Or it means "unseen" or "overlooked," from the word for "showing." Regarding the phrase "outside of," hope belongs to the living. Deilochus also records the history of this battle. However, regarding the killing of Cyzicus and the battle as a whole, there is no agreement. 

Ephorus, in his ninth book, writes that the Doliones, being Pelasgians, were hostile toward those inhabiting Thessaly and Magnesia because they had been driven out by them, and so they attacked the Argonauts by night. Apollonius followed Deilochus. But Callisthenes, in the first book of his *Account of the Voyage*, says the inhabitants of Cyzicus attacked the Argonauts at night out of pure enmity. 

**Telecles and Megasthenes]** Apollonius invented these names; he did not take them from history. So says Tarrhaios. Some say Cyzicus was killed by the Dioscuri <note>Castor and Pollux</note>, others by Jason. The word "his" <note>original: *eoio*</note> is used poorly here; it is a possessive form meaning "his own."

And the ship reached **Artacea**, the harbor of men; where even now
The inhabitants of the sea still honor you with heroic sacrifices.
The others, giving way, fled in fear, just as hawks

**Artacea]** Herodian <note>A 2nd-century grammarian</note> places the grave accent on this name in the third book of his *General Prosody*. For it is Artakes. 
**Like hawks]**
<margin>1050</margin>
A type of falcon. Callimachus discusses the types of hawks in his work *On Birds*.
And Homer also seems to know them: "Not even a hawk." Homer says "Kirkos" <note>original: *Kirkos*</note> is the swiftest of winged creatures.
And, "the Hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo." For the hawk is sacred to Apollo.
**Dove]** <note>original: *Peleia*</note> A species of pigeon, similar to the wood-pigeon, as Aristotle says.
<margin>1060</margin>
**Return]** <note>original: *Hypotropiê*</note> A turning back. That is, in flight.
**At dawn, the ruinous]** Together with the morning light, they saw their terrible mistake. Unspeakable.
**Thrice in bronze armor]** In bronze gear. This is a "hyperbaton" <note>a figure of speech where the natural word order is disrupted for emphasis</note>.
<margin>1070</margin>
The sequence should be: "having marched around in bronze gear." Which means 
running around.
**Performed funeral rites at the tomb]** They established a burial mound. To *tarchysai* means to bury; *ktereïxai* means to make a tomb and perform the rites over it, having made a grave for him.
The word **poured out** <note>original: *ekkekhytai*</note> is used in the Homeric style, referring to the ancient mound of earth safely heaped upon the ground. 
Deilochus <note>An early Greek historian</note> mentions the "meadowed plain" and also writes about the tomb of Cyzicus.
**Nor his wife Cleite]** Apollonius records that Cyzicus was a newlywed and childless, but Euphorion <note>A Hellenistic poet</note> says in his work *To Apollodorus* that he was about to be married. Some say Cleite was the daughter of Merops, others say she was a Thracian, the daughter of Iasus. Some say she did not suffer upon her husband's death, but was sent back home by her father. However, Evaines <note>A mythographer</note> agrees with Apollonius in his *Mythical Accounts*. Deilochus says of Cleite that she died of grief. Apollonius records that Cyzicus was killed childless, but Evaines says he left behind a son with the same name as himself. 
Regarding the fountain: it is a thing of wonder that such intense suffering and grief could stir a divine nature; or perhaps it is simply the nature of women to lament. Thus, the nymphs themselves joined the Doliones in mourning Cleite. Evaines and Deilochus record that Cleite hanged herself, and that there is a "Zote" fountain in Cyzicus which they call by her name.

# ARGONAUTICA

<margin>Regarding the name **Cleite** herself: she was named the same as the child. This was done because they wished to preserve the memory of the tragedy for a longer time; or it means "renowned," signifying something famous or notorious, arising from the extreme nature of her suffering and her devotion to her husband.</margin>
<margin>**Of mill-ground labor]** This refers to the fire—that is, the wheat. It means flour that has been shaped or ground by a millstone. He is referring to loaves of bread.</margin>
<margin>**Libations]** Properly, these are oils poured out along with water, as in this case; they are the offerings for the dead and the ritual pourings.</margin>
<margin>**Meal-cakes]** A certain kind of pastry. The Athenians call anything that has congealed a <unclear>pelanos</unclear>.</margin>
<margin>**Those dwelling in Cyzicus**, all the Cyzicenes. They are **Ionians** because they were colonists from Miletus. For Neleus led a colony to Miletus, and from there they went to Cyzicus after a long time. This is why he called the Milesians Ionians.</margin>

And for the men, the day from Zeus arrived. For not even
Did anyone endure to taste food, nor for a long time,
Out of their grief, did they remember the work of the mill-ground grain,
But they continued to live eating uncooked food just as they were.
<margin>1075</margin> Even now, whenever their annual libations are poured,
The Ionians dwelling in Cyzicus always, without fail,
Grind the meal for cakes at the communal mill.
From that time, harsh storms broke out
For twelve days and nights together; and these held them there,

Mopsus, son of Ampycus <note>Mopsus was the Argonauts' seer, capable of understanding the language of birds</note>, protected as they slumbered deeply.
And then, above the golden head of the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note>,

The ceasing of the stormy winds; and Mopsus understood,
Having heard the favorable omen of the coastal bird.
And the bird was turned back again by a god, and it perched above...

---

**Grinding for meal-cakes]** The whole community grinds and mills meal-cakes at the millstone. A "pelanos" is something congealed and gritty according to the Athenians; as Euripides says, "a foamy <term>pelanos</term> from the mouth" <note>original: "Στόματος ἀφρώδη πέλανον"</note>. He is speaking of unbaked and incomplete loaves of bread, like those Theocritus mentions in his Doric works. 
**Days together]** The word "together" <note>original: "ὁμοῦ"</note> in Homer signifies "in the same place" ("and together they held the swift horses"); but in writers after Homer, it signifies other things. For instance, Sophocles uses it to mean time; and <unclear>Golis</unclear> says "sometimes <unclear/> is full of mixtures, and sometimes of old things and strange things." But here it is used to mean "likewise," as in Euripides: "Old men and young men and mothers together."
**On the following]** This means on the coming night.
**The others indeed]** This type of contraction <note>original: "συναλοιφὴ"</note> belongs to the newer Ionian dialect. Because of this, they criticize Zenodotus <note>An Alexandrian grammarian known for editing Homer</note> for saying, "The other gods and men indeed" <note>original: "Ὦλλοι μέν ῥα θεοί τε καὶ ἀνέρες"</note>; for Homer did not use this form.
**Final bed]** They were taking their later lot and portion of sleep in Dolionia, sleeping there because they were meant to sail away the next day.
**Deeply slumbering]** He was guarding them as they slept greatly and deeply. But Tarrhaeus <note>A Greek grammarian</note> says it means sleeping lightly, like a <unclear>brambles</unclear>.
**The ceasing of the stirring]** The stopping and relief from the violence of the winds. For the bird is a sea-bird and lives on the shores. It is said that Zeus, for fifteen days—or as some say, fourteen—creates a period without wind so that the bird can give birth on the shores. These are called "Halcyon Days" during the time of birth, and some after the birth. The author took these details about halcyons from Pindar’s *Paeans*. He called the voice of the halcyon "the voice of the wives" because it had been sent by Hera, as Pindar says.
**Of the coastal bird]** Having heard the appropriate voice of the bird that lives by the shores and beaches.

<summary>The Argonauts remain stranded in Cyzicus due to storms, observing a ritual fast that becomes a local tradition. The seer Mopsus interprets the cry of a halcyon bird as a sign from the gods that the winds will finally cease.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>
**1090 Of the stern-ornament]** <note>original: Ἀφλάστοιο</note> Apollonius <note>likely Apollonius the Sophist, a grammarian</note> in his *Lexicon* has defined the *aphlaston* as the *akrostolion* <note>the decorative prow-tip</note>. This is not correct; for the *akrostolion* is part of the *stolos* <note>the prow-post</note>. The *stolos* is the wood that projects from the *pyche* and extends to the prow. The *pyche* is where the name of the ship is inscribed. Therefore, the *akrostolion* is at the prow, while the *aphlaston* is at the stern. The poet <note>Homer</note> also presents it as being at the stern, saying: "Hector, once he seized the stern, would not let go, holding the *aphlaston* in his hands" <note>Iliad 15.716-717</note>. The word *aphlaston* is said to be formed by contraction from *a-thlaston* <note>meaning "un-crushed"</note>, used ironically because it is actually very easily crushed <note>original: εὐθλαστόν</note>. Thus, the *aphlaston* is a small decorative board at the stern of the ship.
</margin>

...darting high above the **stern** of the ship.
But he <note>Mopsus the seer</note>, seeing him <note>Jason</note> reclined on soft fleeces of sheep,
Shook him and woke him at once, and spoke thus:
"Son of Aeson, you must climb to this sacred place
On chilly Mount Dindymum to appease the well-throned
Mother of all the blessed gods <note>Rhea, the Mother of the Gods</note>; then the violent
Storms shall cease. For such a voice I just now heard
From the sea-halcyon <note>the kingfisher bird</note>, which, while you slept,
Flew in circles above you, announcing each detail."

<margin>
**1110 For from her, both winds...]** From this goddess, Rhea, the earth, the sea, and the sky are held together. For the natural philosophers <note>scholars who interpreted myths as physical laws</note> explain her through "physiology" as the harmony and bond of all things. They explain her name etymologically as coming from "to flow" <note>original: ῥεῖν, rhein</note> and "to make an attempt" <note>original: πεῖρα, peira</note>. Physically, they say that Cronus is her husband, representing "Time" <note>original: Κρόνον... χρόνον</note>, through a change of a single letter. Time follows the order of the elements by necessity. Furthermore, they say that allegorically, these forms are the parents of the sea, sky, and underworld gods. For after the arrangement and binding of the elements, it happened that men learned of and honored the gods and their divine powers. The word **are bound** <note>original: πεπείρηται</note> is used instead of "are held together" or "are yoked." 
**From the sacred rock]** He mentioned this in the previous lines, saying: "and even now it is called the Sacred Rock." 
**They rowed]** They moved the oars. The author uses a specific past tense <note>the aorist</note> here instead of the imperfect. 
He calls it the **Thracian harbor** because Cyzicus lies at the edge of Phrygia, and Bithynia joins Phrygia. The Bithynians are Thracians living on the right side. Or it is because Thracians once inhabited Cyzicus. 
**And the whole opposite shore]** Meaning the shore of Thrace; all the land facing Thrace. The Macrones are a tribe living near the Black Sea.
</margin>

For from her the winds, the sea, and all the earth
Below are bound, as is the snowy seat of Olympus.
And when she ascends from the mountains into the Great Heaven,
Zeus himself, the son of Cronus, gives way. And likewise the other
Immortal blessed ones attend the dread goddess.
So he spoke; and the word was welcome to him as he heard it.
He rose from his bed with joy; and he roused his comrades,
Urging them all, and as they woke he spoke to them
Of the prophecy of Mopsus, the son of Ampycus.
And quickly the younger men, driving oxen from the stalls,
Led them from there up to the steep peak of the mountain.
While others loosed the cables from the sacred rock,
And rowed to the Thracian harbor; and they themselves
Disembarked, leaving a few of their comrades in the ship.
To them, the Macrian heights and the whole opposite shore...

<margin>
**1114 On their right]** <note>original: χερσυνέ αἷς</note> He means "on their own right hand side."
**Misty mouth of the Bosporus]** <note>original: Στόμα Βοοσπόρου ἠερόεν</note> This means hazy or foggy.
**Bosporus]** This name means "Ox-path" <note>original: βοὸς πόρος</note>, so called because of Io, who swam across it in the form of a cow.
**1120 From the other side]** <note>original: Ἐκ δ᾿ ἑτέρης</note> This refers to the other continent, Europe; for Mysia and the river Aesepus are in Asia. He is speaking of another region, the Troad, through which the Aesepus flows, separating it from Mysia. Homer also mentions the Granicus and the Aesepus. The Troad begins where Mysia [ends]...

Thracian [lands] appeared before their eyes on their right.
The misty mouth of the Bosporus appeared, and the Mysian
hills. From the other side, the stream of the river Aesepus,
The city, and the Nepeian plain of Adrasteia.

---

...beginning from the great [mountains] and ending at the Aesepus. Dolionia and Phrygia begin at the Aesepus and end at the Rhyndacus. There are two Mysias: the European and the Asian. It was the hills of the Asian Mysia that appeared to the Argonauts. **The Nepeian plain** <note>original: πεδίον Νηπήϊον</note> is a plain near Cyzicus. Callimachus also mentions it in his *Hecale*: "the famous Adrasteia beneath the hill of Nepeia." Dionysius of Miletus says that Nepeia is a plain in Mysia. Olympus, the king of the Mysians, married the daughter of Tasos, whose name was Nepeia; he settled in this plain which is now called the Nepeian Plain. Apollodorus, however, says the Nepeian plain is in Phrygia. Callimachus says in his commentaries that Nemesis is the goddess who holds this plain. There is also a city called Adrasteia, named after the man who founded it. Apollonius mentions both: the city and the plain. For he says: "The city and the Nepeian plain of Adrasteia." Homer also mentions the city: "And those who held Adrasteia." **Sturdy stump** <note>original: Στιβαρὸν στύπος</note>: *stypos* means the trunk or stem from which they stripped the wood. **Statue** <note>original: βρέτας</note>: something that resembles a mortal <note>original: βροτῷ ἐοικός</note>. Following this, Euphorion says that the wooden image of the Mother of the Gods is made of vine-wood, perhaps because the vine is sacred to Rhea. **Prochnu** <note>original: πρόχνυ</note> means "entirely." **Ancient tree** <note>original: γεράνδρυον</note> means old wood. **On a hill** <note>original: Κολωνῷ</note>: on the projecting ridge. **Of stones** <note>original: Χεράδος</note>: *cheras* is a collection of small stones, those that can be picked up one by one in the hand; Homer calls these *chermadia*. He uses "altar" to mean the construction of an altar. Or *cherades* are called small heaps of stones. Demetrius of Skepsis says this is an Apollonian dialect; Sappho also mentions it in Pontus: "lest it be empty of stones." And Homer: "you poured heaps of stones around." *Cherados* is a heap of stones. They piled up stones for the construction of the altar. **With oak leaves** <note>original: Δρυΐνοισιν</note>: appropriately, for the oak is sacred to Rhea, as Apollodorus says in the 15th book of *On the Gods*. He says they are crowned with oak because this tree is assigned to the goddess; therefore, it is useful for light, for warmth, and for all things. **Dindymene**: she who is honored on Mount Dindymum, from which she is named and petitioned. **Inhabitant of Phrygia, and Tityas together**: he is clearly speaking about the ones called the **Idaean Dactyls** <note>Legendary metalworkers and attendants of the goddess Mother</note> and companions to the Mother of the Gods. He follows Menander, who says the Milesians, when they sacrifice to Rhea, offer a preliminary sacrifice to Titias.

# BOOK ONE

...and Cyllenus. They are some of the Idaean Dactyls, whom some call the "dispensers of fate" <note>original: moiraghetai</note> and companions of the Mother of the Gods. Callistratus, in the second book of his *History of Heracleia*, says of Tipias <note>likely the hero Tityas, a common attendant of the goddess</note>: "Tipias, a local hero, whom some mythologize as a son of Zeus, and others as the eldest of the Mariandyni, children of Cimmerius; it was because of him that the nation grew, and he is still granted divine honors." Promathidas also speaks of who Tipias was in his works on Heracleia, as does Theophanes. He was deified by the Mariandyni. Stesimbrotus records that a certain nymph of the Oiaxian land <note>Oiaxis is an ancient name for Axos in Crete</note>, having grasped the dust of the Idaean woods, produced the Dactyls; he says they were called "Dactyls" <note>meaning "Fingers"</note> because she squeezed them through her fingers. Sophocles calls them "Phrygians" in his play *The Mute Satyrs*.

**D**actyls of Ida, Cretans, whom once the nymph
Anchiale, in the Dictean cave, with both her hands
Grasping the Oiaxian earth, brought into being.
Jason <note>original: Aisonides</note> prepared many things with prayers to turn aside 
The vengeful spirits <term>ergolas: interpreted as "avengers" or "spirits of labor"</term>, pouring libations upon the burning
Sacrifices. At the same time, the youths, at Orpheus' command,
Leaped in a rhythmic armored dance,
Clashing their swords against their shields, so that the ill-omened
Cry of mourning might be scattered through the air, for the people 
Still wept for their king <note>King Cyzicus, accidentally killed by the Argonauts</note>. Henceforth, the Phrygians evermore
Appease Rhea with the bullroarer and the drum.

...Hellanicus says. Others say they were called Idaean Dactyls <note>Fingers</note> because, meeting Rhea on Mount Ida, they welcomed the goddess by touching her fingers. According to Mnaseas in his first book *On Asia*, they are called Idaean Dactyls after their father Dactylus and their mother Ida. The author of the *Phoronis* writes as follows: "Where the Idaean sorcerers, Phrygian men of the mountains, had their home: Kelmis, and great Damnameneus, and the overbearing Akmon, skillful servants of mountain Adrastina <note>A title for the goddess Rhea or a nymph attendant</note>. They were the first to find the craft of wise Hephaestus in the mountain glens—the violet-colored iron—and they brought it to the fire and demonstrated a magnificent work." <term>Dictean</term>] The Cretan cave. Dicte is a mountain in Crete. <term>Draxamene</term>] (Grasping) It is the custom for pregnant women to hold onto nearby objects to relieve their labor pains, just as Leto held onto the palm tree. It was necessary to say *Oiaxidos*; the *iota* was added. <term>Eblastesen</term>] (Brought forth) instead of "gave birth." <term>Ergolas</term>] This is read in various ways; the heavy <note>grave</note> accentuation prevails. <term>Orpheus' command</term>] At the instruction of Orpheus, as he was the leader of the dance. <term>Betarmon</term>] (Rhythmic dance) The dance itself, named from its "running step." He is referring to the *pyrrhic* <note>warrior</note> dance. The following part means: they danced while striking their shields with their swords because the mourning for Cyzicus was being shouted by the Doliones; this was done so that during the sacrifice, no ill-omened sound would reach the goddess. Hence the Phrygians appease Rhea with cymbals and drums. <term>Rhombos</term>] (Bullroarer) The *rhombos* is a wooden piece <note>original: helix</note> that they whirl, striking it with leather thongs, thus producing a roaring sound. Some call the instrument itself a *rhombos*, including Eupolis in *The Baptists* and Didymus.

# THE ARGONAUTICA

<margin>
**Antaea**] Rhea is called this because she was sacrificed to in **opposition** to the Telchines <note>The Telchines were mythical smiths and sorcerers often portrayed as hostile to the gods</note>. As some say, it is **Autaea**, meaning she who is reached through **litany** and petition.
**The signs were heard**] Through this, the poet says nothing other than the very nature of the goddess. And the natural philosophers say she is the same as the **Earth**. The sign of her peak power is that the trees bore fruit and the grass grew **spontaneously**. 
**Tender**] Meaning soft and green. 
**Lairs**] The hiding places of wild beasts. 
**Thickets**] The wooded places in the mountains. The phrase is "leaving their lairs and their thickets." He demonstrates the wonder through many details: the **thirsty** land, and that the water given was not a small amount, but **ceaseless**. 
**It flowed**] This comes from the word for "it ran," as in Homer: "and all the vessels **flowed** with it." Or, one must interpret "flowed" as "made to flow," so that Dindymon became **overflowing** with water. 
**Gushed forth**] Meaning it was given up from the earth. 
**Thirsty**] This signifies the dry earth. 
**Island**] He seems to be referring to Cyzicus here. 
**Storm-footed**] Meaning the swift ones. 
**Overtook**] Meaning they caught up. 
**Violent breezes**] Those that are heavily burdensome and blowing hard. Properly, **zachrees** refers to what is done violently by the **hands**. For the word is formed from "hands" <note>original: "cheiras"</note> and the intensive prefix "za-". 
**They rested**] Meaning they ceased. 
**He pulled**] In comparison to the momentum of all the others and the resistance of the waves, the word **pulled** provides greater emphasis. Callimachus says this regarding a defeated bull: "he followed, sluggish with pain."
</margin>

> **T**rees poured forth boundless fruit, and around their feet
> **T**he earth spontaneously grew flowers of **tender** grass.
> **W**ild beasts, leaving their **lairs** and their **thickets**,
<margin>1145</margin>

> **M**iracle; for never before did water flow on 
> **D**indymon, but then it **gushed forth** for them; from the **thirsty**
> **P**eak it flowed unceasingly. And men of later times

The word order is changed by transposition, as in: "the earth **flowed** with blood." This always means "blood **ran** upon the earth."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Argonauts' journey. Following their departure from the land of the Doliones, the narrative focuses on Heracles’ immense strength during a rowing competition, which leads to the breaking of his oar near the mouth of the Rhyndacus river.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>
1165 **Rhyndacian**] Rhyndacus is a place in Phrygia mentioned by Bacchylides; in truth, it is the tomb of Briareus <note>A hundred-armed giant of Greek myth</note> at the entrance. Callimachus records the history of the river in his work *On the Rivers of Asia*, as does Demetrius of Scepsis in his *Arrangement*. Alternatively: Rhyndacus is a river of Phrygia now called Megistos <note>The "Greatest" river</note>, near the mouth of which is the tomb of the hero Mysus, son of Aegaeon.
</margin>

> Looking upon the **Rhyndacian** outpourings and the great **mound** of Aegaeon,
> they were just passing out of Phrygia, 
> when then, heaving up the furrows of the roughened swell,
> he broke his oar from the middle; one piece he himself 
> held in both hands as he fell sideways, but the other the sea
<margin>1170</margin>
> washed away, carrying it in the back-surging waves. He sat up in silence,
> gazing around; for his hands, now still, were trembling. 
> As when from the field a gardener or a ditch-digger 
> goes gladly to his hut, craving his supper;
> and there at the entrance he bends his weary knees,
<margin>1175</margin>
> parched with dust, and looking at his blistered hands, 
> he heaps many curses on his belly.

---

**Tomb**] Rhyndacus is similar to the name Aeacus. **And the great mound**] Some manuscripts read "the great peak" <note>original: "rion"</note>. It is possible the poet changed it, or a scribe’s error left the letter "eta" <note>forming "erion," meaning mound or tomb</note>. The myth concerning Aegaeon is reported by Demetrius of Cnidus. Conon, in his *History of Heraclea*, says that Aegaeon was cast into the sea by Poseidon, and was buried at the place now called the "Mound of Aegaeon" by Apollonius, though he also calls him Briareus. Concerning the naming of the Aegean Sea, he writes in his own research on the islands: "Some say the Aegean Sea is named after the goat <note>original: "aigos"</note> of Percania; others after Carisia, who was called Aegaea." Some say the city of Aegae, from which they say Poseidon comes, is in the Peloponnese, others place it near Crisa. Some say it is because the sea looks like a "hand" <note>original: "cheira"</note> stretched out. Hesiod says Aegaeon was the son of Uranus and Gaia <note>Sky and Earth</note>. Briareus, Aegaeon, and Gyges are all names used for the same being. Eumelus, however, in his *Titanomachy*, says Aegaeon was the child of Earth and Sea, dwelling in the deep and fighting as an ally of the Titans. He also says in a dithyramb that he was summoned from the sea by Thetis to ascend and guard Zeus, being a child of the sea. Others call him a sea monster. Tarraeus says that in his old age, fleeing from Euboea, he came to Phrygia and died there.

**Just a little out of Phrygia**] That is, a short distance from Phrygia. For as Homer states, Phrygia lies very close to Mysia. Thus, people say they are both the same region because they are so near. **Passing out**] They were sailing past. **Heaving up**] Moving the oar during the stroke and cutting through the waves and eddies. **Roughened**] Meaning the sea was becoming rough and violent. **Furrows**] The blasts or the rising and lofting of the waves. The phrase **from the middle** emphasizes both the danger of the sea and the hero's strength. **Piece**] The broken fragment of the oar. **Broke from the middle**] For this reason, they say Heracles was left behind in Cius. Others say it happened at Aphetae, because he made the ship *Argo* tip to one side. Ephorus, in his first book, claims he was left behind because of his service to Omphale. **Still, they were trembling**] His hands had a "breathless" quality of stillness <note>original: "aeteson"</note> due to the hero's innate power. **At the entrance**] At the door and the porch. The outer parts of a gate are called *promolai*, as the poet says in the following lines: "He stood at the entrance <note>original: "promolesin"</note>, and they leaned against it." **Weary**] Referring to one exhausted by toil. **Parched**] Dried out and neglected. **Blistered**] Hands squeezed and heavily burdened by labor. **Heaped many curses**] Instead of "he prayed," here it means he cursed his stomach, or spoke to it.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Argonauts’ voyage along the coast of Asia Minor. Having left the land of the Doliones (modern-day Erdek), they arrive at the territory of the Cianians in Mysia. This section provides both the poetic narrative of their arrival and the scholarly commentary (scholia) explaining the geography, local history, and the specific actions of Heracles as he seeks to replace his broken oar.</meta>

# BOOK ONE OF THE ARGONAUTICA

<column-break/>

**The haunts of the Cianian land**] A poetic way of referring to the city of **Cios** <note>original: "Kios"; a Greek city on the coast of Bithynia, modern-day Gemlik in Turkey</note>. This is a city in **Mysia**, named after **Cius**, who led the colony of the Milesians, as **Aristotle** records in his *Constitution of the Cianians*. It was first inhabited by **Mysians**, then by **Carians**, and then by their neighbors the **Milesians**. There is also a river of the same name flowing around Mysia, mentioned by **Scylax of Caryanda** <note>A 6th-century BCE explorer and geographer</note>. This river also flows around the city itself.

**Around the Arganthonian**] A mountain in Cios.

**Provisions for them**] Supplies. Food. It can also mean chaff, as in **Homer**: "as the chaff-heap is shaken."

**Dry**] Completely parched wood.

**Bedding foliage**] Leaves suitable for beds and mats, derived from the word for "bed" <note>original: "lechos"</note>.

**To be spread**] The word "as" is missing; the sense is "so as to be spread."

**They were twirling**] Instead of "they were rubbing." They would rub the wood together to start a fire. For the poet says these **fire-sticks** <note>original: "pyreia"</note> are rubbed against one another to generate fire. One part is the base, called the **spreader** <note>original: "storeus"</note>, and the other is like a **drill**, which they twist while pressing it against the spreader.

**Son of Zeus**] He refers to **Heracles**.

**Might anticipate**] Meaning he might get a head start on the voyage.

**Handy**] That which fits the hand.

**Wandering**] Either because he was unfamiliar with the region, or in the sense of roaming around until he found something suitable.

**Poplar**] Named from "springing up from the earth" <note>original: "era"</note> and moving. Or perhaps from being broken by the winds.

**He stripped off the skin**] The sequence is: "he stripped off the lion’s skin."

**Bronze-weighted**] Meaning strong, or weighted with bronze at the end. **Peisander** <note>An early epic poet</note> says the club of Heracles was made entirely of bronze. Some etymologize the word for club <note>original: "ropalon"</note> from "downward weight" <note>original: "rope"</note> and "threshing."

**From the ground**] From the earth, or the root.

**Trunk**] The stem.

**Obstacle**] A hindrance <note>here referring to the clods of earth clinging to the roots</note>.

**Unexpectedly**] All at once.

<margin>**Which they call Pegae**]</margin> The name of the spring is "Pegae" <note>literally "Springs"</note>, used here as a proper noun. **Neighbors nearby**: those who live in the surrounding area. **Caves**: <note>original: "enaulous"</note> refers here to grottos. **Wood-watchers**: those who dwell in the mountains. **Fair-flowing**: beautiful-streaming. **Watery**: the name [or type] of the nymph. **Radiant**: refers to him [Hylas] being shining or glowing. **Mid-month**: the full moon. **Cypris**: the passion of love. **Leaning to one side**: leaning sideways toward the spring. The meaning is: as he lowered the water-jar into the spring, and as the water filled the vessel with a loud sound, the nymph grabbed his neck with her left hand and kissed him (so he says), and with her right hand she dragged him down into the water. **Immediately she**: Theocritus, in his *Idylls* in the poem titled *Hylas*, says he was snatched by *all* the nymphs. Onasus, in the first book of his *Amazonica*, says that Hylas fell in and remained underwater. Nicander, in the second book of his *Changes*, also says he was snatched by all the nymphs; but Apollonius says it was by only one. **Tender**: soft; this does not just mean "young."

"...does he take heed," because he was focused on the departure of Jason's voyage, and not on the rest of his companions. "Sometimes without stopping, at other times standing still," because at times he ran until he was weary, and at other times he stood. "He sends forth a bellow," because he would occasionally shout, calling for Hylas. "Immediately the morning star," referring to the star of the dawn. The logic of the sequence is: as the morning star appeared by the mountain ridges, immediately the breezes arrived. Quickly Tiphys urged them to go on board and set sail.
**They backed the cables**] He described the subsequent action by means of the preceding one; instead of saying, "they loosened the sail."
**From the ship**] Meaning they hoisted the anchors and moved the ship from its mooring. Ephorus <note>An ancient Greek historian.</note> is ridiculous for thinking that Anacharsis <note>A Scythian philosopher who visited Athens in the 6th century BCE.</note> was the first to invent the anchor for naval travel. For the Argonauts are older than Anacharsis.
**When bright-eyed dawn from heaven**] He calls the dawn "bright-eyed" <note>original: "charope"</note> because it brightens the air and provides light. The terms "gray-blue" <note>original: "glaukon"</note> and "bright-eyed" are used synonymously; for both refer to brightness. Therefore he adds "gleaming" <note>original: "diaglaussoisin"</note> instead of "illuminating" or "shining through." This is also why Athena is "bright-eyed" <note>original: "glaukopis"</note>; the "gleam" <note>original: "glene"</note> is the pupil of the eye, from "to gleam" <note>original: "glausein"</note>, which means to shine. Euripides also used this for the moon: "the bright-eyed moon revolves."
**Horizon**] According to some, this signifies the hemisphere beneath the earth; but primarily it means the East. For it is the limit <note>original: "peras"</note> of the heaven's movement; for it comes from there and ends there.

But he, stunned by helplessness, did not speak a word, not one, the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note>; but he sat eating his heart out with heavy affliction deep within. But anger seized Telamon, and thus he spoke:
<margin>(1290)</margin> "Truly you sit there at ease, since it was convenient for you to leave Heracles behind; your plan has succeeded, so that his glory throughout Greece might not overshadow you, if the gods should grant us a return home. <column-break/>

<margin>1285</margin> **Anger seized Telamon**] For he was a very close companion of Heracles, who also fought alongside him in many labors, sailed with him to Ilium <note>Troy</note>, and fought the Amazons; he also slew Alcyoneus, as Pindar also records. Theocritus showed their friendship, saying, "They both, being companions, always shared <margin>1295</margin> one table." The meaning of the speech is: you sit here quietly as if by chance. Apollonius says that Heracles was left behind at Cios, <margin>1300</margin> having gone out in search of Hylas. Dionysius of Mitylene, however, says that the hero sailed with the best of the men as far as the Colchians, and assisted Jason in the matters regarding Medea. Demaratus says the same. But Herodorus says he did not sail at all with the others. Hesiod, in the *Marriage of Ceyx*, says he went out in search of water and was left behind in Magnesia at the place called Aphetae <note>the "Place of Setting Sail"</note> because of his departure. Antimachus, in the *Lyde*, says Heracles was put off the ship because the *Argo* was weighed down <note>original: "katabareshthai"</note> by the hero’s weight. Posidippus the epigram-writer followed this, as did Pherecydes. Ephorus, in his seventh book, says he was left behind voluntarily with Omphale, the queen of the Lydians. Uniquely, Anticleides in the second book of his *Delian Matters* says it was Hyllus, the son of Heracles, who went for water and did not return. **So that his glory might not [overshadow you]**] This is spoken impiously and craftily by one who is anxious; he brings the argument back to the "sickness" <note>envy</note> of Jason, so as to further disparage the action. For it made no difference to you to be surpassed by Heracles in Scythia, but nevertheless it would bring shame upon you later, when we returned to Greece. Therefore, you have neglected the common safety of all for the sake of your own lack of reputation. **But what use is there in words**] Herodian, in his twentieth book, says that neutral disyllables ending in -os, starting with a naturally long vowel, take the smooth breathing: *aichos* (shame), *ethos* (custom), *ouros* (limit), *eidos* (form). So it is with *edos* (delight/pleasure). But *ethmos* (sieve) takes the rough breathing, even though it has the 'e' before the 'th', because the future *heso* is aspirated. The word "to you" is omitted. The sense is: but what delight is there for me in so many words? For I will go without those who plotted this trick with you. **Gleams** <note>original: "liges"</note>] The flashes. In other places, the word signifies curls of hair—"from the curls <note>original: "osligon"</note> the oil always flows." Herodian says this in the second book of his *General Grammar*. In Apollonius and Philetas, the words *aps* (back) and *opiso* (backwards) are used side-by-side <note>a pleonasm</note>. **Forcing through the deep**] Instead of "fighting against the pressing wind and forcing a way." The "deep" <note>original: "laitma"</note> is the hollow of the sea and its distance, as if it were a "cut" <note>original: "latmema"</note>. Or it comes from being "struck" <note>original: "latypesthai"</note> by the waves, which means to be hit. Silenus, in his *Glossary*, calls it the open sea, and Irenaeus, in the first book of his commentary on Apollonius, has given the same explanation. **Had not the [sons] of Thracian [Boreas]**] Heracles later killed Zetes and Calais, finding them around the island of Tenos, which lies near Delos, because Heracles bore a grudge against them...

# THE ARGONAUTICA

[Notes on] Boreas. Homer [says], "The storm-wind having persuaded you along with the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note>." But Aenesidemus, in his *History of Tenos*, says that they hosted Heracles but then grew restless and wished to kill him.

---

<margin>
Regarding the "Games of Pelias," until the line "Around them": Apollonius says that Heracles killed the sons of Boreas <note>The Boreads: Zetes and Calais</note> because they prevented the ship from turning back to Mysia [to find him].
But Semus says it was because Heracles was beaten by the Boreads in a race. Stesimbrotus says they had a dispute with Heracles regarding the gifts given by Jason to the finest of the heroes.
Nicander of Colophon, in the first book of the *Oetaica*, says that Boreas [the North Wind] himself was the cause of the death of the aforementioned [sons], because he sent a storm against Heracles at Kos as he was returning. "Having fallen" <note>original: "Dedonpotos"</note>] means after his death.

---

[Regarding the line] "Returning from [the games of] Pelias": Heracles encountered the Boreads as they were traveling to their homeland after the funeral games, and being reminded of this very thing—that they had prevented the search for him—he slew them on the island of Tenos. "Two pillars" <note>stelae</note>]: one of the two is a tomb on the island of Tenos and a monument; it happens that one of them is moved by the wind of Boreas, their father. "And these things were destined"]: this line is from Callimachus. It is a common error among all poets after Homer to lengthen the initial vowel of verbs in the present tense because of the 'i' <note>a technical grammatical point regarding the augment in the imperfect tense</note>. "But to them Glaucus"]: Glaucus was the son of Polybus, of the race of Anthedon (Anthedon is a Boeotian city; as Homer says, "and furthest Anthedon"); he was a fisherman by trade. Once, after failing to catch many fish, he grew tired on the road and set down his burden of fish. One of them, having eaten a certain immortal herb, came back to life. Glaucus took some and ate it himself, and he too became a god. Then, as he began to reach extreme old age and could no longer bear it, he threw himself into the sea and was honored as a sea-spirit <note>daimon</note>. They say the "Glaucus fish" is named after him. "Roaring" <note>original: "Brychies"</note>]: sounding deep. "Keel" <note>original: "Neiou"</note>]: he refers to the part of the ship that is dragged through the water. "Why... against the will of great [Zeus]"]: from where, or why ever, do you interpret the will of Zeus in a way that goes beyond it? "At Argos it is his fate"]: Apollonius himself says in the *Catalogue of Heroes* that Heracles, while performing his labors, left them aside to join the best of the heroes. "If he completes a few more"]: meaning if he finishes the small number of labors he has left to do for himself.

> —it is placed there or even for future time, when the joining conjunction "an" is brought out with it. "Whenever [an] you come." It ought therefore to use the joining word "ei" [if]. "If you would not endure it for me, O goddess." Whether alive etc.] "The fate of Hylas" <note>original: "hula moron"</note>; for the rest, one must hear this as "portion" or "fate." For it is shaped from "moira" [fate], like the word for "gate" in Homer, "having thrown it at the gate among the dead" <note>original: "en pulō en nekouessi balōn"</note>. Thus "moron" means fate, whether of one living or dead. Or whatever his fate was, whether living or dead. In exchange for him, they gave pledges] instead of saying they gave hostages to Heracles so that he would not keep searching. The prefix "epi-" is redundant. Seeking] <term>masteuontes</term>; searching. From which "masys" also means the search. Callimachus says, "At another time I grew weary in the wandering of the search" <note>original: "Masuos allot’ ekamon alētui"</note>. This is also why breasts are called <term>mastoi</term>, because they are necessarily "sought" by children <note>This is an example of ancient folk etymology linking the word for "seeking" with "breasts."</note>. And "he shall search the mountain-ridges." He has not used the word "there" <note>original: "autothi"</note> soundly; for it indicates the present place, equivalent to "to remain here." "Lest perhaps we miss one another." He ought to have named the distant place, as in, "where shepherd calls to shepherd." Pledges] <term>rhysia</term>; the things given as security in place of something else to prevent an abduction. Since the people of Cios were at a loss before Heracles, they swore not to stop seeking Hylas, and they maintain a concern for the people of Trachis because the hostages were settled there by Heracles; the assembly of the Cians relates this history. The ship all day long] the sense is this: the wind carried the ship through the whole day and night, blowing violently. But when day appeared, it did not blow even a little, but ceased into stillness. Ran aground] they poured out and were filled. Or, seeing the shore jutting out, seeing it lying open and slanted, and turning to their oars, they brought the ship to harbor.

<column-break/>

COMMENTARY
on the second book of
Apollonius’s
Argonautica.

The main points of the 
second book of the 
Argonautica are these: 
Amycus, the leader 
of the Bebrycians, 
fights a boxing 
match with Polydeuces <note>Also known as Pollux, the twin brother of Castor and a champion boxer</note> 
and is killed. Because of him, 

<column-break/>

a battle breaks out between the Argonauts and the Bebrycians; the Argonauts slay many of them, and the rest flee. Afterward, the Argonauts arrive at the home of Phineus, who had been blinded in his eyes; he begs them to help him. For the Harpies <note>Terrifying winged spirits or "snatchers"</note> would appear from some unseen place and snatch away his food, leaving him without a taste. He knew, being a seer, by whose hands it was fated they would be driven off; when he pleaded, the sons of Boreas <note>Zetes and Calais, the winged sons of the North Wind</note> pursued them. In the meantime, Phineus explains the voyage to Colchis to them. When the sons of Boreas return, they recount how they overcame the Harpies. Next follow the stories concerning Cyrene, daughter of Hypsius, and Aristaeus, the son of Apollo and Cyrene herself; and the myths concerning the Etesian winds <note>Strong, cool seasonal winds of the Aegean</note>; and how they sailed through the Symplegades <note>The "Clashing Rocks" that crushed ships passing between them</note>; and how they arrived at the island in the Thynian region, and Apollo appeared to them; there, after establishing a sanctuary, they named the god "of the Dawn." Then follow the events in Mariandynia and the Acherusian headland there; and how Lycus, the king of this land, received them most kindly; for they had punished his enemy, Amycus; and how Idmon the seer and Tiphys the pilot die in Mariandynia. The following sections tell of the customs of the Chalybes, Tibareni, and Mossynoeci, and the mythical birds on the Island of Ares, and how they were driven off by the Argonauts. And how the sons of Phrixus and Chalciope (Medea’s sister), while sailing to Orchomenus, were shipwrecked. Having been brought to the Island of Ares, they met the Argonauts and recognized one another. "Dwelling" <note>original: "aulis"</note> refers to a place of residence or a lifestyle. "King of the Bebrycians": Amycus ruled the Bebrycians, holding Bithynia and the coastal regions at that time. Some Bebrycians also lived near Lydia in the areas close to Ephesus and Magnesia. Charon <note>Charon of Lampsacus, an early Greek historian</note> says that the land of the Lampsacenes was formerly called Bebrycia, named after the Bebrycians who lived there. Their race vanished because of continuous wars and attacks from other nations. "Haughty" <note>original: "agenoros"</note>: meaning arrogant or proud. "Bithynian Ash-nymph": it is unclear if this is a proper name; he calls her Melia because certain nymphs are called Meliae <note>Ash-tree nymphs</note> after Melia, the daughter of Oceanus, as Callimachus <note>A famous scholar and poet of the Library of Alexandria</note> says.

...either because she spent time around apple trees, like the Hamadryads <note>Nymphs who live in trees</note>. But she is called "Bithynian" because she belonged to the race of the Bithynians. He [the poet] called Poseidon "God of Lineage" <note>original: "Genethlios"</note> because he rules over moisture and all nourishment, and he is the cause of generation, insofar as water is the generator of all things.
