# THE ARGONAUTICA

<page-num>118</page-num>
<header>ARGONAUTICA</header>

<margin>
**The Overseer:** <note>original: "Epopsios"</note> One who watches over or looks upon. **As much as a covering:** A deficient and very small debt or garment. **Having embarked:** This participle is used as a verb, meaning "we have boarded." **1130 Having embarked upon the Ram:** Dionysius says in his *Argonautica* that there was a man named Krios <note>The Greek word for "Ram" is *Krios*</note> who helped Phrixus. This man, feeling shame at the plot of Ino, suggested that Phrixus should make his escape; hence the myth was told that he was saved by a ram. But Herodorus says that children were born to Athamas and Themisto: Schoeneus, Erythrios, Leucon, and Ptoios; the youngest were Phrixus and Helle. They departed because of Ino's plot. They say Helle died at Pantylo, as Hellanicus also testifies. The children of Ino and Athamas were Learchus and Melicertes. **The Golden One:** It is said that the fleece of the ram became gold through the touch of Hermes.
</margin>

"We entreat you by Zeus the Overseer, <note>Zeus *Epopsios* is the god who watches over human conduct and protects those in need.</note> whoever you
Of men may be, to be kind and to help those in want.
For harsh storms, breaking over the rough sea,
Have scattered all the timbers of our reckless ship,
<margin>1130</margin> Wherein we were laboring, having embarked upon a common need.
Therefore we now fall at your knees, if you will listen,
To give us at least some covering for our bodies, and to help us,
Pitying men of your own age who are in misfortune.
But respect us as suppliant strangers for the sake of Zeus
<margin>1135</margin> The Guardian of Strangers <note>original: *Xenios*</note> and of Suppliants. To Zeus belong both suppliants
And strangers; and he, I suppose, is also an Overseer to us."
Then the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note> questioned him wisely in return,
Suspecting that the prophecies of Phineus <note>The blind seer from earlier in the epic who gave the Argonauts directions.</note> were being fulfilled:
"All these things we will provide for you immediately and gladly.
<margin>1140</margin> But come, tell me truly, in what part of the earth
Do you dwell, and what business drove you to sail across the sea?
Tell me also your own famous names and your lineage."
And Argos addressed him, being helpless in his misery:
"That Phrixus, son of Aeolus, reached the land of Aea from Hellas,
<margin>1145</margin> I truly think you have heard for yourselves before now.
Phrixus, who came to the city of Aeetes,
Riding upon a ram; which Hermes then made golden,
And the fleece you might even now still see,
Stretched out with its thick wool upon the branches of an oak.
<margin>1150</margin> This ram he then sacrificed, by its own promptings,
To Zeus, the God of Flight <note>original: *Phyxios*</note>, above all others. And him
Aeetes received in his palace, and gave him his daughter
Chalciope in marriage without a dowry, in the gladness of his heart."

---

**By his own promptings:** He sacrificed the ram (the poet says) according to the ram's own suggestions. That is, according to the advice of the ram itself. For the ram itself, having used a human voice, commanded him to do this. **The God of Flight above all:** Zeus Phyxios <note>The protector of those in flight or exile.</note> among the Thessalians, either because they once fled the flood in the time of Deucalion, or because Phrixus fled to him for refuge. **Chalciope:** Pherecydes says in his sixth book that she was called Iolia. Her surnames were Chalciope and Ophiousa.

### BOOK TWO

...in the foothills of the Caucasus, where the Typhaonian rock stands.
There, they say that Typhaon <note>Also known as Typhon, a monstrous giant with a hundred dragon heads who challenged Zeus for control of the cosmos</note>, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus, son of Cronus,
When he stretched out his mighty hands against the god,
Dripped warm blood from his head; and in this state he reached
The mountains and the Nysaean plain, where even now
He lies submerged beneath the waters of the Serbonian lake <note>A vast coastal lagoon in ancient Egypt, often associated in myth with the burial of monsters</note>.
So he spoke; and a pale chill seized the cheeks of many
At once, when they heard of such an ordeal. But Peleus
Answered boldly with words, and spoke thus:
"Do not, noble youth, be so greatly disheartened in your soul.
For we do not expect to be so lacking in strength as to be
Inferior to those who have never been tested in immortal armor.
But I believe that we too, being skilled in war,
Will go there, having been born from the blood of the blessed gods.
Therefore, if he does not grant the Golden Fleece out of friendship,
I do not expect the tribes of the Colchians to be of any help to him."
Thus they spoke to one another in turn,
Until they had had their fill of dinner and fell asleep.
But at dawn, a favorable wind blew for them as they awoke.
They raised the sails, and the canvas was stretched tight
By the force of the wind; quickly they left behind the Island of Mars.
And as night came on, they passed the Island of Philyra.
There, the son of Uranus, Cronus, once lived with Philyra, not in Olympus—

<column-break/>

<margin>1215</margin> **In the foothills of Caucasus:** It is said that in the region of Caucasus, at the Typhaonian rock, Typhaon was struck by a thunderbolt and released certain fluids <note>original: "ichoras", the golden blood of gods or immortals</note>, from which the serpent guarding the Fleece was born. Some say Typhaon fled to Caucasus <margin>1220</margin> while being pursued, and that while the mountain was burning, he fled from there to Italy; there, the island of Pithecousa <note>Modern Ischia</note> was thrown around him, <margin>1225</margin> as Pherecydes <note>A 6th-century BC mythographer</note> records in his *Theogony*. Other myths say he was driven to the regions around Syria, as Apollonius says. <margin>1230</margin> **Typhaon:** The verse says that having been struck by Zeus, he went just as he was to the regions around Syria and reached Pelusium, pursued by Zeus; there he lies submerged in the <margin>1235</margin> Serbonian lake. This lake extends from Syria to Pelusium. Herodorus <note>A Greek historian from the 5th century BC</note> says the same things about Typhaon. There he also records things about Nysa, saying: "There is a certain Nysa, a mountain peak reaching the high air with its woods, far from Phoenicia, near the streams of Egypt." The Caucasus extends from the land of the Armenians to the Colchians. The Serbonian lake is located near Pelusium in Egypt.

**Do not, noble youth:** Peleus answered the concern about how they would sail for their own interests by telling him not to fear. Therefore, it should be written as "in your soul" <note>original: "thymō"</note>. However, some write it as "by his word" <note>original: "mythō"</note>, meaning: "Do not let him frighten us with stories about Aeetes." But in all versions it is carried as "be disheartened in your soul." For he says that we are in no way inferior to Aeetes. The word for "noble youth" <note>original: "ēïtheë"</note>, I believe, was formed by the insertion of the letter 'eta', just as "small" <note>original: "baios"</note> becomes "very small" <note>original: "ēbaios"</note>. The word "ēïthe" also means someone related to a beggar. Or it can mean "wonderful one" (as in, "by no means, O wonderful one") or "noble one."

**Island of Philyra:** He speaks about the Philyres, named after Philyra the daughter of Oceanus, who lived in these regions. When Cronus was lying with her, back when he ruled the Titans, Rhea <note>The wife of Cronus</note> caught them in the act. Therefore, Cronus, feeling ashamed, transformed into a horse, while Philyra fled to Thessaly. Pherecydes says that Cronus, having taken the likeness of a horse, coupled with Philyra daughter of Oceanus...

### THE ARGONAUTICA

This double-natured one is Chiron <note>Chiron was a centaur, famously wise and the tutor of many heroes like Achilles and Jason. Unlike most wild centaurs, he was immortal and scholarly</note>. Suidas, in the first book of the *Thessalian History*, says that Chiron was the son of Ixion and the brother of Pirithous. "Cretaean mountain" refers to the Cretan range. It was formed by similarity to Mount Sinaus.

---

<margin>
The word "shaggy" (chaitēeis) means "having a mane"; derived from "mane" (chaitē), just as from "dew" (ersē) comes "dewy" (ersēeis), and from "fat" (pimē) comes "fatty" (pimēeis). Concerning the Macrones, Becheiri, and Sapeiri, they have been mentioned previously. When he said, "the recess of the sea appeared," he showed that the land of Colchis is located in the innermost corner of the sea.
</margin>
...under the Cretan steep, where <gloss>truly</gloss> Zeus was still being raised by the Idaean Curetes <note>The Curetes were semi-divine guardians who clashed their shields to drown out the cries of the infant Zeus so his father Cronus would not find and eat him</note>, while Cronus, deceiving Rhea, lay beside Philyra. <gloss>Or</gloss> in those very beds, the goddess caught them in the act. But he, springing up from the bed,
<margin>1240</margin>rushed off <gloss>looking</gloss> like a long-maned horse.
And she, the Oceanid Philyra, leaving that place and those haunts out of shame, came to the long Pelasgian mountains, where she gave birth to the monstrous Chiron, half <margin>1245</margin>horse and half <gloss>equal to</gloss> a god, the offspring of that transformed bed.
From there they passed the Macrones and the vast land of the Becheiri, and the arrogant Sapeiri, and the Byzeres after them. For they were ever cutting through the waves swiftly, carried by a gentle wind.
<margin>1250</margin><margin>
**And now the Caucasian]**
Those peaks called the Caucasian mountains, Eratosthenes says, are near the sea called the Caspian.
</margin>

<margin>
**Rising up]**
The sheer cliffs and outcroppings of the Caucasian mountains. Some say "rising peaks" (eeipnai) refers to the rugged rocks that reach into the heights.
</margin>
"And now the towering peaks of the Caucasian mountains rose up," where Prometheus, his limbs <margin>
**Where the limbs]**
Prometheus was bound in the
</margin>
wrapped in unbreakable bronze chains around the harsh crags, fed the eagle with his liver as it darted back and forth.

---

Caucasus, and the eagle ate his liver. Agētas, in the thirteenth book of his *Scythian History*, says it was thought that the liver of Prometheus was devoured by the eagle because a river called "The Eagle" was destroying the most fertile region <note>original: "kratinēn," meaning the best or strongest land</note> of Prometheus's territory. He notes that "liver" is used by many, just as "udder" (euthar) is, to signify fertile and green land. When Heracles diverted the river with channels, it was thought the eagle had been driven away by him and Prometheus was released from his bonds. Theophrastus says that Prometheus, being a wise man, was the first to share philosophy with mankind; from this, the myth was spread that he shared "fire." Herodorus the stranger says this about the binding of Prometheus: he was a King of the Scythians and, being unable to provide necessities for his subjects because the river called "The Eagle" flooded the plains, he was imprisoned by the Scythians. When Heracles appeared, he diverted the river into the sea, and because of this it was mythologized that he had slain the eagle and released Prometheus from his bonds. Pherecydes, in his second book, says the eagle sent against Prometheus was the child of Typhon and Echidna, daughter of Phorcys. He says the eagle ate the liver during the day, and what remained grew back at night until it was whole again. **Wrapped in bronze]** Hesiod says Prometheus was bound and the eagle sent against him because of the theft of fire. But Duris says it was because he fell in love with Athena. Therefore, some who live around the Caucasus sacrifice only to Zeus and Athena, because they were the cause of Prometheus's punishment. But they worship Heracles exceedingly, out of gratitude for the destruction of the eagle. It is fitting then that Apollonius, having arrived at the Caucasus, mentions these things now.

### BOOK TWO

Towards the very peak they saw the eagle at evening time with a sharp whirring, flying over the ship near the clouds; yet even so, it shook all the sails as it rushed past with its wings. For it did not have the nature of an airy bird, but moved its swift wings like well-polished oars. Not long after, they heard the mournful cry of Prometheus as his liver was torn out <note>Prometheus was a Titan punished by Zeus for giving fire to humanity; an eagle was sent daily to eat his liver, which regrew every night</note>. The air rang with his scream, until they saw the flesh-eating eagle darting back from the mountain along the same path. By night, through the guidance of Argus <note>This Argus is the son of Phrixus, who joined the Argonauts later in their journey and knew the way to Colchis</note>, they reached the wide-flowing Phasis and the furthest boundaries of the sea. Immediately they furled the sails and the yardarm within the hollow mast-hold. Then they quickly lowered the mast itself to the side. With oars they drove into the great stream of the river, which gave way, bubbling all around. On their left hand they had the steep Caucasus and the Cytaean city of Aea. From there, they saw the Plain of Ares and the sacred groves of that god, where the serpent guarded the fleece, watching it as it hung upon the thick branches of an oak. Jason himself <gloss>poured libations</gloss> from a golden cup, pouring honey-sweetened draughts of unmixed wine to the Earth and the local gods, and to the souls of dead heroes. He prayed for them to be kindly <gloss>come as</gloss> protectors, and to receive the ship's cables with good omens. Immediately Ancaeus spoke these words among them: "We have reached the land of Colchis and the streams of Phasis; now is the time for us to deliberate whether we shall try to persuade Aeetes with gentle words..."

<column-break/>

<margin>1255</margin> **Towards the peak:** The poet says that around evening the leaders saw the eagle [approaching] Prometheus. **Fluttering past** means breathing upon them; that is, by creating a blast of wind through the force of its wings, it shook the sails.

**Like well-polished:** He means the feathers in the wings were like "oars," a metaphor for the blades of the wings.

<margin>1260</margin>

<margin>1265</margin> **For a long time:** He uses this phrase to reveal the massive size of the bird.

**Aetherial:** Meaning "air-traveling." In the phrase "Not long after," the word order should be understood as "Then, after no long time."

<margin>1270</margin> **Argus:** Referring to the son of Phrixus. **Guidance** refers to his experience and knowledge of these difficult regions.

**Spreading:** The grammarian Herodian <note>A famous Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD</note> places the accent on the penultimate syllable. **Honey-sweetened:** Simply meaning "sweet."

<margin>1275</margin> **Inhabitant gods:** The local or indigenous deities. It was the custom for those arriving in a foreign land to sacrifice to the local gods and heroes. They say Alexander the Great also did this at Ilion <note>The ancient name for Troy; Alexander visited the site to honor the heroes of the Trojan War</note>.

**Ship's favorable cables:** Meaning things that are fitting, leading to good and acceptable outcomes.

<margin>1280</margin> **Whether by mildness:** Meaning "gently." **Successful** (epibolos) means "secure" or "attaining a goal."

...as we approach, we might test Aeetes to see if he will be persuaded by us, or if some other way is needed. Thus also Amerias <note>An ancient scholar known for his work on rare vocabulary</note> explained this in his *Glossary*.

# APOLLONIUS OF RHODES
## The Third Book of the Argonautica.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'E' within a square frame, decorated with scrolling vine and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

Come now, Erato, 
stand by my side, and tell me
How from there he brought to Iolcos
<gloss>the land of Iolcos</gloss>
the fleece, did Jason,
through the love of Medea. For you also...

<column-break/>

->SCHOLIA<-
<note>Scholia are ancient marginal commentaries or explanatory notes written by scholars to help readers understand the text.</note>
on the third book of
Apollonius's 
Argonautica.

->The chapters of the third book of the Argonautica are as follows:<-

---

Hera and Athena, having consulted together, persuade Aphrodite to send love upon Medea. Jason, arriving with the sons of Phrixus <note>Phrixus was the hero who originally flew to Colchis on the Golden Ram; his sons joined the Argonauts to return to Greece.</note> to Aeetes, asks to receive the fleece. Aeetes, becoming indignant, surrounds him with great labors: such as to yoke the fire-breathing bulls, and to sow the teeth of the dragon, from which giants were produced. He had not only to withstand them, but also to harvest the "crop" of the earth-born men. Medea, because of her love for Jason, is led by Chalciope <note>Medea's sister and the mother of Phrixus's sons.</note> to help her own sons. And indeed, she will meet Jason at the temple of Hecate, and gives him the drugs <term>pharmaka: medicines, charms, or poisons</term>, and suggests the manner in which he must prepare for the harvest of the giants. Using the drugs, Jason accomplished the proposed labors, contrary to all the expectations of Aeetes.

**Come now, Erato** and so forth. They say Erato discovered the dance; because of this, Apollonius says Erato "shares in the rites of Aphrodite," by which I mean the marriage rites; and dancing follows marriages. Regarding those who follow the writings attributed to Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and seer of early Greece.</note>, two generations of Muses are recorded. The elder, born with Cronus; the younger, those from Zeus and Mnemosyne. 

**Come now**—it is said of the Muses that Clio discovered history; Thalia, agriculture and the study of plants; Euterpe, lessons; Terpsichore, education; Erato, dance; Polyhymnia, the lyre; Melpomene, song; Urania, astrology; Calliope, poetry.

It is questioned first why he called upon the Muses at the start of the poem's journey, but now makes mention of only one of them. Second, why he calls upon Erato and not the others. It must be said regarding the first point that at the start of the journey, he reasonably called upon Apollo, the leader of the Muses; but here, since he is about to speak of marriages and festivities, and the Muses are protectors of festivities, he calls upon the Muse now for this reason. That the Muses are protectors of festivities is made clear in the Orphic poems: "Nor do mortals ever cease from the Muses, who are the Rulers, who care for the dance and lovely festivities." 

Regarding the second point, since in the Orphic poems Erato is given as the inventor of dance, and Apollonius is about to narrate the marriage of Medea and Jason, for this reason he calls upon the Muse who is the inventor of the dance that belongs to a marriage. Wherefore also a little later he added that she "shares in the rites of Aphrodite." For dancing follows the marriage. Rhianus <note>A poet and scholar of the 3rd century BCE.</note>, however, says it makes no difference whether one calls upon one or all the Muses, saying thus: "All listen, when you have spoken the name of one." And perhaps also because he is speaking about love, and Erato is named from "to love" <note>original: "eran"</note>, for this reason he mentions her, ascribing this common interest to her because of her name. Erato comes from *eran* ("to love"), in the Attic dialect. The sequence of the text is: "Stand by me and tell."

q.iii.

### ON THE ARGONAUTICA

**Unlooked-for**: unexpectedly. <note>original: "Ανώιστως"</note> **After Greece**: instead of "into Greece." <note>original: "Μεθ' Ἑλλάδα"</note> **To turn away**: to turn back. **The sense is**: nevertheless, one must not let any trial pass by. **Her near at hand**: instead of "immediately" or "quickly." Or perhaps the word "sitting" is omitted. **Unreservedly**: means truly and simply, and also clearly; but here it means "abruptly." For she adds, *but I do not yet perceive what to devise.* **Pondering in two ways**: worrying with divided minds.

**After Cypris**: towards Cypris <note>Another name for Aphrodite, the goddess of love, referencing her birth on Cyprus.</note>. **Approaching**: coming upon and having come to. **To her son**: Apollonius makes Eros the son of Aphrodite; but Sappho says he is the child of Earth and Heaven; Simonides says of Aphrodite and Ares, quoting:
> O cruel child of crafty Aphrodite,
> whom Ares of the wily schemes begot.
But Ibycus and Hesiod say Eros comes from Chaos. In the writings attributed to Orpheus, he is the son of Cronus:
> But Eros,
> Cronus and all the winds
> brought forth.

**To charm by shooting**: here it means to beguile, so that she might not control herself because of love. **Dense**: instead of "rightly" or "well." The plan was "dense" <note>In the sense of "shrewd" or "solid."</note> and wise, and it pleased her.

<margin>35</margin> **So that he might build for her**: <note>original: "Ὀφρά τέ οἱ δείμῃ"</note> The followers of Aeisarchos write such words with one ‘r’; but Herakleon uses two. As also in the poet [Homer]: “Then at that time taking from the chest...” 
**In the porch**: <note>original: "Αἰθούσῃ"</note> the colonnade or portico. 
<margin>40</margin> **But he [went] to the forge**: Of the Aeolian islands, the one called Hiera, in which they say Hephaestus forges. He called it “wandering,” <note>original: "πλαγκτῆς"</note> 
<margin>45</margin> following those who tell myths about Italy and Sicily regarding the wandering of Odysseus. Or because in ancient times all islands wandered and had no fixed foundations. 
**Callias**, in his work on *Hiera*, says it is dedicated 
<margin>50</margin> to Hephaestus, but mentions Lipara. “On the island of Lipara.” These are the seven Aeolian islands: Strongyle, Euonymos, Hiera, Lipara, Didyme, Erikodes, and Phoinikodes, near Sicily. 

---

**But he**: Regarding the Aeolian islands, that the one called Hiera is where they say Hephaestus forges. Callias relates this in the tenth book of his history *On Agathocles*, saying there is also a high roof on which there are two craters; one of which has a circumference of four stades <note>A Greek unit of distance; four stades is approximately 740 meters or half a mile.</note>, from which a great light is carried, so that the illumination reaches over a large area. Then from the chasm, glowing stones of immense size are thrown up. And such a roar occurs at the time when Hephaestus happens to be working, that the sound is heard for five hundred stades <note>Approximately 90 kilometers or 57 miles.</note>. The lumps of metal thrown up from the blast are always rust-colored due to the fire and scorched in appearance, and they have power in the sun. At night, everything moving around the god's work is clearly revealed; by day, from the peak where the flame shoots up, something like a cloud is seen lying beneath. By saying, “he forged curious things with the blast of fire,” the poet points to what is described by Callias as the blowing up of fire from the chasm. 

**He had gone**: <note>original: "Ἠει"</note> at dawn. 
**She stopped**: <note>original: "Ἕσχεθεν"</note> she ceased combing her hair. 
**With uncombed [hands]**: <note>original: "Ἀψήκτοις"</note> unbrushed. 
**O divine one**: <note>original: "Η̄ θεία"</note> An address used in Homer from younger people to elders. But Apollonius has used a collective phrasing. For what belonged to Hera, he also applied to Athena. These things are fitting to be said according to Homer’s poetry. And regarding the younger ones, this applies not only to Athena and Hera, but also for Zeus, because Aphrodite is considered older. But Hesiod says she was born from the genitals of Uranus. 
**After a long time**: <note>original: "Δηναίας"</note> seen after a long interval. 
**Not formerly**: <note>original: "Οὔ τι πάρος γε"</note> This mimics the Homeric line: “Formerly you did not visit often.” 
**You will mock**: <note>original: "Κερτομιείς"</note> you speak ironically or teasingly.

**Righteousness**: <note>original: "εὐνομίης"</note> lawfulness, justice, and noble goodness. **Covered in snow**: <note>original: "Νιφετῷ παλύετο"</note> it was concealed by the snow.

Will return to Iolcus; for she is fashioned as one of many wiles <note>original: "δολόεσσα" (dolóessa). The poet suggests Medea is not just clever, but possessor of a 'crafty' wisdom.</note>.”
So she spoke; and Cythereia <note>A common title for Aphrodite, referring to her sacred island of Cythera.</note> said to them both:
“Hera and Athena, he might obey you more
Than me. For before you, even though he is shameless,
There will be a small measure of shame in his eyes; but for me
He has no regard, and always strives against me and ignores me.
And indeed I intended, being hemmed in by his wickedness,
To break his ill-sounding bows and arrows
Openly. For in such a way he threatened me when ‘angered’ <note>original: "χαλεφθείς" (chalephtheís)</note>,
That unless I kept my hands far off, while he still restrained his temper,
Afterward I would ‘blame’ <note>original: "ἀτεμβοίμην" (atemboímēn)</note> myself.”
So she spoke, and the goddesses smiled and looked at
One another. But she again addressed them, grieving:
“My sorrows are a source of laughter to others; nor should I
Tell them to everyone; I know enough of them myself.
But now, since this is indeed pleasing to both of you,
I will try, and I will soothe him; and he will not disobey.”
So she spoke. And Hera took her by her slender hand,
And gently smiling, she spoke ‘in reply’ <note>original: "παραβλήδην" (parablēdēn)</note>:
“Perform this task now, Cythereia, just as you say,
Straightway, and do not be angry, nor strive
In wrath with your son; for he will cease his behavior later.”
She spoke, and left her seat; and Athena set out with her.
And they both went out ‘rushing back’ <note>original: "παλίσσυτοι" (palíssuytoi)</note>. And she herself...

**Daughter of Aeetes**] <note>original: "Παρθένον Αἰήτεω"</note> Simply in place of "daughter." But it can also be understood this way: of the daughters of Aeetes, the one who is still a virgin <note>This identifies Medea as the younger, unmarried daughter compared to her sister Chalciope.</note>.
85 **Wily**] <note>original: "Δολόεσσα"</note> In place of "prudent." For *dolos* <note>craft or trickery</note> is sometimes used for wisdom. **I intended**] <note>original: "Μενέηνα"</note> I was angry; I was exceedingly pained. **Angered**] <note>original: "Χαλεφθείς"</note> 90 The sense is: having become angry, he threatened, unless I held back my hands, while he still mastered his temper, that I would blame myself. **In reply**] <note>original: "Παραβλήδην"</note> Instead of "adding to" what was said. For it can be understood as "to deceive." But the scholar Palamedes says, "from comparison" or "deceitfully." **Helpless:** That is, being in a state of loss, having been unable to defeat Eros, he departed. For Ganymede plays with Eros. **Approaching:** Instead of "coming upon him," or having arrived there. **Why do you smile:** Why do you laugh, you great and unspeakable evil? Either you have cheated him in vain and outwitted him, nor did you deal with him fairly, but you tricked him since he was inexperienced. **Adrasteia:** She was the nurse of Zeus.
<margin>*</margin> Callimachus says: "Adrasteia, sister of the Curetes, put you to sleep." **In the Idaean cave:** Either the one in Crete, or the one in Troy. For the Trojans also claim the birth of Zeus, as Demetrius of Scepsis says. **Hoops:** He calls the rhombs "hoops" or "circles." In the Ionic dialect, he uses the neuter plural *kykla* instead of the masculine *kyklous* (circles), just as one says *lychna* (lamps) and *diphra* (chariots). **Bands:** The joints or connections. **Circular:** Rounded, or running around the perimeter.

# ARGONAUTICA

<margin>
And the water flowed <note>original: 225</note> | Apollonius is referring to the setting of the Pleiades <note>A star cluster in the constellation Taurus.</note> when he says it flowed warm, and when they rose, he says it was cold, by which he clearly establishes the season. For there are two risings of the fixed stars and two settings. The morning rising is when a star first stands outside the rays of the sun and is seen rising around dawn. The morning setting is when the sun is toward the east and a star is seen setting for the last time around the west on that night. The evening rising is when
</margin>

And the water flowed forth; much of it grew warm
When the Pleiades <note>The "Seven Sisters" star cluster.</note> were setting; but in turn, as they rose,
It bubbled up from the hollow rock like ice.
Such were the wondrous works that the skillful Hephaestus <note>The god of fire, smithing, and craftsmanship.</note>
Had fashioned in the halls of Aeetes of Cyta.
<margin>230</margin> He also fashioned for him bulls with feet of bronze; and bronze
Were their mouths, from which they breathed a terrible flame of fire.
Furthermore, he forged a plow of solid adamant, all in one piece, <note>A mythical, indestructible metal.</note>
As a favor to Helios <note>The Sun god, who was the father of King Aeetes.</note>, who had taken him up in his chariot
When he was exhausted from the battle on the Phlegraean plain <note>The site of the war between the Gods and the Giants.</note>.
<margin>235</margin> There too, the central courtyard had been built; and upon it were many
Well-fitted double doors and chambers here and there.
And a beautifully decorated portico was fashioned along both sides.
And at an angle, taller buildings stood on either side.
In one of these, because he was the most excellent,
<margin>240</margin> Lord Aeetes dwelt with his wife;
But in another dwelt Apsyrtus, the son of Aeetes,

---

the sun is setting and a star is seen in the east as the first of those rising during that night. The evening setting is said to occur when the sun is setting and a star is seen near the west, setting with it, so that it is hidden by the rays of the sun. All the time spent under the rays is called "hiding."
The Pleiades are the daughters of Pleione the Oceanid and Atlas. According to some, they take their name from their mother; or rather, from the word *pleion*, which means "year." For these stars indicate both winter and summer. They always move in the opposite direction to Orion. It is said that Orion once met Pleione with her daughters in Boeotia; falling in love with her, he pursued her, and she fled. They say her flight was continuous. And thus, the Pleiades were turned into stars as they fled from Orion. Pherecydes <note>An early Greek mythographer and genealogist.</note> also states that the bulls are bronze-footed and breathe fire. **Furthermore, a plow of solid adamant.** There are two types of plows. One is "joined" <term>pekton: a plow made of separate pieces of wood joined together</term>, and the other is "naturally-curved" <term>autoguon: a plow where the main body and the pole are made from a single, naturally curved piece of timber</term>. The "joined" one has the sole-piece attached by a joint. The sole-piece is where the plowshare is placed. The wood extending from the sole-piece to the oxen is called the pole. The piece extending from the pole is the "ox-driver." The parts of the yoke placed upon the necks of the oxen are called "yoke-straps" by some, and "pegs" by others. Such is the joined plow. The naturally-curved one is that in which the sole-piece is not joined by a fitting. Eratosthenes <note>The famous scholar and librarian of Alexandria.</note> describes the construction of plows in his work *On Architecture*. **As a favor to Helios.** This myth was fashioned because of the lameness of Hephaestus' feet. Or perhaps it is simply plausible. For Hephaestus had greater power than the Giants, by which he could have turned them back. However, Apollonius has given the reason why Hephaestus constructed the bronze-hoofed bulls and the plow for Aeetes. Homer also showed that Hephaestus was powerful in the scene with the River Xanthus. **Phlegraean.** Phlegra is a plain in Thrace, near Pallene, where the gods fought the Giants. **Central courtyard.** The middle of the court where the stalls for the oxen were. The Attic writers call the passage leading to both the men's and women's quarters the *mesautos*. **Beautifully decorated portico.** A colonnade of varied design on both sides of the house. **At an angle.** On the sides of the portico, there were taller structures. These are towers.

"Get out of my sight, you scoundrels! Out of this land, you and your tricks, before someone sees a 'miserable fleece' and a Phrixus <note>Aeetes implies the fleece belongs to his family through Phrixus, and Jason has no right to it</note> indeed! You have come here from Greece—not for the fleece, but for my scepter and my kingly honor.

375

If you had not already shared my table, I would surely have cut out your tongues and lopped off both your hands, leaving you only your feet to sail away on—so that you might be prevented from making such a move again. What lies you have told even against the blessed gods!"

380

So he spoke in his anger. The heart of the son of Aeacus <note>Peleus, father of Achilles and one of the Argonauts</note> swelled with fury from deep within; his spirit longed to hurl back a deadly word in defiance. But the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note> restrained him, for he himself first replied with soothing words:

385

"Aeetes, bear with me in this anger. For we have not come to your city and your home with the intent you imagine. No one would willingly endure crossing such a vast swell of foreign sea for another man's property. But a divine power and the chilling command of a cruel king <note>Pelias, who sent Jason on the quest</note> drove me.

390

Grant us this favor as we ask it. I will spread your wondrous fame throughout all of Greece. Moreover, we are ready now to offer you a swift repayment in war—whether you wish to subdue the Sauromatians <note>a nomadic people from the Eurasian steppe</note> or some other tribe under your scepter."

395

He spoke, flattering him with a gentle voice. But the King’s heart within his breast brooded with a twofold intent: whether he should spring upon them and slaughter them where they stood, or whether he should make a trial of their strength. As he pondered, this latter course seemed better; and so he spoke to Jason, addressing him craftily.

400

<column-break/>

**Immediately]** <note>original: Αὐτίκα</note> used here in the sense of "now." Regarding the phrase "to go," the word "I expect" <note>original: ἔολπα</note> is understood from the common context. **Otherwise:** In the phrase "having set out at once," one must note that it is phrased unclearly. Perhaps "again" should be said instead of "immediately." And instead of "from Greece," it should be "to Greece," so that it means: "return immediately to Greece." Or, "having come to Greece with the spoils," one must then add the following: "you come back here for the fleece, for the scepters, and for the kingly honor." Thus, one should either read "that there is a fleece" but "not for the fleece," or "not scepters" but "at least scepters." The commentators seem to have encountered a different reading. For they say that the word "I expect" is understood from the common context, yet the word "I expect" appears nowhere in this section.

**Aeetes, bear with me]** <note>original: Αἰῆτα, σχέο μοι</note> O Aeetes, restrain or hold back from me this form of anger. **Neither indeed desiring]** <note>original: Οὐδὲ μὲν ἱέμενοι</note> not desiring your kingdom. **Your own]** <note>original: Σφωϊτέροισιν</note> he used the word "your own" <note>a dual possessive pronoun</note> incorrectly. He should have said "those." The word **spoke]** <note>original: ἴσκεν</note> is used in the Homeric style. **Make a trial of strength]** <note>original: Πειρήσαιτο βίης</note> let him take a trial of the strength of the heroes. **Craftily]** <note>original: ὑποβλήδην</note> the word "craftily" (or "interrupting") is placed poorly here. It refers to someone anticipating and cutting off the other person while they are speaking.

<header>ARGONAUTICA, SECOND</header> <note>original: "ΑΡΓΟΝΑΥΤ. ΔΕΥΤ." – Although the header says "Second," this text corresponds to the famous trial of Jason in Book Three of Apollonius Rhodius's epic.</note>

<margin>
The phrase "why do you speak at such length": means you are being long-winded. "Ruling over Hellas": he refers here to Pelias <note>Jason's uncle, the usurper king of Iolcus</note>. The word "begrudge" means I do not envy you, unlike Pelias. By "taking a trial of your courage I will provide the fleece," he means that "envying is not a trait I hold dear." "Deadly": refers to the labor. "Two for me in the field": Antimachus in his poem *Lyde* declared these bulls were fashioned by Hephaestus <note>the god of fire and smithing</note>. "Hard": means rough. Pherecydes says in his sixth book that the field is fifty *gyai* <note>a unit of land measure</note>. "Seed": refers to wheat. "In the furrows": the marks made by the plow; for as the plow is dragged, the earth is broken open. "Deo": the goddess Demeter <note>goddess of the harvest</note>. "I mow down": I kill. "Standing around": refers to those standing around and surrounding one equally. "Turn" <note>original: "Γύρος"</note>: refers to the place before; it is also used regarding time. "You hem me in too much": he means, "you press me too hard with your conditions/justice." Therefore, even though the labor exceeds my strength, know that I will face it until death; he uses the masculine word for "fate" <note>original: "μόρον"</note>. "For there is nothing else": nothing is worse for men than Necessity, by which we have arrived here, forced by the king.
</margin>

"Stranger, why do you speak of each of these matters at such length? 
If you are truly of the race of gods, or if you have come as 
strangers in no way inferior to me, 
I will give you the gleaming golden fleece to take, if you wish, 
once you have been tested. For I do not begrudge noble men anything, 
unlike that man you describe who rules over Hellas. 
The trial of your courage and your strength shall be a labor, 
one which I myself perform with my own hands, deadly though it is. 
Two bulls with feet of bronze graze on the Plain of Ares for me, 
breathing out flames of fire from their mouths. 
These I yoke and drive over the "hard fallow field of Ares," 
and quickly plowing it to the end of the field, 
I do not cast the "seed" of Demeter <note>wheat</note> into the "furrows," 
but instead the teeth of a terrible serpent, which grow up 
into the forms of armed men. These, as they rise up against me 
from all sides, "I mow down with my spear," 
slaying them as they confront me. 
At dawn I yoke the oxen, and by the evening hour 
I cease from the harvest. If you can fulfill such tasks as these, 
you may carry away the fleece to the king's house on this very day. 
But before then I will not give it; do not hope for it. For it is unseemly 
for a brave man to yield to one who is his inferior."

So he spoke. Jason fixed his eyes on the ground before his feet 
and sat there just as he was, speechless, helpless in his misfortune. 
He turned the plan over in his mind for a long time; he did not see any way 
to accept the challenge with confidence, for the task seemed immense. 
At last, responding with cunning words, he addressed him: 
"Aeetes, you hem me in very closely with your conditions. 
Therefore I will endure this labor, even though it is monstrous, 
even if it is my fate to die. For nothing else 
more chilling will be imposed on men than cruel Necessity, 
which forced me to come here at the command of a king."

So he spoke, struck down by helplessness. But the King...

**495: Inquiring]** [Means] searching out, or speaking. For the sense is: it is contrary to us. For that which is to be fulfilled is not for me to say, nor for you who inquire with your mouths afterward.
**500: He commanded]** he gave orders.

"Taught" <note>original: "daei"</note> instead of "he taught." 
"Abundant water" <note>original: "nechyton hydor"</note> means "poured-out-much." The prefix "ne-" <note>original: "nē"</note> signifies both lack and intensity. 
Also "un-poured water" <note>original: "achyeton hydor"</note> means "much water," according to the Ionians and Sicilians. 
Dionysius of Clazomenae writes: "where they loosened the abundant water they had thrown."
"Stars and the moon": he refers to the traditional myth that sorceresses can draw down the moon. 
Some also called solar and lunar eclipses "withdrawals" <note>original: "kathaireseis"</note> of the gods. 
In ancient times, people thought sorceresses could withdraw the moon and the sun. Therefore, even until the time of Democritus, many called eclipses "withdrawals." 
Sosiphanes in *Meleager* says: "By the Magi’s incantations every Thessalian girl is a false bringer-down of the moon from the ether."
"Perhaps" <note>original: "tacha"</note>: the word "perhaps" is used here in a sense of doubt. But the Ionians also use it to mean "quickly." 
Apollodorus says in his work *On the Gods* that the dove is sacred to Aphrodite. For this reason, it is considered lustful. For he says that "to act like a dove" <note>original: "peleiassai"</note> means "to love." 
"And my heart": as my soul foresees, so may it happen.

**Furious** <note>original: "Memaws"</note>: used instead of "angry." For he is one who is prudent in the face of evils.

**He threatened** <note>original: "Steuto"</note>: from the same root as "to rush" <note>original: "seuto"</note>. 
**Vomit out** <note>original: "apophlyxosin"</note>: used instead of "blow out" or "escape." It can also mean to "overturn." From this root we get the word for "babbler" <note>original: "phlyaros"</note>. 
**For he never [would have] received**: the word "endured" is missing from the sense. 
**Unless Zeus**: he says that the messenger **Hermes** was sent by Zeus, ordering Aeetes to receive Phrixus so that Phrixus might marry Aeetes' daughter. But the author of the *Aegimius* <note>An ancient lost epic</note> says that because of the **Golden Fleece**, he was received voluntarily. It was said that after completing the sacrifice and obtaining the fleece, he then entered Aeetes' halls carrying the skin. 
**So that [he] might meet**: so that Phrixus might meet with a fitting reception from Aeetes.

Resounding; and silence held the darkening gloom.
<margin>750</margin> But sweet sleep did not at all take Medea.
For many cares for the son of Aeson <note>Jason, son of Aeson</note> in her longing kept her awake,
fearing the strong might of the bulls, by whom he was destined
to perish by a shameful fate in the field of Ares.
Thickly her heart within her breast throbbed,
<margin>755</margin> just as a ray of the sun flickers in a house,
rising from water that has newly been poured into a cauldron
or perhaps a pail; it tosses here and there,
darting with a swift whirl.
So too the heart in the girl's breast was shaken,
<margin>760</margin> and tears of pity flowed from her eyes; and within,
pain was always wearing her down, smoldering through her flesh,
around the slender nerves and down to the very base of the neck;
there the most painful ache sinks in, whenever tireless
loves <note>original: *erōtes*</note> strike into the wits.
<margin>765</margin> She said at one time she would give him the soothing drugs for the bulls,
at another time not; and that she herself would die with him.
Then immediately, that she would neither die herself, nor give the drugs,
but just as she was, she would endure her doom in quiet.
Sitting then she wavered, and she spoke:
<margin>770</margin> "Wretched me, now here or there shall I pour out my evils?
My mind is altogether helpless; there is no defense
against the pain, but it burns just as it is. Would that I
had been slain before by the swift arrows of Artemis,
before seeing him, before the sons of Chalciope reached the Achaean land;
<margin>775</margin> whom a god or some Fury brought here from there 
to be much-lamented sorrows for us."

<column-break/>

**But sweet sleep did not take Medea** — The word <term>mala</term> <note>original: *μάλα*, meaning "very" or "at all"</note> is redundant here. The sense of the passage is: "But sweet sleep did not at all take Medea, because she was fearing the strong might of the bulls."

**Longing for the son of Aeson** — The poet does not use the word <term>pothos</term> <note>original: *πόθος*</note> correctly here in place of <term>eros</term> <note>original: *ἔρως*, passionate love</note>. For *pothos* refers to a "seeking" or "yearning" for something absent, while *eros* is an intense, present longing.

**Fearing** — This comes from the verb *deidō*; the perfect tense is *dedoika*. From this, the participle is formed by shortening it to *deidiōs*; the feminine form is <term>deidiua</term> <note>the form used in line 752</note>.

**Throbbed** — It was rushing or moving. From this word comes the name <term>Thyiades</term> <note>The Bacchantes, female followers of Dionysus known for their frenzied movement</note>.

**Just as a ray of the sun in a house** — A downward ray of sunlight in a house is reflected upward from water toward a wall—water that has been recently poured into either a cauldron or a bucket; it moves continuously to both sides in a turning motion.

**Pain wearing her down** — The pain was exhausting her as it burned. Homer says: "to consume <note>original: *katasmyxai*</note> the ships with fire." <meta>εε</meta>

**There the most painful** — In the place where the soul’s most sensitive part is, whenever one is gripped by love with great distress. 

<insert>
The poet plausibly maintains the character of the girl: she is being dragged along by her passion, yet she is still trying to be controlled by her reason.
**Strike into** — Meaning "to fall upon."
**To perish** — Clearly, to perish because of love.
**Endure** — She considered enduring the ruin/doom.
**Achaean** — Used here instead of "Thessalian." Homer says: "They were called Myrmidons and Hellenes and Achaeans."
</insert>

### COMMENTARY

**Having devised drugs**] <note>original: "Φάρμακα μησαμένη"</note> The word "to give" is understood here.

**She might trust**] <note>original: "πιθῇ"</note> This refers to the act of persuasion or placing trust.

**What counsel?**] What deceptive plan of help will there be for me?

**To us**] <note>original: "ἄμμι"</note> The plural "to us" is used here instead of the singular "to me."

**They will leer**] <note>original: "Ἐπιλλίζουσιν"</note> They will mock or blame. Literally, it means to turn one’s eyes aside in a mocking or leering way.

**And misery**] <note>original: "Καὶ οἰζὺ"</note> The text is corrupted; "misery" is poorly placed. It is better read as "alas, misery," so that the speech belongs clearly to the women.

**Casket**] <note>original: "Φωριαμὸν"</note> Here he refers to a small chest or jewelry box. This is clear from the description of the contents. Eratosthenes, in his work *Hermes*, provides an etymology for the word *phōriamon* (casket): "They named it a casket because it hid a 'thievish darkness' <note>original: "phōreion achlin"</note>; from 'thievish' it is called a casket by men."

**Unceasing**] <note>original: "Ἀσχεγὲς"</note> This is used instead of "much-held." The prefix "a-" here is "intensive" <note>term: intensive alpha; a linguistic feature in Ancient Greek where the letter "a" at the start of a word makes the meaning stronger rather than negating it</note>, similar to how one might describe a forest as "impassably" wooded.

**So long as she might taste**] The word "so long as" <note>original: "τόφρα"</note> is used in place of "until" <note>original: "ὄφρα"</note>. Sometimes "until" indicates purpose (as in Homer: "until the seed should not be scattered"), and sometimes it is preceded by "so long as." Homer says: "So long as it was morning, and the sacred day was increasing."

**Might taste**] This word is not used correctly here, for the physical impression of "tasting" does not fit the sense of reaching satiety or fullness.

<column-break/>

"Let him perish in his contest, if it be his fate to die. For how could I hide it from my parents <margin>780</margin> after having devised these drugs? What story shall I tell? What trick, what cunning plan will serve as my aid? Shall I greet him alone, apart from his comrades? Wretched me! I truly hope that even if he is dead, I might find relief from my griefs. But then evil would come to me when <margin>785</margin> he is deprived of life. Away with shame! Away with glory! Let him be saved by my will, unharmed, and let him go wherever his heart desires. But on that very day, when he has finished the contest, let me die—either by hanging my neck from the roof-beam <margin>790</margin> or by tasting drugs that destroy the soul. But even so, once I am dead, they will leer at me with insults afterward; from afar the whole city will shout about my fate. And the Colchian women, carrying my name in their mouths, will mock me here and there with sharp words: <margin>795</margin> 'This girl, caring so much for a foreign man, died; she who shamed her home and her parents, yielding to madness.' What shame will not be mine? Oh, my ruin! It would be much better to leave life in this very chamber this night, <margin>800</margin> escaping all these wicked reproaches by an unexpected death, before accomplishing these shameful and unmentionable things."

She spoke, and went to the casket <note>original: "phōriamon"</note> in which lay many of her drugs, some healing, some deadly. Placing it upon her knees, she wept; she soaked her lap <margin>805</margin> with unceasing tears. They flowed uncontrollably as she piteously mourned her own fate. She was eager to choose a soul-destroying drug, so that she might taste it. Already she was undoing the fastenings of the casket...

<margin>**To Hellas]** He refers now to the whole region of Phthiotis <note>A region in central Greece</note> as 'Hellas,' using the same name for the country as the city which Argos founded.</margin>

<margin>**Indeed once even Theseus]** Through these words, Jason invites Medea to sail away with him, offering Ariadne as an example—the savior of Theseus. He mentions that her crown was turned into a constellation <note>The Corona Borealis</note>; yet he does not tell the whole truth, for Ariadne was abandoned by Theseus on Naxos. According to some, she was wedded by Dionysus, by whom she bore Oenopion, Thoas, Staphylus, Latramys, Euanthes, and Tauropolis. Homer testifies that Theseus did not actually bring her to Athens, but that she died after being abandoned, in the passage where Odysseus says: *'I saw Phaedra and Procris and beautiful Ariadne, daughter of baneful Minos, whom Theseus once tried to carry off from Crete to the hill of sacred Athens, but he had no joy of her.'* <note>Odyssey 11.321</note>. Regarding the crown being placed among the stars by Dionysus, Aratus <note>An ancient Greek didactic poet</note> says: *'And that very crown, which Dionysus set as a glorious sign when Ariadne passed away.'*</margin>

<margin>**But she]** Through these lines, he urges Medea to sail with him, using the love of Ariadne as an example, implying she went with Theseus to Athens.</margin>

<margin>**Courtesy]** Refers to her manner of conversation and wisdom. As Homer says: *'You seem like a courteous person.'*</margin>

<margin>**Nectarean]** Instead of "pleasant." I say it is delightful, like nectar.</margin>

<margin>**Without hesitation]** Some write "smiling forth." The doubling of the preposition is emphatic; it shows more clearly the haste and readiness with which the gift was stripped bare.</margin>

<margin>**Unsparingly/Without hesitation]** She spoke to him without further thought; she, no longer hesitating to look at him or overthinking, took the drug from her breast-band. This shows the intensity of her love.</margin>

<margin>**Drawing out]** Instead of "taking away," or "draining," or "emptying."</margin>

**Sparkling** <gloss>original: "amarygas"</gloss> ] these are <gloss>to the</gloss> continuous movements. It is also said of fire that it "sparkles" <note>original: "amaryssien"</note>, from the way the flame continuously leaps. Homer says, "He watched the sparkling <note>original: "marmarygas"</note> of their feet," either indicating continuous or rapid movement. **Melting** <gloss>original: "tekomene"</gloss> ] he paraphrases the Homeric line, "his heart was warmed <note>original: "iainthe"</note> as when the dew on the ears of corn falls upon the ripening harvest." Therefore, that which is "melting" is certainly pouring itself out. Homer says, "and straightaway the wax was warmed," when the great strength of the sun called upon it. However, "warmed" is not in every case the same as "melted." Whence Homer, having said "was warmed," added "as if," using a metaphor for when the stalks of grain are held upright or raised up. Thus, the moisture is an emphatic expression of the pleasure of the stalks, as is the case with living things when the dew clings to the fruit. So also the...

<margin>1015</margin> ...soul, she would have bestowed it upon him in her joy as he sat there.

---

...and the soul of Menelaus was moved to delight by the words of Antilochus. To "fix" <note>original: "pēxai"</note> is to compare either a soul that has been shaped or one that is persuasive. Therefore, the word "melted" <note>original: "teketai"</note> can also be read in the sense of pleasure. For that which is melting is certainly being dissolved and softened. Thus, one can say that Medea was entirely dissolved and set afloat. **Having watched for the middle of the night** <gloss>original: "diammoireda phylaxas"</gloss> ] some observe certain constellations when they reach the mid-heaven and midnight, and those near the horizon, some setting and others rising, or the heights of the Great Bear. **Otherwise:** "divided into parts" <note>original: "diammoireda"</note> instead of saying the heaven is divided into equal portions of the zodiac, so that the rising of the stars and the zodiacal signs are at the mid-heaven. **Circular** <gloss>original: "periegea"</gloss> ] that which is rounded and spherical. **Sacrifice a ram** ] place the slaughtered and untamed animal upon the fire. **To lay the raw pieces** <note>original: "omothetein"</note> is to offer the first-fruits of the limbs of the sacrificial victim while raw. **Only-begotten** <gloss>original: "mounogene"</gloss> ] Hesiod says, "Nor did the only-begotten goddess have a lesser share of honor." Musaeus records that Zeus, having fallen in love with Asteria, lay with her and gave her to Perses, and from her Hecate was born to him.

## BOOK THREE

**Or even the island of Aiaia** <note>original: "Ἠὲ καὶ Αἰαίης νῆσος"</note>] Aiaia is an island located in the Phasis river, where the Golden Fleece was kept. This is the capital city of the Colchian people. **In the high [mountains]** <note>original: "αἰπεινοῖσιν"</note>] Herodotus records that Thessaly is surrounded on all sides by mountains. Hellanicus states that Deucalion, the son of Prometheus, ruled over Thessaly, and that he established an altar to the twelve gods. Although other rivers flow into it—four of which are particularly notable: the Peneus, the Apidanus, the Panisus, and the Enipeus—when these waters mingle, the Peneus prevails in name, making the others anonymous. **And well-pastured** <note>original: "Καὶ εὔβοτος"</note>] This means the land is suitable for grazing or possesses fine livestock. **There Prometheus** <note>original: "Ἔνθα Προμηθεὺς"</note>] [He notes] that

<column-break/>

"Houses—where will you pass from here across the sea in your ship?

Of Pasiphae, who is a kinsman of my father."

---

Deucalion was the son of Prometheus and Pandora, as Hesiod says in the first book of the *Catalogues*; others say Hellen was the son of Prometheus and Pyrrha. Hellanicus, in the first book of his *Deucalionea*, says that Deucalion ruled over Thessaly. In the same work, Hellanicus states that Deucalion established the altars of the twelve gods. **Son of Iapetus** <note>original: "Ἰαπετιονίδης"</note>] It is not mentioned from which woman Prometheus begat Deucalion. There is also another Deucalion about whom Hellanicus writes. And yet another, the son of Minos, whom Pherecydes mentions in his fourth book, and whom Acantus or Aesippus remembers in the *Arcadics*. **This land Haemonia** <note>original: "Αἱμονίην δή"</note>] They used to address Thessaly as Haemonia. It had other names as well. It was also called Pyrrhodia, after Pyrrha, the wife of Deucalion. 
> In ancient times, Thessaly was called Pyrrha; as Rhianus says: "The ancients once called it Pyrrha, from Pyrrha, the ancient wife of Deucalion; but later Haemonia, from Haemon, whom Pelasgus begat as his strongest son. Haemon in turn begat Thessalus. From this Thessalus, the people changed their name." 
Others say the land was named after Thessalus the son of Pheidippus, the son of Heracles, after the Trojan War. It is divided into four parts: Pelasgiotis, Thessaliotis, Iolcitis, and Phthiotes. Apollodorus sets these out in the *Catalogue of Ships*.

**Son of Aeolus** <note>original: "Αἰολίδεω"</note>] [The poet means] not directly the son of Aeolus, but a descendant of Aeolus. For Sisyphus was the son of Aeolus, and his children <margin>1095</margin> were Almus and Porphyrion. From Chrysogone (daughter of Almus) and the god Poseidon, Minyas was born, who founded the city of Orchomenus. It is for this reason he is called **Son of Aeolus** <note>original: "Αἰολίδης"</note>, <margin>1100</margin> because Sisyphus was known as the son of Aeolus. Thus, Minyas is a descendant of Aeolus on his mother’s side, though his father was Poseidon. This is why Apollonius says that upon entering <margin>1105</margin> Boeotia, he founded Orchomenus as a neighbor to the Thebans.

**Would that as to Theseus** <note>original: "Αἴθε γὰρ ὡς Θησεῖ"</note>] Jason very persuasively brings this up to her to encourage her to agree <margin>1110</margin> with his plan, as she is already gripped by love.

**Soothing** <note>original: "Καταψύχων"</note>] This means softening or calming.

**Vehement** <note>original: "Ἀδινῷ"</note>] Here, the word means <margin>1115</margin> pitiful and sorrowful.

**They will attend** <note>original: "Πορσανέουσι"</note>] Here used in the sense of "they will honor," and they will regard her as a goddess; with reverence. When Jason later says, "You shall **prepare** <note>original: "Πορσανέας"</note> our marriage bed <margin>1120</margin> in our bridal chambers," it signifies how she will be received, etc.

**Alone from his companions**] The phrase "alone from himself" <note>original: οἰόθεν οἶος</note> does not quite fit here. For he is one man apart from many. Specifically, one should say, "alone from the others."

**In peace they cared**] This is a solecism <note>A grammatical error or intentional quirk in usage.</note>. For the logic is that they, being quiet, were cared for by themselves, as if they were caring for one another. It should have said they cared for "their own affairs," as is proper for themselves.

**Of the Aonian dragon**] Instead of saying "the Boeotian dragon." For Aonia was the later name for Boeotia. He calls Thebes **Ogygian** <margin>1170</margin> after Ogygus, who was their king. Regarding Europa and the arrival of Cadmus <margin>1175</margin> at Thebes, Lysimachus in the first book of *Thebaica* has collected much conflicting material in a surprising way.

» The Sun indeed from afar] He calls the "dark earth" the place below the horizon. For he has used "setting" to refer to the horizon as handed down by the ancients. And he calls those toward the west "Ethiopians." By "dark earth," he means the unseen hemisphere near Erebus <note>The primordial deity representing darkness; a region of the underworld.</note>. Some understand this as the place below the horizon in Apollonius. He calls the sun "Evening" <note>original: Ἑσπέριον</note>, signifying the hour at which the setting follows it. "The furthest peaks of the Ethiopians" refers to the outermost parts, as they lie at the edge of the inhabited world. He did not speak correctly, however, in saying the sun sets "beneath the peaks of the Ethiopians." For the horizon circle is marked by nature, and indicated by sight. 

» Night with her horses] The yoking of a chariot to Night is a concept more recent than the time of Homer. 

» Immediately when] He says that Jason, having gone out at the turning of the Bear, noted the time that had been told to him by Medea. 

» Under clear skies] Under the clear air of men. "By the clear sky," meaning a moist place due to the silence of men. <note>The commentator is interpreting the quiet, open meadow as a place of ritual purity.</note>

### THE ARGONAUTICA

<margin>
**Like when [he goes to] the Isthmus:** The Isthmian games are those held at the Isthmus of Corinth. They were originally dedicated to Poseidon, but later to Melicertes, by the command of Sisyphus (the son of Aeolus), who was then king of Corinth. When the body of Melicertes was washed ashore and appeared to Sisyphus at Corinth, he honored him—being his nephew and the son of Athamas—with the Isthmian games. In ancient times, the victors were crowned with pine; later, with dry celery <note>Often referred to as wild parsley.</note>. Musaeus says in his work *On the Isthmian Games* that there are actually two contests held at the Isthmus: one for Poseidon and one for Melicertes.
</margin>

Stand by the contest. Along with them, a vast crowd rushed.

Very steadily they went, for the well-wrought plow-handle, made of adamant <note>Adamant was a mythical, indestructible metal, often associated with diamonds or tempered steel in ancient literature.</note>, guided them. For a while, the bulls raged in vain, breathing out a violent flame of fire; and the blast rose up like the roar of night winds, which sailors, fearing greatly, have furled their large sail to avoid. Not long after, urged by the spear-point, they moved on; and the **rough** <margin>**The rough ground was split:** Now used to mean the harsh earth was being divided.</margin> ground was broken open behind them, split by the strength of the bulls and the mighty plowman. 1330

encouraged him with words. But he, scooping up water from the river’s currents in his helmet, quenched his thirst.

against the hunters, while much foam flows from its mouth to the ground in its rage.

1375 And like a star of fire that leaps from heaven,

---

The poet uses the word "trail" to describe the light dragged along by the object's speed. Musaeus <note>A legendary semi-mythical poet of early Greece.</note> says such apparitions are carried away from the Ocean and extinguished in the upper air. Apollonius has persuasively called the stars mentioned by Musaeus "glittering flashes" (marmarugas). For the Greeks call those flashes that become impossible to catch with the eye due to their speed *marmarugas*. 

However, some critics find it unconvincing to compare Jason to such a star when he is embarking on a dangerous labor, since a shooting star is extinguished as soon as it appears. But if someone argues that he is being compared to the "Fiery One" <note>Pyroeis: The ancient Greek name for the planet Mars, named for its reddish, fire-like glow.</note>, about which Pericleites writes in his mathematical work *On the Chalcidians*—speaking of the planets—he says that the "Fiery One" is held in a single harmony, called "Mars" by the Greeks and "Hercules" by the Chalcidians; and that as it moves, flashes and stars are produced in its wake. Yet the "Fiery One" is actually slow-moving. Finally, the word "Trail" can also refer to a furrow in the earth.

> Now you yourself, Goddess Muse, child of Zeus, tell of the labor
> and the schemes of the Colchian
> maiden. For truly, my
> mind within me wavers in speechless doubt, as I ponder
> whether I should call it the lovesick grief of ruinous folly, or
> 5 a shameful flight, by which she left the tribes of the Colchians.
> Now he [Jason], among the men of the people who were the best

formerly called the Cronian. There, they also kill Apsyrtus by a trick. Because Zeus was angry at this and wished to turn back the Argonauts with a foul wind, Hera sends them to the winds; the ship is carried through the Eridanus [Po River] into the sea around Sardinia. They are purified by Circe and sail through the Wandering Rocks, with Thetis and the other Nereids escorting them. They sail past the Sirens. Having been saved, they reach the place formerly called Drepane, and later called Corcyra, where the Colchians who had been pursuing them through the Symplegades catch up to them; these Colchians demanded Medea from Alcinous. He, having postponed the judgment until the next day, said that if she were still a virgin, she must be sent back to her father; but if she were a wife, she should be given to her husband. Therefore, the marriage takes place that night. And so the Colchians, having failed in their purpose, remain in Scheria, fearing to return to Aeëtes; but the Argonauts, having sailed away, are dragged down to the Syrtis of Libya. And there Canthus and Mopsus die. As the Argonauts are in despair about their safety, Triton appears and shows how they will be saved. Having carried the ship, they brought it to Lake Tritonis. Then they arrive in Crete, where they were forced to flee by Talos; whom Medea destroyed with incantations. After these things, they arrive in Aegina. And from there they are saved to Thessaly. **Now you yourself, Goddess... tell of the labor:** the vocative particle "O" is missing here. It should be understood as: "O Goddess." The meaning is: "Now, O Muse, tell me of the labor and the plans of Medea." I am in doubt whether she left her fatherland because of a passion of love or to flee from mistreatment. **In speechless doubt:** <note>original: amphasie</note> this means in a state of difficulty or speechlessness. Thus, he is unable to say whether she left her fatherland because of a passion of love or by making a flight from mistreatment (that is, fearing lest she be mistreated by her father). In the word for speechless doubt, the *a* signifies negation [a-], and the *m* was inserted. **The word "shameful":** <note>original: aeikeliou</note> this is used as an adjective modifying "flight," and therefore matches its case; however, it should be understood as a common noun in the genitive case, so that it means "a flight of shamefulness." In this way, the meaning is preserved.

### F O U R T H   B O O K. 175

All night long, King Aeetes was plotting a deep snare against the heroes in his halls, his spirit stirred with heavy anger over the hateful contest. He did not believe for a moment that these feats had been accomplished without the help of his own daughters. 

But Hera cast a most painful fear into Medea's heart. She trembled like a nimble fawn <note>original: κεμάς</note> that the cry of hounds has terrified in the deep thickets of the wood. For she immediately sensed the truth: that her aid to Jason would not remain hidden, and soon she would face the full weight of her father’s wrath. 

She lived in terror of her handmaidens who were her confidants; her eyes were filled with fire, and a terrible ringing sounded in her ears. Often she clutched at her throat, and often she tore at her hair by the roots, groaning in bitter pain. And truly, the maiden would have perished there beyond her fated time by drinking poison—thwarting Hera's designs—if the goddess had not stirred her to flee with the sons of Phrixus <note>Medea's nephews, who were also fleeing Aeetes</note> even in her state of terror. 

Her fluttering heart grew warm within her breast. Turning back, she gathered all the drugs from her chest and poured them together into the fold of her robe. She kissed her bed and the double doors on either side of the entrance, and she touched the walls with her hands. Tearing off a long lock of hair, she left it in her bedchamber for her mother as a memorial of her maidenhood. She lamented with a sobbing voice:

"I go, leaving behind this long tress for you in my place, O my mother. Farewell to you as I go on my long journey. Farewell, Chalciope, and all this house. Stranger, I wish the sea had shattered you before you ever reached the Colchian land!" 

So she spoke, and from her eyelids, she poured a flood of tears.

<column-break/>

**Over the hateful contest:** He calls it a "hateful" labor because he himself was full of hatred and distress regarding it.

**Most painful:** This is either formed by negation <note>original: "ἀλγεινότατον," from algein, to feel pain</note> or it refers to something that occupies one’s thoughts, so that one might say it comes from "taking care" <note>original: "alégein"</note>.

**Fawn:** A <term>kemas</term> is a young deer. Scholars say there is a difference between a *kemas* and a *nebros*. A *kemas* is one still sleeping in the cave (derived from the word for "lying down"), while a *nebros* is one that is older, going out to graze and feed.

**Thickets:** Meaning denseness or thick growth.

**Sensed:** This comes from the verb "to think" <note>original: "οἴω"</note> by a grammatical division. The word "sensed" <note>original: "ὀΐσατο"</note> uses a long *iota*. This is similar to how "dark water" is related to "cloud," or how Sophocles in his play *Ixion* uses a term for "damaged," and Homer uses a term for "much-damaged."

**Confidants:** Those who know a secret along with someone; witnesses.

---

**Her ears rang:** Her hearing was ringing as if people were already coming to drag her away to her father.

**Of her throat:** The <term>laikanie</term> refers to the windpipe through which the breath is carried from the lungs.

**By the hair:** Specifically, tearing at the hair on the temples.

**Her heart was winged:** Meaning her heart became light or was relieved. Her soul quickly shifted from its previous reasoning and turned toward a sense of hope or cheerfulness.

**Having slipped away** | Secretly passing out of the house; having run away, fleeing.

**Around difficult** | Troublesome or evil, or those roots given up from the earth for an evil purpose. For destructive drugs are more numerous than those that bring safety. Or, it refers to roots that are pulled up from the ground with great difficulty.

**I am not the only one [to wander] toward the Latmian...** | Latmos is a mountain in Caria <note>modern-day Turkey</note> where there is a cave in which Endymion used to dwell. There is also a city there called Heracleia. Hesiod says Endymion was the son of Aethlius (son of Zeus) and Calyce, and that he received a gift from Zeus to be the "steward of his own death," dying only when he wished. The historians Peisander, Acusilaus, Pherecydes, and Nicander (in the second book of his *Aetolica*), and Theopompus all agree. 
However, in the poem *The Great Eoiae*, it is said that Endymion was taken up by Zeus into heaven, but he fell in love with Hera. He was deceived by a cloud-phantom (Nephele) into believing his love was returned, and for his presumption, he was cast down into the underworld. 
Regarding the Moon’s love for him, Sappho <note>The famous lyric poet from Lesbos</note> and Nicander (in the second book of his *Europa*) provide the history. It is said the Moon descends into this cave to visit Endymion. Epimenides says that while Endymion lived among the gods, he fell in love with Hera, and because Zeus was angry, Endymion asked to sleep forever. Ibycus says he ruled over the region of Elis. Others say he was granted divinity because of his great justice.

# BOOK FOUR

They say that he was deified, and that he asked Zeus for the gift of eternal sleep. Some say he was a **Spartan**, others an **Elean**. <note>A person from Elis, a region in the Peloponnese.</note> However, some reject the myth of **Endymion’s sleep** entirely. They claim he was actually a hunter who hunted by moonlight because that is when the wild beasts come out to graze; during the day, he would rest in a cave, which led people to believe he was always sleeping. Others interpret the myth allegorically, saying that Endymion was the first to attempt the study of the heavens through **natural philosophy**. <note>The ancient precursor to science and astronomy.</note> The moon provided him with the opportunities for his study through its illumination and movements. Because of this, he spent his nights occupied with celestial patterns and did not sleep, resting instead during the day. Others say it was simply because Endymion was a man who loved to sleep. From this comes the proverb, "**Endymion’s sleep**," used for those who sleep a great deal, or those who do something so lazily that they seem to be asleep. Theocritus also mentions this: *“Enviable to me is he who sleeps the sleep that knows no turning, Endymion.”* <note>original: "Zalōtos men emin o ton atropon hypnon iauōn Endymiōn"</note>

***

"Nor am I the only one who burns with love for the beautiful Endymion.
Truly, how often have you, you dog <note>A harsh address common in ancient epic to denote a shameless or persistent person.</note>, with your deceitful songs,
Reminded me of my own love, so that in the dark night
You might perform your sorcery undisturbed? These were the deeds dear to you.
But now, it seems, you yourself share in a similar ruin.
A painful deity has given you Jason to be your miserable affliction.
But go now, and endure,
Wise though you may be, to bear this much-sighed-for grief."
So she spoke; and Medea’s feet swiftly carried her as she hurried along.
Gladly she climbed the banks of the river,
Looking across to the bright gleam of the fire, where through the night
The heroes were celebrating their victory with festivities.
Then, through the darkness, she called out with a piercing, high-pitched voice
To the youngest of Phrixus' sons on the opposite shore.

<column-break/>

**"Truly, how often"** | It is a myth that sorceresses <note>original: "pharmakides"</note> pull down the moon with their incantations. This is what the **Thessalian women** are thought to do, though they are mistaken in their belief. For instance, **Aglaonice**, daughter of Hegemon, <margin>65</margin> was skilled in astronomy; knowing when lunar eclipses were about to occur, she would claim that she was pulling down the goddess. Immediately after, she happened to fall into **misfortunes** <margin>70</margin> because she lost some of her family members, for which she paid the penalty to both <note>Likely referring to paying a penalty to both the gods and her reputation.</note>. From this, a proverb is used in life for those burdened by misfortunes, saying: "**She pulls down the moon.**" In the author of the *Naupaktika* <note>A lost epic poem often attributed to Carcinus or Hesiod.</note>, Medea does not leave of her own choice, but is called out in the evening. The Argonauts, by a plan, find the right time for her removal—as a parody of Aeëtes’ union with his wife Eurylyte—and with Idmon advising them, they flee, and Medea sails with them. **"Reminded me of my own love"** | This refers to the love of Endymion, caused by your spells. **"In the dark"** | That is, when the moon is absent, due to my own preoccupation with my lover. Some take this to mean the **eclipse** of the moon, which is said to be "taken down" by sorceresses. Therefore, the ancients called eclipses "takings-down" <note>original: "kathaireseis"</note>. **Otherwise:** **"Truly, how often"** and the following lines should be understood thus: you truly frequent the cave often, remembering the love of Endymion, and remembering him, O you dog, so that you may perform your sorcery undisturbed in the dark night with deceitful songs, which were the deeds dear to you. **"Miserable"** | He means that which is incurable. **"They were celebrating"** <note>original: "edaon"</note> | Instead of saying "they were burning" <note>as in a fire</note>, it means "ethereal." **"High-pitched"** | Intensely, loudly. **"From the other side"** | Directly from the mainland; from the words *peran* (beyond) and *peras* (limit) comes *peraiothen* (from the opposite side). From this, the word **Mainland** <note>original: "Epeiros"</note> is used for all land by extension; but strictly it refers to land that extends into the **infinite** <note>original: "apeiron"</note>. As Euripides made clear, "Calling the land 'Mainland' because it is 'Infinite'."

“Let us flee before he comes...” Apollonius says that Medea fled to the ship at night while Aeetes was holding a council of the Colchians <note>The people of Colchis, where the Golden Fleece was kept.</note> concerning the dispute with the heroes. <column-break/>

Phrontis recognized the girl’s voice, and he pointed out the sound to his brothers and the son of Aeson <note>Jason.</note>. The comrades watched in silence and wonder when they realized it was truly her. Thrice she cried out, and thrice Phrontis answered her in turn at the urging of the group. Meanwhile, the heroes were rowing with swift oars toward the sound. They had not yet cast the ship's mooring lines onto the opposite shore when **Jason** leaped with swift feet from the high deck to the land. After him, Phrontis and Argus—the two sons of Phrixus—sprang to the ground. Medea, clasping both their knees with her hands, addressed them:

“Save me, my friends, in my misery, and save yourselves as well from **Aeetes**. For everything has been revealed and no remedy remains. Let us flee upon the ship before he can mount his swift horses. I will give you the **Golden Fleece**, for I shall lull the guardian serpent to sleep. But you, stranger <note>She addresses Jason directly.</note>, take the gods you worship as witnesses to the promises you made to me. Do not let me, having fled so far from home for your sake, become a thing of scorn and shame for lack of a protector.”

She spoke in deep distress. The heart of the son of Aeson <note>Jason</note> rejoiced. Immediately, as she lay prostrate at his knees, he raised her up gently and embraced her, offering words of encouragement:

“Lady, let **Zeus** of Olympus himself be my witness, and **Hera**, the goddess of marriage and wife of Zeus, that I will truly establish you as my wedded wife in my own halls when we have returned home to the land of Greece.”

So he spoke, and immediately joined his hand with hers.

***

The scholar Apollonius has depicted Medea promising the Fleece to Jason after she has fled from the house of Aeetes. However, the author of the *Naupactica* depicts her bringing the Fleece with her during her flight, as it was kept inside the house of Aeetes. Herodorus, on the other hand, says that after the Argonauts had departed, Jason was sent by Aeetes to get the Fleece; Jason then went and killed the dragon, brought the Fleece back to Aeetes, and Aeetes then deceitfully invited them to dinner.
