# ARGONAUTICA

It is called Tithonis, as Eratosthenes mentions in his *Geography*. The river Lycus, flowing from the Araxes, mingles with the Phasis and then, losing its own name, empties into the sea. Others say this same thing happens with the Inachus, the Pamissus, and the Spercheius in Thessaly. For when they all flow into the same place, they are called the Spercheius. The Araxes is a river of Scythia <note>A region of Central Eurasia</note>. Metrodorus, in the first book of his *History of Tigranes*, says that the Thermodon is also called the Araxes. He calls the Caspian the "Caucasian Sea" because it borders the Caucasus. **Another view:** It is better to understand the "Caucasian Sea" as the Euxine <note>The Black Sea</note>, which is near the Caucasus; for the Phasis does not empty into the Caspian, but into the Euxine.

**Swirls of smoke:** These are the coils of thick smoke, used as a comparison. Because the text says, "one after another rises," it shows the continuous nature of the repetition. **Coiled:** Refers to the turnings and windings of the heavy smoke. **High-floating:** Suspended in the air. **He shook his vast coils:** He said this hyperbolically, describing the monstrous size of the dragon. **Coils** (*rhumbonas*): The turnings of the spiral, the laboring movements. Even Euripides in his *Heracles* says: "You, the self-begotten [source] of all things, in the ethereal whirl <note>original: "rumbos"</note>." This means motion. This is also why the small wheel moved by sorceresses is called a *rhymbion*. From this, they speak of circular motions. **Dry:** Parched. **Overarching:** Covered or protected. **Approached:** Rushed forward. **Soothe:** To put to sleep. **Night-wanderer:** Referring to the goddess <note>Hecate</note> who dwells underground. **Successful onset:** Either a meeting that is not to be appeased, or one that is sought after. **Charmed by the spell:** Humbled by the incantation. **Spine:** The bones of snakes are called the "spine" <note>original: "akantha"</note>, and "earth-born" is used generally, as with other reptiles. **Snap around:** To seize from both sides.

But Hecataeus of Miletus says they passed from the Phasis river into the Great Ocean, then from there into the Nile, and from there into our sea <note>the Mediterranean</note>. But Artemidorus of Ephesus says this is a falsehood, for the Phasis does not meet the Ocean, but flows down from the mountains. Eratosthenes says the same in his *Geography*. Timagetus, in the first book of his *On Harbors*, says the Ister <note>the Danube</note> flows down from the Celtic mountains, then empties into a Celtic lake; after this, the water splits in two, one part flowing into the Euxine <note>Black</note> Sea, and the other into the Celtic Sea <note>the Adriatic</note>. He says the Argonauts sailed through this mouth and reached Tyrrhenia <note>Etruria, Italy</note>. Apollonius follows him in this. Cosmos in the eighth book of his *Egyptian History*, and Leon in the first book of his *To His Mother*, and Knosos in the first book of his *Geography of Asia*, all call them the most ancient of all.

<meta>This page continues the speech of Argos to the Argonauts, explaining the ancient history of Egypt and Arcadia to justify their return route via the Ister (Danube) and the antiquity of the Egyptian maps. # BOOK FOUR

Some say the Egyptians were the first of men; and that in Egypt, the first city to be built was Thebes. Nicanor agrees with these accounts, as does Archemachus in his *Metonymies*, and Xenagoras in the first book of his *Chronicles*. Hippys also says that the Egyptians were the most ancient of peoples, a conclusion reached by considering the temperament of their air and the extreme fertility of the water of the Nile. Apollonius says they existed before any of the stars appeared in the sky; for this reason, they are thought to have understood the nature of the stars and to have given them names. The twelve signs of the Zodiac they called "Counseling Gods" <note>original: "theous boulaious"</note>, and the planets they called "Rod-bearers" <note>original: "rabdophorous"</note>. 

However, Herodotus says that the Phrygians were more ancient. He tells how Psammetichus, the king of the Egyptians, wishing to determine which people were the eldest, gave two infants to a shepherd; he ordered that no one should speak any word to them, and that they should only be given the milk of a goat. After two years had passed, the children let out a cry, saying "bek." It is said that among the Phrygians, this is the word for bread. Therefore, they concluded from this that the Phrygians were the first people. Others, however, say it is foolish to believe this. They argue that the children, hearing the bleating of the sheep, and being driven by their natural instincts, turned their voices toward that articulate sound.

<margin>
**Such were the Arcadians]** He says that the Arcadians alone of the Greeks were the most ancient.
**265 Of the Apidaneans]** This refers to the Peloponnesians, named after Apis, the son of Phoroneus.
**Arcadians, who previously]** The Arcadians are thought to have existed before the moon, as Eudoxus also says in his *Circuit*. And Theodorus in...
</margin>

> **P**ondering: "What sort were the Apidanean Arcadians,
> **A**rcadians, who even before the moon, it is told,
> **L**ived eating acorns in the mountains. Not yet was the Pelasgian
> **L**and ruled by the glorious sons of Deucalion;
> **A**t that time, the fertile land of Eeria <note>An ancient name for Egypt</note> was called
> **M**other Egypt by the men of earlier generations;
> **A**nd the fair-flowing river Triton, by which all
> **E**eria is watered; for never does rain from Zeus soak it."

...his twenty-ninth book, says that the moon appeared only a little before the war of Heracles against the Giants. Chios in his *Positions* and Dionysius of Chalcis in the first book of his *Foundations* say the same thing; they even say there is a tribe in Arcadia called the "Selenites" <note>Moon-people</note>. Mnaseas says that Arcadian kings ruled before the moon existed. Aristotle, in his *Constitution of Tegea*, says that barbarians inhabited Arcadia but were driven out by the Arcadians who attacked them before the moon rose. Because of this, they were named "Proselenes" <note>original: "proselēnoi" — meaning "before the moon"</note>. 

Doris, in the fifteenth book of his *Macedonian History*, says that Arcas, from whom Arcadia takes its name, was the son of Orchomenus; for this reason, there is also a city in Arcadia called Orchomenus. Some say that Endymion <note>A figure often associated with the moon in myth</note> discovered the cycles and paths of the moon, and for this reason the Arcadians were called "Proselenes," since Arcas was related to Endymion. Others say they were called this because of Typhon, while Xenagoras says it was because of Atlas. 

**Ruled by the sons of Deucalion]** Those descended from Deucalion held power and ruled over Thessaly, as Hecataeus and Hesiod say. Thessaly was called Pelasgia after Pelasgus, who ruled there. 

**And the river Triton]** Various causes were given by the ancients for the flooding of the Nile. Anaxagoras says it overflows because of the melting of snow; Euripides follows him, saying: "The beautiful maiden-stream is filled when the white snow melts and moistens the soil." Aeschylus and Sophocles also assumed that it did not snow in the regions of Egypt itself, but that the flooding of the Nile was caused by the melting of snow elsewhere. Nicagoras says it flows from the land of the Ethiopians. Democritus the natural philosopher says the Nile receives its overflow from the sea that lies to the south; he claims the water becomes fresh because of the distance and the length of its passage, being drawn up by the heat. Because of this, he says, it has a distinct taste. Akion of Chios says that in winter, the sun being beneath the earth sends the water up, but in summer, being above the earth, it draws it out.

# THE ARGONAUTICA

## THE NILE AND THE CONQUEROR SESONCHOSIS

...years, because the earth is heated more [in the south]. For this reason, the ground becomes relaxed and gives up more water. Ephorus, however, says that Egypt is "river-silt" <note>original: "potamochoson"</note>. He claims that when the earth is cracked by the sun in the spring, the water breaks out and increases the flow. Thales of Miletus says that the "Etesian" winds <note>The seasonal Mediterranean winds</note> drive clouds toward the mountains of Ethiopia, where they break apart. Furthermore, when these winds blow against the current of the river, they push back the sea and cause the Nile to flood as the water is held up. Diogenes of Apollonia believes that the sun snatches water from the sea, which then falls into the Nile. He thinks the Nile fills in the summer because the sun turns the moisture from beneath the earth into the river. The Nile was formerly called the Triton; it was renamed after Nile, the son of Cyclops and grandson of Tantalus, who ruled the country, as Hermippus tells us.

<margin>
**Rain enough]** There is an ambiguity in the grammar here. It means either "the fields sprout enough" or "the rain does not wet them enough," since it does not rain continuously in Egypt.
**Thence some say]** Sesonchosis, king of all Egypt after Horus (the son of Isis and Osiris), set out and conquered all of Asia and most of Europe.
</margin>

> "Rain enough falls, and from the outflows the fields sprout their grain.
> "From there, they say a certain man traveled all around
> "Europe and Asia, trusting in the strength and power of his people
<margin>Line 275</margin>
> "And in his own courage. Countless cities did he
> "Found as he went; some are still inhabited,
> "And some are not—for a long age has passed since then.
> "Yet Aea remains firm even now, and the descendants
> "Of those men whom he settled there to dwell.
> "Indeed, they preserve the written records of their fathers,
<margin>Line 280</margin>
> "The pillars <note>original: "kyrbias"</note> on which are all the paths and boundaries of the world."

More accurate details about this king are found in Herodotus. Theopompus, in his third book, calls him Sesostris. Herodotus says that in the lands he conquered through war, he set up pillars describing how he won. But if they surrendered without a fight, he added the image of female genitalia to the pillars as a symbol of their "softness" <note>An ancient way of mocking those who would not fight</note>. Regarding the era of Sesonchosis, Apollonius says only that "a long age has passed." But Dicaearchus, in his second book, says that Sesonchosis took an interest in the Greek way of life and established laws so that no one could abandon the trade of their fathers—for he believed this was the beginning of greed. **"And some are not"]** This means either the cities have perished or they have been renamed and are no longer recognized by their current inhabitants. Time is the cause of this.

Dicaearchus, in his first book, says that Sesonchosis became king after Horus, the son of Isis and Osiris. He calculates that from the reign of Sesonchosis to the reign of Nilus was 2,500 years; from the reign of Nilus to the first Olympiad was 436 years. Thus, the total time is 2,936 years. **"Aea remains firm"]** He means that Aea <note>The capital of Colchis, where the Golden Fleece was kept</note> has remained undisturbed from the time of Sesonchosis until his own day, inhabited by the descendants of those settled by the king. He uses the term "descendants" <note>original: "uionoi," literally 'grandsons'</note> loosely, just as the "Heraclidae" refers not only to the children of Hercules but to all his later progeny. Apollonius says the Colchians are Egyptian colonists; Scymnus also says this in his work *On Asia*. Herodotus confirms it, noting that they practice circumcision, weave linen in the same way, and follow Egyptian laws. **"Indeed, they preserve the written records"]** This refers to their written laws. He says they also have the laws of their ancestors and pillars <note>stelae</note> on which are recorded the maps of land and sea. **"Pillars"]** <note>original: "kyrbias"</note> Stelae. He is referring to the revolving tablets <note>axones</note> on which laws are written, as the comic poet Aristophanes mentions. Apollodorus says that every public writing or law is called a *kyrbis*, because the ancients, when setting up stones, used to record their decisions on...

<meta>catchword: ...the [ταῖς]</meta>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Book 4 of the *Argonautica*. The previous page discussed the ancient records of Egypt and the conquests of Sesonchosis. ### BOOK FOUR

...those who record things. **Kyrbeis** <note>original: "kyrbeis"; ancient tablets of law or ritual</note>, derived as if from *korypheis* <note>original: "korypheis"; meaning "peaks" or "summits"</note>, by shortening the word and changing the 'p' to 'b', results in *kyrbeis*. Later, when they wrote on whitewashed wooden boards, they called those *kyrbeis* as well. Specifically, *kyrbeis* are the tablets that contain sacred records. Some say, as **Eratosthenes** <note>A famous 3rd-century BC scholar and head of the Library of Alexandria</note> claims, that the pillars called *axones* <note>original: "axones"; literally "axles"</note> in Athens, which contain the laws, are also *kyrbeis*. However, more precise scholars say that *axones* were square stones, while *kyrbeis* were triangular. Laws were written on both in Athens. **Horn]** They call all rivers "horns" of the Ocean because they are carried down from it. The **Ister** <note>The ancient Greek name for the lower Danube River</note> is a river in Scythia. As for the phrase "recognized the river from afar," it means they identified it and knew its course even from a distance.

<margin>
**Calling it sacred]** He says the **Ister** flows down from the land of the **Hyperboreans** <note>A mythical people of the far north</note> and the **Ripaean Mountains** (speaking this way in imitation of **Aeschylus** in his play *Prometheus Unbound*). He says that as it pours out between the **Scythians** and the **Thracians**, it splits: one stream empties into the sea near us <note>The Mediterranean/Aegean</note>, another falls into the "bitter sea," and a third into the **Adriatic Gulf**.
</margin>

> "Around the moist and gloomy [region] for those who observe it.
> "There is a certain river, the topmost **horn of the Ocean**,
> "Broad and deep enough to sustain a merchant ship;
> "Men call it the **Ister**, and they recognized it from afar.
> "For a time, it cuts through a vast expanse of land
<margin>285</margin>
> "As a single stream (for its springs murmur far off 
> "In the **Ripaean Mountains** under the blast of the North Wind),
> "But when it enters the borders of the **Thracians** and **Scythians**,
> "There its water splits in two; one part throws its stream 
> "Into the **Ionian Sea** <note>Here referring to the Adriatic</note>, and the other behind it
<margin>290</margin>
> "Is sent through a deep gulf, emptying into the **Trinacrian Sea** 
> "Which lies alongside our land; if this is indeed the truth."

**Scymnus** says in his sixteenth book *On Europe* that the Ister flows solely from a desert. The **Ripaean Mountains** are in the north, as **Callimachus** says: "From the Ripaean mountain of the fifth," or something similar. **Eratosthenes**, in his *Geography*, says it flows from desert places and surrounds the island of **Peuke**. No one except **Timagetus** records that the **Argonauts** sailed into our sea through this route; **Apollonius** followed him in this. For Scymnus says they sailed through the **Tanais** <note>The River Don</note> to the Great Sea <note>The Outer Ocean</note>, and from there came into our sea. He even digresses to say that when the Argonauts reached the mainland, they carried the *Argo* on rollers until they reached the sea. **Hesiod**, however, says they sailed through the **Phasis** <note>A river in Colchis, modern Georgia</note>. **Hecataeus** refutes him, recording that the Phasis does not empty into that sea, nor did they sail through the Tanais, but rather they took the same return voyage they had taken before; **Sophocles** in his *Scythians* and Callimachus record this as well. Because of this, some of the Scythians who sailed into the Adriatic did not find the Argonauts, while those who went through the **Cyanean Rocks** <note>The "Clashing Rocks" at the mouth of the Black Sea</note> found that they had sailed down to **Corcyra** <note>Modern Corfu</note>. The Ister, flowing from the Hyperboreans, when it reaches the area between Scythia and Thrace, splits into two: one part empties into the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note>, and the other into the **Tyrrhenian Sea**. **Trinacrian]** The Tyrrhenian Sea lies next to **Sicily**. It was formerly called **Trinacria** because it has three capes: **Pachynus**, **Lilybaeum**, and **Pelorus**. Apollonius, wishing to say something novel about the Ister, further subdivides the stream that flows into the Adriatic into two: saying one part goes to the Adriatic and the other to the Tyrrhenian Sea. For this reason, describing the outpouring, he called it "Trinacrian." **Which lies alongside our land]** If it is written "your land" <note>original: "hymeterēi"</note>, it would mean Greece; if "our land" <note>original: "hēmeterēi"</note>, it would mean the land of the Ister, for it lies near the **Colchians** in that way.

...further, because the earth becomes more heated. For this reason, the earth, being loosened, gives up more water. **Ephorus** <note>A 4th-century BC Greek historian</note> says that Egypt is "silted up" by the river. When the earth is cracked by the sun in the spring, the water is drawn up, and the stream increases. **Thales of Miletus** <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, often called the first philosopher</note> says that the clouds are driven by the **Etesian winds** <note>original: "etesiai"; annual Mediterranean winds</note> toward the mountains of Ethiopia, where they break apart. For when the gusts blow from the opposite direction of the river and fall upon the sea from the receding flood, the Nile receives the backflow. **Diogenes of Apollonia** <note>A 5th-century BC philosopher known for his theories on air and moisture</note> believes the water of the sea is snatched up by the sun, and then carried down into the Nile. He thinks the Nile fills up in the summer because the sun turns the moisture from beneath the earth toward that region. The Nile was previously called the **Triton**, but was renamed after **Neilos** the son of the Cyclops, son of **Tantalus**, who ruled the land, as **Hermippus** <note>A 3rd-century BC biographer and scholar</note> says.

—likewise most of Europe. More accurate details about him can be found in **Herodotus**. **Theopompus** <note>A 4th-century BC historian</note> calls him "Sesostris" in his third book. Herodotus says that if he conquered some people in war, he would set up pillars recording how he won; but if they surrendered without a fight, he added the image of female genitals to the pillars as a symbol of their "softness" or cowardice. Regarding the time in which Sesonchosis lived, Apollonius says only this: "for a vast age has passed since then." But **Dicaearchus** <note>A student of Aristotle and a geographer</note> says in his second book, *On the Greek Life*, that Sesonchosis concerned himself with Greek lifestyle and established laws so that no one could abandon their ancestral trade; for he thought this was the beginning of greed. He also says Sesonchosis was the first to discover how to ride horses. Others attribute these things to Horus.

<margin>**Or not.]**</margin> Either some of the cities have already disappeared, or having been renamed, they are unknown to the current inhabitants. The time elapsed since then has become unbelievable. Dicaearchus says in his first book that after Horus, the son of Isis and Osiris, Sesonchosis became king; thus from the reign of Sesonchosis until the reign of **Neilus** <note>The king for whom the river was renamed</note> there are 2,500 years. From the reign of Neilus until the first **Olympiad** <note>776 BC</note>, there are 436 years. So the total time is 2,936 years.

<margin>**But Aea indeed]**</margin> He says that Aea remains unbroken from the times of Sesonchosis until his own day, as do the descendants of those settled by Sesonchosis. He uses the term "grandsons" loosely, just as the "Heracleidae" refers not only to the children of Heracles, but to all his descendants. That the **Colchians** are colonists of the Egyptians, as Apollonius says, is also stated by **Scymnus** <note>A 2nd-century BC geographer</note> in his works on Asia; and Herodotus confirms it, mentioning their circumcision, their weaving of linen, and saying they use the same laws as the Egyptians.

<margin>**Who indeed [have] written]**</margin> He calls the laws "written." He says there are also laws from their ancestors among them, and pillars on which the maps of land and sea are recorded.

<margin>**Kyrbias]**</margin> Pillars. He refers to the *axones* <note>original: "axonas"; rotating tablets</note> on which laws are written, as **Aristophanes** the comic poet does. **Apollodorus** says that every public writing or law is called a *kyrbis* because the ancients, when setting up stones, used to record what had been decided on them...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the fourth book of Apollonius Rhodius’s *Argonautica*. Having discussed the Nile and the legendary migrations of the Egyptians, the commentator now turns to the ancient Greek legal tablets known as *kyrbeis* and the mysterious geography of the River Ister (the Danube), which the Argonauts are said to have navigated on their return journey.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR
### PAGE 187

...to record on **tablets** <note>original: "kyrbeis"</note>, which are like "summits" <note>original: "korypheis"</note>; through a contraction and the change of the letter *phi* to *beta*, they became *kyrbeis*. Later, when people wrote on whitened wooden boards, they called those *kyrbeis* as well. However, *kyrbeis* specifically are those which contain sacred records. As **Eratosthenes** <note>A famous polymath and librarian at Alexandria</note> says, people also call the **axles** <note>original: "axones"; revolving wooden beams used for displaying laws</note> in Athens *kyrbeis*, as they contain the laws. More precise scholars distinguish them: they say *axones* were square stones, while *kyrbeis* were triangular. In both cases, the laws of Athens were written upon them. **Horn** <note>original: "Keras"</note>: They call all the rivers that flow down from the Ocean "horns" of the Ocean. The **Ister** <note>The ancient name for the lower Danube River</note> is a river of Scythia. The phrase "known from afar" means that even from a great distance, people had labored to understand and recognize the river's course.

<margin>
**Calling it Ister]** He says that the Ister flows down from the land of the **Hyperboreans** <note>A mythical people of the far north</note> and the **Rhipaean Mountains** <note>A legendary mountain range in the north, possibly the Urals or Carpathians</note>. He says this following **Aeschylus** in his plays *Lycurgus* and *Prometheus*. He describes it as pouring between the **Scythians** <note>Nomadic people of the Eurasian steppes</note> and the **Thracians**, where it splits: one stream empties into "our sea" <note>The Mediterranean</note>, another falls into the **Pontic Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note>, and a third into the **Adriatic Gulf**. **Scymnus** <note>A Greek geographer</note>, however, in his...
</margin>

> Around the moist and murky sea they sailed.
> There is a certain river, the highest horn of Ocean,
> Wide and very deep, and suitable for a merchant ship;
> Calling it Ister, men have known its course from afar.
> For a long time it cuts through the boundless land
> All alone—for its springs murmur far off
> Beneath the breath of the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note>
> In the Rhipaean mountains—
> But when it steps upon the borders of Thracians and Scythians,
> There it splits in two; one part throws its water here
> Into the Ionian Sea, and the other part behind
> It sends through a deep gulf, splitting as it emerges
> Into the Trinacrian Sea, which lies beside our land, if this be true.

...sixteenth book *On Europe*, says that the Ister flows alone from a desert. The Rhipaean mountains are in the East, as **Callimachus** <note>A major Hellenistic poet and scholar</note> says: "they send from the Rhipaean mountain, where it is most [distant]." **Eratosthenes**, in his *Geographies*, says it flows from desert places and surrounds the island of **Peuke** <note>An island in the Danube delta</note>. No one records that the Argonauts sailed through this river into our sea, except for **Timagetus**, whom **Apollonius** followed. For **Scymnus** says they sailed through the **Tanais** <note>The Don River</note> into the Great Sea <note>The Outer Ocean</note>, and from there came into our sea. He adds a detail that when the Argonauts reached the mainland, they carried the ship **Argo** on rollers until it was launched back into the sea. **Hesiod** says they sailed through the **Phasis** <note>A river in modern Georgia (Caucasus)</note>. **Hecataeus** <note>An early Greek historian and geographer</note>, refuting him, records that the Phasis does not empty into that sea, nor did they sail via the Tanais, but rather took the same route they had taken before. **Sophocles** in his play *The Scythians* and **Callimachus** agree on this. For this reason, some of the Scythians who sailed as far as the Adriatic did not find the Argonauts; others, sailing through the **Cyanean Rocks** <note>The "Clashing Rocks" at the mouth of the Black Sea</note>, arrived at **Corcyra** <note>Modern Corfu</note> looking for them. The Ister, flowing from the Hyperboreans, when it reaches the region between Scythia and Thrace, splits into two: one part empties into the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note>, and the other into the **Tyrrhenian Sea** <note>The sea west of Italy</note>.
**Trinacrian]** The Tyrrhenian sea lies beside Sicily. It was formerly called **Trinacria** because it has three capes: **Pachynus**, **Lilybaeum**, and **Pelorus**. Apollonius, wishing to say something novel about the Ister, further divides the stream that flows into the Adriatic into two: one part flows into the Adriatic, and the other into the Tyrrhenian sea; he uses the term "Trinakeian" loosely. **Beside our land]** If it is written "your land," it refers to Greece; if "our land," it refers to the land of the Ister, for it lies near the **Colchians**.

**From your land]** The **Achelous** <note>The largest river in Greece</note> is the most distinguished of all the rivers in Greece. The **Trinacrian Sea** <note>The sea around Sicily</note> lies adjacent to the land of the Greeks. If, therefore, the Achelous exists, it is in your land. They hear the name, but **Argos** <note>The builder of the ship Argo, acting here as a geographical guide</note> is unaware that the river springs from the land itself. He says that the **Ister** <note>The Danube</note> flows into the Achelous because it provides the Achelous with its sources.

**Lucky]** <note>original: "Aision"</note> That which is fitting or proper.

**Trail]** <note>original: "Holkon"</note> The path or streak left by a shooting star.

**Since the breezes]** For the same winds continued to blow. And a heavenly radiance appeared to them, signaling the voyage across the Ister. Those who have written about the departure of the **Argonauts** and the **Colchians** <note>The people of Colchis, modern-day Georgia, who were pursuing the fleece</note> disagree. **Others of the Colchians]** That is, they came by land to the region as far as the **Cyanean Rocks**, as **Callimachus** <note>A famous scholar-poet from Alexandria</note> also says. Apollonius says they turned back, contrary to Callimachus, who says they went into the Ister with **Apsyrtus** <note>The brother of Medea and leader of the pursuit</note>. **Through the Fair Mouth]** The Ister has three mouths. One of them is called the **Fair Mouth**, as **Timages** says in his work *On Harbors*; he says Apsyrtus sailed into this one. **The furthest Ionian]** The Ionian Sea is near Italy, into which the **Adriatic** flows. Because of this, some call it the Adriatic, sharing the name. Since the Adriatic joins the Ionian, they sometimes call the Adriatic "Ionian" and the Ionian "Adriatic." It was named after **Ionius**, the son of **Illyrius**, as **Theopompus** says in his twenty-first book. The Ionian Sea near Italy is so named from Ionius, an Illyrian man. Some, however, say it comes from the wandering of **Io** <note>A priestess of Hera who was turned into a cow and wandered the world</note>. **Three-pointed]** **Eratosthenes** <note>The geographer</note> says in the third book of his *Geography* that there is a triangular island in the Ister, equal in size to **Rhodes**. He calls it **Peuke** <note>meaning "Pine-island"</note> because it has many pine trees. He called the peak of its triangle, where the river splits, the "elbow" <note>original: "angkona"</note>, and the base facing the sea, the "boundary" <note>original: "ouros"</note>. **Around it, two]** Regarding this island Peuke, he says there are two mouths of the Ister; one is called **Arekos** and the other the **Fair Mouth**. The Colchians with Apsyrtus sailed through one of these. **High on the island]** Seeing Jason, they sailed through the Arekos mouth of the island. The **shepherds** <note>original: "nomeis"</note> (referring to everyone there), thinking the ships were sea monsters, were terrified and turned to flight.

**Marshy meadows** <note>original: "Eiamenaí"</note>, well-watered and sheltered places. One must understand that the shepherds fled from both sides of the river. **Mixed with Thracians]** The Scythians are neighbors to the Thracians who live in Europe. **Neither those around Lauion]** The Lauion plain is in Scythia. **Timonax** records fifty nations of Scythia in the first book of his work *On the Scythians*. **The plain of the Sindi is divided]** The River **Ister** <note>The Danube</note> divides it; one of its streams flows into the **Adriatic**, and the other into the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note>. **Sindi]** Herodian, in the sixth book of his *General Grammar*, says the word should have the accent on the first syllable; however, some accent the last syllable. Even **Hipponax** mentions them, comparing the name to a "cleft" or "fissure." **Hellanicus** says in his work *On Nations* that the Sindi are reached by sailing the **Bosphorus**; above them are the Maliote Scythians. There is also a type of spear called a **sigynos**, which shares its name with the tribe.
</margin>

From afar, in the **marshy meadows** <note>low-lying riverbanks</note>, the rustic shepherds left behind their countless flocks for fear of the ships, watching them like wild beasts emerging from the monster-teeming sea. For never before had they seen seafaring ships: neither the Scythians mixed with Thracians, nor the Sigynni, nor the Graukenii, nor the **Sindi** who now dwell around the great, deserted **Lauion plain**.

But when they passed the **Silver Mountain** and the distant cliff of **Mount Angouron**, near the **Kauliakos** rock (around which the sacred river divides its flow, casting it here and there into the sea), and crossed the Lauion plain—then indeed the Colchians emerged into the **Cronian Sea** <note>An ancient name for the Adriatic Sea</note>. They cut off all the paths, lest the Argonauts should escape them.

The Argonauts came down the river from behind and passed the two islands of **Bryteian Artemis** <note>Islands in the Adriatic associated with the goddess</note>. In one of these was a sacred temple; on the other, they landed, avoiding the great multitude of **Apsyrtus** <note>Medea's brother and leader of the Colchian pursuit</note>. For the Colchians had left those islands far behind in the interior, out of reverence for the daughter of Zeus <note>Artemis</note>; but the other paths were crowded with Colchians guarding the passages of the sea.

So too they left a multitude on other islands nearby, as far as the **Salangon River** and the island-land. # THE ARGONAUTICA
### BOOK FOUR

<column-break/>

->**ARGONAUTICA**<-

With sails set, they entered the deep stream of the Eridanus <note>The Eridanus was a mythical river, often identified by later Greeks with the river Po in northern Italy.</note>. There, once upon a time, smitten in the chest by a blazing thunderbolt, half-consumed Phaethon <note>Phaethon was the son of Helios (the Sun) who attempted to drive his father’s chariot but lost control, nearly scorching the earth before Zeus struck him down.</note> fell from the chariot of the Sun into the mouth of that deep lake. Even now, the lake exhales a heavy vapor from his smoldering wound. No bird can stretch its light wings to fly across that water; instead, mid-flight, it plunges into the flames. 

All around, the Heliades <note>The "daughters of the Sun" and sisters of Phaethon.</note>, encased in tall poplars, groan in their wretched wailing. From their eyes they shed gleaming drops of amber onto the ground. These are dried by the sun upon the sands; but whenever the waters of the dark lake wash against the shores under the breath of the echoing wind, then all the amber rolls in a mass into the Eridanus <margin>The Celts say that amber is not from the Heliades, but is the tears of Apollo, son of Leto, which are carried in the eddies—the countless tears he shed in times past when he came to the sacred race of the Hyperboreans. He had left the shining heavens at the rebuke of his father, angry on account of his son [Asclepius], whom divine Coronis bore in shimmering Lacereia at the mouth of the Amyros. This is also said to be when he was ordered to serve as a laborer because of the murder of the Cyclopes.</margin> with its swelling current. 

The Celts have a different tradition: they say that these are the tears of Apollo, the son of Leto, which are carried along in the swirls—tears he shed without number in the days of old when he reached the sacred land of the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people living in the far north "beyond the North Wind."</note>. He had left the bright heavens because of the harsh words of his father [Zeus], grieving for his son [Asclepius] whom divine Coronis had borne by the streams of the Amyros. Such is the story told among those people. 

But for the heroes, there was no desire for food or drink, nor did their minds turn to joyful things. Instead, they were exhausted during the days, weighed down by the wretched stench which the streams of the Eridanus gave off unceasingly from the smoldering Phaethon. At night, they heard the piercing lament of the Heliades wailing shrilly. <margin>As the Heliades mourn, their tears mix with the waters like drops of oil. "Staxes" is the term used, as if from the word for a "dropping" or "falling drop."</margin> Their tears, as they mourned, were carried upon the water like drops of oil.

From there, they entered the deep stream of the Rhodanus <note>The river Rhône.</note>, <margin>The Rhodanus is a river of the Celtic lands which mixes with the Eridanus. It branches out: in one direction it flows toward the Ocean; in another, into the Ionian Gulf; and in another, into the Sardinian Sea.</margin> which flows through the land of the Celts.

# FOURTH

### BOOK FOUR

The river flows on until it meets the Eridanus; there, the waters roar as they are churned together in a narrow pass. But the river itself springs from the deepest recesses of the earth, where the gates and the dwellings of Night are located <margin>630</margin>. Starting from that point, it surges forth, pouring out onto the shores of the Ocean on one side, while on another it empties into the Ionian Sea. On a third side, it sends its stream through seven mouths into the Sardinian Sea <note>The Sardinian Sea refers generally to the waters of the western Mediterranean near modern-day Italy and Sardinia.</note> and its boundless gulf <margin>635</margin>. From there, the heroes sailed into the stormy lakes that spread across the vast and measureless land of the Celts. 

There, they would have met an undignified end. For a certain branch of the river led toward a gulf of the Ocean, which they were about to enter without knowing better; from there, they would never have returned safely <margin>640</margin>. <margin>640 Hercynian] The Hercynian mountain of the Celts, or a forest.</margin> But Hera leaped down from heaven and shouted from the Hercynian rock <note>The Hercynian Forest was a vast, ancient forest in central Europe, often used by Greek writers to describe the wild northern frontier.</note>. All were shaken alike with fear at her cry, for the great sky rang out with a terrifying sound. By the goddess’s command, they turned back and realized the path that was their true route home. 

By Hera’s counsel, they reached the salt-sprayed shores, passing through the countless tribes of the Celts <margin>645</margin> and the Ligurians <note>The Ligurians were an ancient people inhabiting the northwestern Mediterranean coast of Italy and south-eastern France.</note>, traveling undisturbed <margin>Undisturbed] unknown. unsearched. unmolested.</margin>. The goddess poured a thick mist around them every day as they traveled. Deep in the river's mouth, they steered their ship and arrived safely at the Stoechades islands <note>The Stoechades are the modern Îles d'Hyères off the coast of the French Riviera.</note>, thanks to the sons of Zeus <margin>650 Because of the sons of Zeus] The Dioscuri, who prayed on their behalf.</margin>. Altars and sacred rites have been established there for them, remaining firm to this day. Nor was it only on that voyage that they followed as helpers; Zeus granted their protection to the ships of later generations as well <margin>Gave the ships] to save them, clearly. The phrasing is an ellipsis <note>original: "ὁ τύπος ἔλλειψις" — a grammatical term meaning the text is shortened for effect.</note>.</margin>.

Leaving the Stoechades, they crossed over to the island of Aethalia <note>Aethalia is the ancient name for the island of Elba.</note>. There, exhausted from their toil, they wiped away their sweat with pebbles <margin>655</margin>; even now, the stones along the shore are colored like human skin <note>This refers to the spotted or multicolored pebbles of Elba, which legend claimed were stained by the Argonauts' sweat.</note>. Their stone quoits and marvelous weapons are still there, and a harbor called "Argous" <note>The "Argo's Harbor," often identified with modern Portoferraio on Elba.</note> takes its name from them. From that place, they quickly sped away once more across the swelling waves of the sea.

She bid them sit upon thrones, though they hesitated as they came in.
But the two of them rushed to the hearth and sat there 
in silence and without a word (as is the custom for wretched suppliants). 
She, Medea, hid her face in both her hands, 
while he, Jason, fixed his great hilted sword in the ground—
the very sword with which he had killed the son of Aeetes <note>This refers to Apsyrtus, Medea’s brother, whom Jason murdered to aid their escape.</note>. Never did they
raise their eyes to meet her gaze. Immediately 
Circe recognized their fugitive fate and the guilt of murder. 
Therefore, respecting the law of Zeus, the god of suppliants—
who is greatly angered by murderers but also offers them aid—
she performed the sacrifice by which ruthless suppliants 
are cleansed when they approach the hearth. 
First, to provide atonement for the unrepented murder,
she held above them the offspring of a sow whose teats 
were still swollen from a recent birth; she cut its throat 
and moistened their hands with the blood. Next, she 
appeased the god with other libations, calling upon 
Zeus the Purifier, the avenger of murderous supplications. 
Then the handmaid Nymphs, who attended to all her needs, 
carried all the ritual remains out of the house in a mass.

Iris went on her way. And Hera spoke once more, urging her:
"Dear Iris, go now, if ever you fulfilled my bidding;
Go, hasten on swift wings,
And command Thetis to come here to me, rising from the sea.
For I have need of her. Afterward, then,
Go to the shores where the bronze anvils of Hephaestus
Are struck by heavy hammers.
Tell him to quiet the bellows of his fire until the *Argo*
Has passed them by. Then also go to Aeolus,
Aeolus who rules the winds born of the clear sky.
And to him, speak my mind: that he should
Cease and still the blasts in the air, and that no breeze
Should blow, nor any gale from the West over the rough sea,
Until they reach the Phaeacian island of Alcinous."
So she spoke. Immediately Iris, leaping down from Olympus,
Cut through the light air with her outspread wings. She dove into the
Aegean Sea, where the halls of Nereus <note>The "Old Man of the Sea" and father of the Nereids, including Thetis.</note> are located.
First she came to Thetis, and delivered the message
Of Hera’s counsel; and she stirred her to set out on her way.
Next she went to Hephaestus; and she quickly made him
Cease his iron hammers; and the soot-covered bellows
Stayed their breath. And thirdly she came to
Aeolus, the famous son of Hippotas. And when to him
She had spoken her message and rested her swift knees from her journey,
Thetis, meanwhile, leaving Nereus and her sisters,
Had come from the sea to Olympus to meet the goddess Hera.
Hera sat her down close to herself and spoke her word:
"Listen now, divine Thetis, to what I desire to tell you.
You know how much the hero, the son of Aeson <note>Jason.</note>, is honored
In my heart, and the others who assist him in his labor."
